leads.text:
If this opinion indicates that it is “FOR PUBLICATION,” it is subject to

-1- 
S T A T E O F M I C H I G A N 

C O U R T O F A P P E A L S 

DILLION WERTH, 

 Plaintiff-Appellee, 

UNPUBLISHED 
November 25, 2026 
10:29 AM 
v No. 375651 
Macomb Circuit Court 
THE LASALLE GROUP, doing business as 
LASALLE CONSTRUCTION SERVICES, 

LC No. 2023-000546-NO 
 Defendant/Cross-Plaintiff/Third-Party 
Plaintiff, 

and 

HASTINGS INSURANCE COMPANY, 

 Cross-Plaintiff-Appellant, 

and 

METRO CONCRETE CORPORATION, 

 Defendant/Cross-Defendant-Appellee, 

and 

MASTERCRAFT & ASSOCIATES, 

 Third-Party Defendant. 

Before: ACKERMAN, P.J., and BORRELLO and KOROBKIN, JJ. 

PER CURIAM. 
-2- 
 In this negligence and premises -liability action, cross -plaintiff, Hastings Insurance 
Company (Hastings),1 appeals as of right from the trial court’s final order dismissing this action, 
preserving the right of defendant/cross-plaintiff/third-party plaintiff, The LaSalle Group, doing 
business as LaSalle Construction Services (LaSalle), to appeal the trial court’s earlier dispositive 
ruling on LaSalle’s cross-claim against defendant/cross-defendant, Metro Concrete Corporation 
(Metro), and substituting Hastings, as LaSalle’s assignee, for purposes of pursuing this appeal. On 
appeal, Hastings specifically challenges the trial court’s earlier order granting Metro’s motion for 
summary disposition with respect to Lasalle ’s cross -claim seeking contractual indemnity from 
Metro for any damages stemming from plaintiff’s claims of injury and the costs of defending the 
principal lawsuit, as well as further alleging that Metro breached its contractual obligation to 
provide insurance covering LaSalle from personal injury claims . For the reasons set forth in this 
opinion, we affirm. 
I. FACTS AND PROCEDURAL HISTORY 
 This case arises out of injuries that plaintiff, Dillion Werth, suffered while working on a 
construction site. Werth was employed as a painter by third -party defendant, Mastercraft & 
Associates (Mastercraft). While working on the mezzanine floor of a renovation project , Werth 
fell through a hole that had been created for a stairway and suffered injuries. LaSalle was the 
general contractor for the project. 
At the present juncture, details regarding the underlying factual circumstances of plaintiff’s 
injuries are relatively unimportant because the dispute before us only concerns the allotment of 
financial responsibilities stemming from this litigation. Relevant to this dispute, LaSalle and Metro 
had entered into a subcontract for the project at issue, under which Metro would perform certain 
concrete work. The subcontract also included certain indemnity provisions in favor of LaSalle. 
After incurring his injuries, plaintiff filed this lawsuit against both LaSalle and Metro , 
alleging that both parties had created the hazardous condition at issue and breached their duty to 
keep the construction site free from dangerous conditions. Specifically, Werth alleged that Metro 
had, during the course of its work on the site, moved barriers protecting workers from falling 
through the hole in the mezzanine deck. Werth also alleged that he was injured in a common work 
area under LaSalle’s dominion and control, which LaSalle had failed to keep reasonably safe and 
free of hazards. 
LaSalle filed a cross-claim against Metro, claiming that LaSalle was entitled to complete 
indemnification from Metro, under the parties ’ subcontract, for any liability LaSalle was 
determined to have to Werth for his injuries. LaSalle also alleged the terms of the subcontract 
obligated Metro to defend LaSalle in the principal lawsuit at Metro ’s sole expense and further 
required Metro to “procure and maintain insurance providing coverage to [LaSalle] for the claims 
of the principal Plaintiff in the principal Complaint.” LaSalle alleged that Metro had breached the 
contractual duty to provide such insurance coverage to LaSalle. 

1 Because there are multiple defendants with different designations on appeal, we refer to the 
parties by name to avoid confusion. 
-3- 
LaSalle cited a provision of the subcontract stating that Metro, as subcontractor, agreed to 
“assume entire responsibility and liability for all damages or injury to all persons[] . . . arising out 
of or in any manner connected with the execution of the Work under this Subcontract” and further, 
“to the fullest extent permitted by law,” agreed to “defend and indemnify” LaSalle, as contractor, 
“from all such claims, including without limitation claims for which the Contractor may be or may 
be claimed to be liable by reason of its own independent negligence. ” This provision also stated 
that “The Subcontractor’s obligation under this paragraph expressly excludes only total liability 
created by the sole and exclusive gross negligence of the Contractor.” LaSalle additionally cited 
another provision of the subcontract providing that Metro agreed to “procure and maintain, at its 
own expense, such insurance as will protect against suits and claims for [b]odily injury or death[] 
. . . that may arise in any manner out of the Subcontractor’s operations and completed operations, 
or by any sub-subcontractor or by anyone employed by any of them, or by anyone for whose acts 
anyone of them may be liable.” 
 Metro moved for summary disposition of LaSalle’s cross-claim under MCR 2.116(C)(10) 
(no genuine issue of material fact) , arguing that the subcontract did not require it to indemnify 
LaSalle because Werth’s injuries arose out of LaSalle ’s negligence, not Metro ’s work on the 
project. Metro claimed it did not install the precast floor, did not create the stairway hole, and was 
not responsible for installing barriers around the hole in the floor. In response, LaSalle argued that 
Metro was required to indemnify it because Werth alleged that his injuries arose out of Metro ’s 
actions, specifically Metro’s employees negligently placing concrete forms around the hole in the 
floor, and Metro still had a common -law duty to act so as to not unreasonably endanger other 
employees or subcontractors. 
 The trial court granted Metro summary disposition and dismissed LaSalle ’s cross-claim. 
The trial court reasoned that LaSalle had admitted that it was “primarily responsible for safety at 
the subject worksite ,” that the record was “devoid of any evidence suggesting defendant Metro 
Concrete disturbed the warning line [of construction barrels and caution tape surrounding the 
stairway hole] in any manner,” that the presence of concrete forms in the vicinity was irrelevant 
because plaintiff did not trip over a cement form before falling in the hole, and that LaSalle had 
therefore not established that Metro breached any common-law duty not to endanger plaintiff. 
 We now turn to Hastings’s appellate challenge to this ruling. 
II. JURISDICTION 
As a threshold matter, Metro challenges this Court’s jurisdiction, arguing that Hastings is 
not an aggrieved party entitled to appeal. Metro asserts that LaSalle suffered no injury from the 
dismissal of its cross -claim because Hastings acknowledges that it paid LaSalle ’s defense costs 
and a portion of the settlement on LaSalle ’s behalf. Metro further contends that, as LaSalle ’s 
assignee, Hastings stands in LaSalle’s shoes and therefore cannot qualify as an aggrieved party if 
LaSalle suffered no pecuniary loss. 

This Court has jurisdiction over an appeal as of right from a final judgment or order only 
when the appeal is “filed by an aggrieved party.” MCR 7.203(A)(1). An aggrieved party must have 
“some interest of a pecuniary nature in the outcome of the case[] . . . .” Federated Ins Co v Oakland 
Co Road Comm’n, 475 Mich 286, 291; 715 NW2d 846 (2006) (quotation marks and citation 
-4- 
omitted). The litigant must also have suffered “a concrete and particularized injury” arising from 
the trial court’s action or the appellate judgment, rather than from the underlying facts of the case. 
Id. at 291-292. As LaSalle’s assignee, Hastings “stands in [LaSalle’s] position . . . , possessing the 
same rights and being subject to the same defenses. ” Fed Home Loan Mtg Corp v Werme , 335 
Mich App 461, 471; 966 NW2d 729 (2021) (quotation marks and citation omitted). 

Metro’s argument rests on Hastings ’s representations in its appellate brief that, as 
Mastercraft’s insurer, it “provided a defense to LaSalle on the basis that LaSalle was potentially 
an additional insured pursuant to the Mastercraft subcontract terms” and, after settlement, paid “a 
portion of the settlement amount on behalf of LaSalle based on LaSalle’s additional insured status 
under the Mastercraft subcontract.” From these payments, Metro reasons that LaSalle has already 
been indemnified and that any separate obligation Metro may owe is immaterial. That argument is 
foreclosed by this Court’s decision in Eller v Metro Indus Contracting, Inc , 261 Mich App 569; 
683 NW2d 242 (2004). 

In Eller, as here, the dispute concerned indemnification arising from a construction 
accident. Id. at 570. Metro Industrial Contracting, Inc., sought indemnification from Mid –
American Gunite, Inc. (Gunite). On appeal, Gunite argued that the trial court should have granted 
summary disposition because Metro Industrial2 had “already had been fully indemnified by Power 
Process Piping, Inc. (PPP), a co-indemnitor.” Id. at 570-571. 

Because both PPP and Gunite were potentially liable under their respective subcontract 
indemnity provisions, this Court explained: “[W]here two or more insurance companies are in the 
same tier of priority—for example, both are primarily liable or both contain irreconcilable escape 
clauses—an insured’s loss is to be apportioned or prorated among the insurance companies on the 
basis of policy limits.” Id. at 572. Applying that principle by analogy, the Court concluded that, 
because PPP and Gunite had agreed to identical indemnity provisions, they were equally liable to 
indemnify Metro Industrial and should share the cost equally. Id. 

The Court further held that “PPP’s indemnification of Metro in full did not necessarily 
extinguish Gunite’s otherwise proven obligation of indemnity ” and that “[e]xposure to legal 
defense costs and liability on a judgment triggered Gunite’s indemnity obligation, even if Metro 
[Industrial] was indemnified by PPP.” Id. at 572-573 (quotation marks and citation omitted). At 
the same time, the Court recognized that Metro Industrial could not recover twice for the same 
loss. Id. Because PPP had satisfied Gunite ’s indemnity obligation, PPP became equitably 
subrogated to Metro Industrial’s rights against Gunite. Id. Thus, Eller treated the existence of a 
co-indemnitor’s obligation and the allocation of any recovery between the indemnitee and the party 
that paid its loss as distinct questions. 

That distinction answers Metro ’s jurisdictional argument. Hastings ’s payments on 
LaSalle’s behalf do not, by themselves, establish that Metro had no obligation under the indemnity 
provision or that dismissal of LaSalle ’s cross -claim caused no cognizable injury. As in Eller, 
payment by one potentially responsible party may affect who is entitled to recover and the amount 

2 We will use “Metro Industrial” to distinguish the party in Eller from the party in the present case. 
-5- 
recoverable without necessarily extinguishing another party’s alleged indemnity obligation. Here, 
the order dismissing the cross-claim foreclosed adjudication of the claim against Metro. Hastings 
asserts the assigned claim and represents that it paid LaSalle ’s defense costs and part of the 
settlement; those alleged payments give the claim a pecuniary dimension, while the dismissal 
supplies the injury arising from the trial court’s action. See Federated Ins Co, 475 Mich at 291 -
292. 

This conclusion is limited to appellate standing. Whether the ind

OF ILLINOIS

 JUSTICE GRISCHOW delivered the judgment of the court. 
 Justices Doherty and Vancil concurred in the judgment. 
 Justice Doherty also specially concurred. 

ORDER 

¶ 1 Held: The appellate court concluded defendants were not entitled to relief from default 
judgment because plaintiff complied with the requirement to perform a reasonable 
inquiry into the address most likely to provide actual notice of service under the 
Limited Liability Company Act (805 ILCS 180/1-1 et seq. (West 2024)), 
defendants’ statutory right of redemption was not modified, and the trial court did 
not abuse its discretion when it denied defendants’ motion to disqualify plaintiff’s 
counsel. 

¶ 2 In April 2025, plaintiff, Reliable Home Repairs Plus, Inc. (Reliable), filed a 
complaint for the foreclosure of a mechanic’s lien against defendants, Catharsis Holdings, LLC 
(Catharsis), Double D Financial, LLC (Double D), unknown owners, and unknown necessary 
parties. Defendants failed to appear and were found in default, and the trial court entered an 
order of foreclosure of the mechanic’s lien and for judicial sale of the property described therein. 
In February 2026, defendants filed a petition to vacate the court’s orders for lack of jurisdiction

and argued they were never served notice. Defendants also moved to disqualify plaintiff’s 
counsel. The motions were denied. Defendants filed a subsequent petition to vacate the default 
order, the order of foreclosure, and the order of judicial sale, arguing the orders granted more 
relief to plaintiff than requested in the complaint, and therefore, defendants were entitled to new 
notice before entry of the orders. All motions were denied. 
¶ 3 Defendants appeal, arguing they are entitled to relief from default judgment 
because they were not properly served with notice, they were not provided new notice when the 
order granted relief beyond that requested in the complaint, and the trial court abused its 
discretion when it denied the motion to disqualify plaintiff’s counsel. For the following reasons, 
we affirm. 
¶ 4 I. BACKGROUND 
¶ 5 Reliable is an Illinois corporation in the business of home repair and renovation. 
Catharsis is a foreign limited liability company registered in California. Catharsis, at the time the 
complaint was filed, owned real estate in Illinois for use as rental properties, including 1015 
Wilcox Avenue in Peoria, Illinois (the property). In July 2024, Reliable and Arla Jeanes, the 
agent and manager of Catharsis, engaged in a discussion for Reliable to perform repairs and 
renovations at the property. In August 2024, Reliable sent an invoice in the amount of 
$15,999.43 to Catharsis at 621 Via Alondra, Suite 611A, in Camarillo, California (Camarillo 
address) for materials and labor related to the renovations discussed at the property. 
¶ 6 In September 2024, Reliable recorded a mechanic’s lien against Catharsis and the 
property. In December 2024, Catharsis transferred ownership of the property via general 
warranty deed to Double D, a foreign limited liability company registered in Montana. The deed 
listed the mailing address for Catharsis at the Camarillo address and the mailing address for 
- 3 - 
Double D at 2814 Brooks Street, Suite 516, in Missoula, Montana (Brooks Street Address). 
¶ 7 In April 2025, Reliable filed a complaint against Catharsis, Double D, unknown 
owners, and unknown necessary parties. In the complaint, it sought foreclosure of the mechanic’s 
lien and argued breach of contract for defendants’ failure to pay the $15,999.43 invoice, 
fraudulent transfer of the property from Catharsis to Double D, and quantum meruit as a claim in 
the alternative. Attached to the complaint was an invoice that Reliable purported to have sent to 
Catharsis at the Camarillo address. The invoice contained the Camarillo address, along with a 
phone number and an e-mail address for Catharsis. 
¶ 8 In August 2025, Reliable filed a motion for default judgment. Reliable argued it 
attempted service multiple times on Catharsis and Double D at multiple mailing addresses 
purported to be those of each defendant, as included on documents submitted and signed by 
Jeanes in California and Montana, and the agents for Catharsis and Double D were not found. 
Attached to the complaint and the motion for default, Reliable included business records and the 
attempted service of process records for both Catharsis and Double D. The California record for 
Catharsis listed Jeanes as the manager and the Camarillo mailing address. The Montana record 
for Double D listed Jeanes as a member, and the mailing address was the Brooks Street address. 
Additionally, the Double D Montana business record listed the registered agent of Double D as 
Andrew Deichl, with an address of 2301 Larch Camp Road in Missoula, Montana (Larch Camp 
Road address). 
¶ 9 Reliable attempted to serve summons to Catharsis and Jeanes as its agent at the 
Camarillo address in April 2025. The summons was returned with an affidavit of nonservice that 
explained the process server attempted service, but neither Catharsis nor Jeanes were found at 
the Camarillo address. The affidavit noted neither the “business nor agent is known here.” 
- 4 - 
Summons was sent to Double D in April 2025 at the Larch Camp Road address. An alias 
summons was also issued to Catharsis and Jeanes at the Brooks Street Address in April 2025. 
The affidavit of nonservice for the Larch Camp Road address stated the process server found an 
empty lot and spoke to a neighbor, who confirmed the registered agent for Double D, Deichl, 
owned the property, but that the “empty lot on the side of the mountain” had “no home on the 
property.” An affidavit of nonservice for the Brooks Street address noted that the address was a 
UPS Store, and the suite number provided was the post office box number at the UPS Store. 
¶ 10 Reliable’s motion for default judgment asserted it next served Catharsis and 
Double D through the Illinois Secretary of State pursuant to section 2-204 of the Code of Civil 
Procedure (735 ILCS 5/2-204 (West 2024)) and section 1-50(b)(1) of the Limited Liability 
Company Act (Act) (805 ILCS 180/1-50(b)(1) (West 2024)). Attached to the motion were 
affidavits of compliance for service on the Secretary of State for Catharsis and Double D. The 
affidavits indicated the Secretary of State was appointed as an agent for Catharsis and Double D 
because both Catharsis and Double D failed to appoint and maintain a registered agent in Illinois. 
The affidavit for Catharsis indicated a copy of the process required to be delivered by certified or 
registered mail was sent to the Camarillo address, and the affidavit for Double D indicated the 
process was sent to the Larch Camp Road address. Reliable asked the trial court to grant its 
motion for default and to enter an order in favor of Reliable’s motion to foreclose on the 
mechanic’s lien. 
¶ 11 In August 2025, the trial court granted plaintiff’s motion for default and entered a 
judgment order of foreclosure and sale. The order found defendants failed to appear and were in 
default, required defendants to pay the amount owed to plaintiff “before expiration of any 
redemption period,” and stated that if such payment was not made, the property would be 
- 5 - 
ordered sold. In the event of such a sale, defendants were “barred and foreclosed of any right, 
title, interest, claim, lien[,] or right to redeem in and to the Property.” 
¶ 12 Five months later, notice of judicial sale was filed in January 2026, and in 
February 2026, counsel for defendants entered an appearance and filed a petition to vacate the 
order of default because defendants were not served with notice of the proceedings. Defendants 
argued they maintained no offices in Illinois, and their “only connection to Illinois” was 
“through successive ownership of certain real estate parcels in Peoria County.” Defendants 
maintained only ownership, without more, did not amount to transacting business in the state, 
and therefore, they did not subject themselves to appointment of the Secretary of State as their 
agent for service of process. 
¶ 13 Alternatively, defendants argued that if they subjected themselves to service 
through the Secretary of State, plaintiff failed to follow the statutory requirements for service. 
Defendants maintained plaintiff knew the addresses in the affidavits for service on the Secretary 
of State were faulty and would not result in notice because those addresses had already resulted 
in nonservice, and therefore, plaintiff did not follow the statutory requirement to send the notice 
to an address where it believed defendants were most likely to receive notice. See 805 ILCS 
180/1-50(c)(2)(B) (West 2024). Additionally, defendants argued they first received notice of the 
proceedings from “their Tenant” after a note was posted at the property indicating the impending 
judicial sale, but plaintiff had alternate means of notifying them of the proceedings, including the 
e-mail address on the business records from California and Montana attached to the complaint 
and an e-mail address of Jeanes in the possession of plaintiff’s counsel. 
¶ 14 Defendants also filed a motion to disqualify plaintiff’s counsel. Defendants 
argued the law firm representing plaintiff in this case, Heyl, Royster, Voelker & Allen, P.C. 
- 6 - 
(Heyl Royster), represented Jeanes, their manager, in a 2024 eviction proceeding concerning the 
property involved in this dispute. Defendants contended, although the eviction proceedings 
ended in June 2024, Jeanes did not receive notification of the termination of the law firm’s 
representation. In support of the motion, defendants attached an affidavit of Jeanes that stated she 
was the manager of Catharsis and Double D, she retained Heyl Royster for an eviction matter at 
the property involved in these proceedings, she never received formal communication 
terminating the attorney-client relationship, she was not notified of plaintiff’s attorney’s 
representation of plaintiff in a matter materially adverse to her, and she did not give “informed 
consent to [Heyl Royster] to permit them to represent an adverse interest.” 
¶ 15 In response, plaintiff argued defendants transacted business in the state of Illinois, 
defendants were properly served under the statutory framework for service on a limited liability 
company, and plaintiff’s counsel should not be disqualified because the eviction matter was not 
substantially related to the pending litigation and disqualification is an “extreme and unwarranted 
measure.” Plaintiff attached an affidavit of Brian Mooty, who stated he was an attorney 
employed by Heyl Royster and provided legal services for evictions at the property for Jeanes 
individually from October 2023 through May or June 2024. Mooty attested the file for those 
evictions was closed in August 2024. Mooty indicated he was unaware the firm was representing 
a client adverse to Catharsis or Jeanes until February 20, 2026. He stated the firm closed the files 
involving his representation of Catharsis, and those files were “restricted from access” by him, as 
well as attorneys at the firm working on this matter. Further, Mooty attest

leads.text:
Amos Fin., LLC v Crapanzano 
 2026 NY Slip Op 07046 
 November 25, 2026 
 Appellate Division, Second Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 Amos Financial, LLC, appellant, 
 v 
 Sharon K. Crapanzano, et al., defendants, DGW South Street, LLC, respondent. 

 Supreme Court of the State of New York, Appellate Division, Second Judicial Department 
 Decided on November 25, 2026 
 2023-11296, (Index No. 32407/22) 
 Betsy Barros, J.P. 
 Linda Christopher 
 Janice A. Taylor 
 Laurence L. Love, JJ. 

 Greenspoon Marder LLP, New York, NY (Angelo A. Regina and Raspreet Bhatia of counsel), for appellant. 
 Solomon Rosengarten, Brooklyn, NY, for respondent. 

 [*1] 
 DECISION & ORDER 
 In an action to foreclose a mortgage, the plaintiff appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Rockland County (David Fried, J.), dated September 22, 2023. The order, insofar as appealed from, granted the motion of the defendant DGW South Street, LLC, for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against it. 
 ORDERED that the order is affirmed insofar as appealed from, with costs. 
 In June 2022, the plaintiff commenced this action against, among others, the defendant DGW South Street, LLC (hereinafter the defendant), to foreclose a mortgage on certain real property located in Rockland County. The defendant interposed an answer asserting affirmative defenses, including that the action was barred by the statute of limitations. 
 The defendant moved for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against it as time-barred. In an order dated September 22, 2023, the Supreme Court, inter alia, granted the defendant's motion. The plaintiff appeals. 
 An action to foreclose a mortgage is governed by a six-year statute of limitations ( see CPLR 213[4]). Even if a mortgage is payable in installments, once a mortgage debt is accelerated, the entire amount is due and the statute of limitations begins to run on the entire debt ( see U.S. Bank N.A. v Connor , 204 AD3d 861, 862-863 ; Bank of N.Y. Mellon v Mor , 201 AD3d 691, 694 ). The entire mortgage debt will be deemed to have been accelerated by, as relevant here, the commencement of a mortgage foreclosure action in which the complaint seeks payment of the full outstanding loan balance ( see U.S. Bank, N.A. v Connor , 204 AD3d at 863 ). 
 Here, the defendant established, prima facie, that the six-year statute of limitations began to run in July 2009, when the plaintiff's predecessor in interest commenced a mortgage foreclosure action against the defendant's predecessor in interest and elected to call due the entire amount secured by the mortgage ( see DLJ Mtge. Capital, Inc. v Pittman , 252 AD3d 474 , 475). The defendant further demonstrated that this action was commenced in June 2022, more than six years later ( see id. ). 
 In opposition, the plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact. 
 Contrary to the plaintiff's contention, it was not entitled to commence a new foreclosure action pursuant to either CPLR 205(a) or 205-a. The Foreclosure Abuse Prevention Act (FAPA) (L 2022, ch 821 [eff Dec. 30, 2022]) replaced the savings provision of CPLR 205(a) with CPLR 205-a in foreclosure actions ( see US Bank, N.A. v Benjamin , 248 AD3d 961 , 963). CPLR 205-a, like CPLR 205(a), states that a plaintiff may not take advantage of the six-month savings provision if the prior action was dismissed upon "a final judgment upon the merits." Here, the record demonstrates that the prior action was dismissed upon the merits after the plaintiff's predecessor in interest failed to adduce evidence of a default at a hearing ( see Hausch v Clarke , 8 AD3d 436, 437 ). 
 The plaintiff's contentions on appeal challenging FAPA's retroactive application and constitutionality under the United States and New York Constitutions are without merit ( see Van Dyke v U.S. Bank, N.A. , 45 NY3d 461 , 474-479; Article 13 LLC v Ponce De Leon Fed. Bank , 45 NY3d 441 , 454-459). 
 Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly granted the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against it. 
 The plaintiff's remaining contention is without merit. 
 BARROS, J.P., CHRISTOPHER, TAYLOR and LOVE, JJ., concur. 
 ENTER: 
 Darrell M. Joseph 
 Clerk of the Court

leads.caseName: Carver Fed. Sav. Bank v. 2181 Pac. St. Hous. Dev. Fund Corp., Inc.
leads.court: Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York
leads.text:
Carver Fed. Sav. Bank v 2181 Pac. St. Hous. Dev. Fund Corp., Inc. 
 2026 NY Slip Op 07049 
 November 25, 2026 
 Appellate Division, Second Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 Carver Federal Savings Bank, respondent, 
 v 
 2181 Pacific Street Housing Development Fund Corporation, Inc., etc., et al., defendants; Michael Findley, etc., et al., intervenors-appellants. 

 Supreme Court of the State of New York, Appellate Division, Second Judicial Department 
 Decided on November 25, 2026 
 2025-07886, (Index No. 505619/24) 
 Mark C. Dillon, J.P. 
 William G. Ford 
 Lourdes M. Ventura 
 Elena Goldberg Velazquez, JJ. 

 Anderson Law, PLLC, New York, NY (Gregory A. Byrnes and Sam Caldarone of counsel), for intervenors-appellants. 
 Westerman Ball Ederer Miller Zucker & Sharfstein, LLP, Uniondale, NY (Frank C. Dell'Amore of counsel), for respondent. 

 [*1] 
 DECISION & ORDER 
 In an action to foreclose a mortgage, the intervenors, Michael Findley, Allan Newby, Fernando Delacruz, and Benjamin Salters, individually and derivatively on behalf of 2181 Pacific Street Housing Development Fund Corporation, Inc., appeal from an order of the Supreme Court, Kings County (Lawrence Knipel, J.), dated May 21, 2025. The order, insofar as appealed from, granted those branches of the plaintiff's motion which were for summary judgment on the complaint and dismissing the affirmative defenses of the intervenors alleging invalidity of the mortgage and for an order of reference. 
 ORDERED that the order is affirmed insofar as appealed from, with costs. 
 The plaintiff commenced this action to foreclose a commercial mortgage encumbering certain real property located in Brooklyn. The property was owned by the defendant 2181 Pacific Street Housing Development Fund Corporation, Inc. (hereinafter HDFC). The complaint alleged that HDFC defaulted under certain loan documents. Those loan documents were executed by Amina Emanuel as HDFC's Vice President. Michael Findley, Allan Newby, Fernando Delacruz, and Benjamin Salters, individually and derivatively on behalf of HDFC (hereinafter collectively the intervenors), intervened in the action and interposed an answer asserting, inter alia, affirmative defenses alleging invalidity of the mortgage based on Emanuel's claimed lack of authority to act on HDFC's behalf. The plaintiff moved, among other things, for summary judgment on the complaint and dismissing the intervenors' affirmative defenses alleging invalidity of the mortgage and for an order of reference. The intervenors opposed the motion. By order dated May 21, 2025, the Supreme Court, inter alia, granted those branches of the plaintiff's motion. The intervenors appeal. 
 Contrary to the intervenors' contention, a temporary receiver appointed for HDFC in a related action was not a necessary party in this action ( see RPAPL 1311). Title to the property remained with HDFC, and the temporary receiver merely assumed custodial rights to protect and manage the property ( see NYCTL 2005-A Trust v Rosenberger Boat Livery, Inc. , 96 AD3d 425, 425 ; Bate v Brenack Stevedoring Co. , 197 App Div 194, 195 ; see also HSBC Bank USA, N.A. v Rubin , 210 AD3d 73, 80 ; Meltzer v Grazi , 10 AD2d 869, 869 ). 
 There is no merit to the intervenors' contention alleging invalidity of the mortgage based on Emanuel's claimed lack of authority to act on HDFC's behalf. "Actual authority granted to an agent to bind his [or her] principal is created by direct manifestations from the principal to the agent, and the extent of the agent's actual authority is interpreted in the light of all the circumstances attending these manifestations, including the customs of business, the subject matter, any formal agreement between the parties, and the facts of which both parties are aware" ( New York Community Bank v Woodhaven Assoc., LLC , 137 AD3d 1231, 1233 [internal quotation marks omitted]; see Demarco v Edens , 390 F2d 836, 844 [2d Cir]). "In the absence of actual authority, words or conduct by the principal that are communicated to a third party may create the apparent authority of the agent to act on behalf of the principal" ( New York Community Bank v Woodhaven Assoc., LLC , 137 AD3d at 1233 ; see Hallock v State of New York , 64 NY2d 224, 231 ; Schwartz v WFG Natl. Tit. Ins. Co. , 192 AD3d 713, 715 ). 
 Here, the plaintiff established its prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law on the question of authority. The plaintiff submitted, among other things, a notarized Secretary's Certificate from the Secretary of HDFC's Board of Directors, HDFC's Board of Directors' Resolution authorizing Emanuel to execute the loan documents, and an affidavit of Emanuel, together with identification, attesting that she was HDFC's Vice President ( see Vermont Equity & Funding Corp. v Brown , 235 AD3d 808 , 811; New York Community Bank v Woodhaven Assoc., LLC , 137 AD3d at 1233 ; 334 Corp. v Jericho Plaza, LLC , 128 AD3d 679, 679 ). In opposition, the intervenors failed to raise a triable issue of fact. 
 The intervenors' remaining contentions are without merit. 
 Accordingly, we affirm the order insofar as appealed from. 
 DILLON, J.P., FORD, VENTURA and GOLDBERG VELAZQUEZ, JJ., concur. 
 ENTER: 
 Darrell M. Joseph 
 Clerk of the Court

Filed 11/25/26 Lowry v. Hope and Trust Trading CA4/2 
Opinion following rehearing 
NOT TO BE PUBLISHED IN OFFICIAL REPORTS 

California Rules of Court, rule 8.1115(a), prohibits courts and parties from citing or relying on opinions not 
certified for publication or ordered published, except as specified by rule 8.1115(b). This opinion has not been 
certified for publication or ord ered published for purposes of rule 8.1115. 

IN THE COURT OF APPEAL OF THE STATE OF CALIFORNIA 

FOURTH APPELLATE DISTRICT 

DIVISION TWO 

KARL LOWRY, 
 Plaintiff, Cross-defendant and 
Respondent, 

 v. 

HOPE AND TRUST TRADING, INC., 
et al., 
 Defendants, Cross-complainants 
and Respondents; 

NEWREZ, LLC, 
 Cross-defendant and Respondent; 

SAMMY CILING et al., 
 Cross-defendants and Appellants; 

ULTIM8 EQUITIES, LLC, 
 Movant and Appellant. 
E086596 

(Super.Ct.No. CVSW2207261) 

OPINION 

E086740 

(Super.Ct.No. CVSW2207261) 

2 
 APPEAL from the Superior Court of Riverside County. Frederick P. Horn (retired 
judge of the Orange Super. Ct. assigned by the Chief Justice pursuant to art. VI, § 6 of the 
Cal. Const.) and Raquel A. Marquez, Judges. Dismissed in part, reversed in part. 
 No appearance for Plaintiff, Cross-defendant and Respondent Karl Lowry. 
 Debbie Sutz for Defendants, Cross-complainants and Respondents Hope and Trust 
Trading, Inc., and Seyedjalil Firoozabadi. 
 No appearance for Cross-defendant and Respondent Newrez, LLC. 
 Alvarenga Law and Dania M. Baker for Movant and Appellant Ultima8 Equities, 
LLC. 
 Corey Parker; Sean Perdomo for cross-defendants and appellants Sammy Ciling, 
Anke Ciling and Tekfur, LLC. 
 Plaintiff, cross-defendant and respondent Karl Lowry (Lowry) sued defendants, 
cross-complainants and respondents Hope and Trust Trading, Inc., Seyedjalil Firoozabadi 
(Firoozabadi), cross-defendant and appellant Anke Ciling (Wife), and others for, among 
other things, a declaration that Lowry’s deeds of trust on Wife’s real property took 
priority over a judgment lien on the same property recorded by Hope and Trust Trading, 
Inc. and Firoozabadi (collectively, Trading). In a first amended cross-complaint against 
Lowry, Wife, Sammy Ciling (Husband), Tekfur LLC (Tekfur), and others, Trading 
alleged that several deeds of trust executed by Wife were fraudulent and requested that 
the deeds of trust and Wife’s homestead exemption be declared void. 
 Movant and appellant Ultim8 Equities, LLC (Ultim8) applied ex parte for leave to 
intervene in the case on the basis that it was assigned the beneficial interest in the deeds 
3 
of trust at issue in the case. The trial court denied Ultim8’s ex parte application. In Court 
of Appeal case No. E086596, Ultim8 contends the trial court erred because Ultim8 is the 
beneficiary of the deeds of trust at issue in the case and therefore would be directly 
impacted by the judgment. Trading contends this court lacks jurisdiction because the 
record does not indicate that the trial court’s denial of Ultim8’s ex parte application was 
based on the application’s merits.1 Trading also requests an award of attorney’s fees as a 
sanction for Ultim8’s allegedly frivolous appeal. In case No. E086596, we dismiss the 
appeal. 
 While Ultim8’s appeal was pending, the trial court entered (1) a stipulated 
judgment involving Lowry and Trading on the complaint and first amended cross-
complaint, and (2) a default judgment against Husband, Wife, and Tekfur on Trading’s 
first amended cross-complaint. In Court of Appeal case No. E086740, Husband, Wife, 
and Tekfur assert the trial court’s default judgment is erroneous. We reverse the default 
judgment in case No. E086740. 
FACTS 
 A. REAL PROPERTY AND UNDERLYING LOS ANGELES COUNTY 
LITIGATION 
 Wife owned real property in Temecula (the Residence). In 2019, Lowry allegedly 
lent Wife $450,000, and the Residence secured the loan. That deed of trust constituted 
the third deed of trust secured by the Residence (the third deed of trust). 

1 Trading’s request for judicial notice, filed on September 12, 2025, is granted. 
4 
 In Los Angeles County Superior Court (the LA Court), Trading sued Wife, 
Husband, and others for breach of contract and fraud. The contract pertained to 
Trading’s purchase of shares of California Medical Imaging Corp. On April 12, 2021, 
Lowry recorded the third deed of trust. On April 13, 2021, the LA Court entered 
judgment against Wife, Husband, and others, jointly and severally, in the total amount of 
$2,640,584.84. 
 On April 30, 2021, Trading recorded the $2,640,584.84 abstract of judgment in 
Riverside County, creating a judgment lien against the Residence. Lowry purchased the 
$175,000 second deed of trust that was held against the Residence and recorded that 
assignment in August 2022 (the second deed of trust). 
 B. CANCELLATION OF THE DEEDS OF TRUST 
 In October 2022, in the LA Court, Trading sought cancellation of the third deed of 
trust. Trading asserted that Lowry never lent Wife $450,000 and that Wife and Lowry 
conspired to execute and record the third deed of trust in order to conceal Wife’s equity 
in the Residence, thereby obstructing Trading’s effort to collect on its judgment. On 
October 14, 2022, the LA court canceled and expunged both the third deed of trust and 
the second deed of trust (collectively, Both Deeds of Trust) forthwith. 
 On November 14, 2022, in the Riverside County trial court (the trial court), Lowry 
sued Trading and others seeking reinstatement of Both Deeds of Trust and a declaration 
that Both Deeds of Trust have priority over Trading’s judgment lien. Lowry recorded a 
5 
lis pendens against the Residence. (Code Civ. Proc., § 761.010.)2 In December 2022, the 
LA court vacated its order cancelling and expunging Both Deeds of Trust due to Lowry 
claiming lack of notice of the expungement proceedings. 
 C. ORIGINAL CROSS-COMPLAINT, HOMESTEAD EXEMPTION, 
AND ASSIGNMENT 
 In January 2023, Trading cross-complained against Lowry, Husband, Wife, and 
others. Trading alleged that Lowry and Wife conspired to conceal Wife’s equity in the 
Residence by falsely executing the third deed of trust. Trading also alleged that the 
second deed of trust was fraudulent because it was created to avoid creditors. Trading 
sought compensatory damages, punitive damages, and cancellation of the third deed of 
trust. 
 Also in January 2023, the LA court granted Wife a homestead exemption on the 
Residence. In June 2023, Lowry assigned Both Deeds of Trust to Blue Vibe, LLC (Blue 
Vibe). 
 D. FIRST AMENDED CROSS-COMPLAINT 
 In March 2024, Trading filed a first amended cross-complaint against Lowry, 
Husband, Wife, Tekfur, and others. The amended cross-complaint concerned three 
parcels of property: (1) the Residence, (2) approximately 20 acres of agricultural land, at 
Assessor’s Parcel Number 933-110-049 (Land-049), and (3) another approximately 20 
acres of agricultural land, at Assessor’s Parcel Number 933-080-011 (Land-011). 

2 All subsequent statutory references are to the Code of Civil Procedure unless 
otherwise indicated. 
6 
Trading alleged that in 1999, Land-049 and Land-011 (collectively, the Land Properties) 
were deeded by Husband and Wife to a shell corporation to defraud creditors. Trading 
alleged that the Land Properties were repeatedly conveyed to shell corporations over the 
years to avoid creditors. 
 Trading asserted, “Cross-Defendants forged a promissory note for $500,000 
allegedly executed by [Wife] on February 28, 2019, falsely reflecting that Lowery [sic] 
lent [Wife] the sum of $450,000. Further, pursuant to this conspiracy, these Cross-
Defendants prepared three separate trust deeds executed by [Wife] on March 24, 2021, 
and on April 12, 2021[,] recorded those three deeds against the [Residence] and the Land 
Properties in order to falsely encumber these properties, and reduce, and hopefully 
eliminate, any equity in these properties available for enforcement of the LA Judgment.” 
 Trading also alleged, “Lowry received the aforesaid security interests and Tekfur 
LLC received title to the aforesaid Land Properties.” Trading asserted that Tekfur was 
“an empty shell” that was formed “for the sole purpose of defrauding [Trading].” 
 Trading sought a declaration that the third deed of trust was void, a declaration 
that the two deeds of trust secured by the Land Properties were void, general damages, 
and punitive damages. 
 Tekfur defaulted on Trading’s first amended cross-complaint in June 2024. 
Husband and Wife defaulted on Trading’s first amended cross-complaint in September 
2024. During a mandatory settlement conference on June 20, 2025, Trading and Lowry 
reached a settlement on Trading’s first amended cross-complaint. 
7 
 E. CONTRACT BETWEEN BLUE VIBE AND ULTIM8 
 On July 16, 2025, in a written contract, Blue Vibe agreed to purchase, from 
Ultim8, a 2.5 percent interest in Watchtower Group, LLC. As payment, Blue Vibe 
agreed to give Ultim8 $100,000 in cash and $650,000 in security interests. Blue Vibe 
agreed to “execute for the benefit of [Ultim8] . . . deeds of trust/mortgages (the ‘Security 
Documents’) on the following Propert[ies] and as further described in the Security 
Documents: 
 “Property Address 1: [Land-011] Value: $150,000 (one of three properties 
pledged together for $450,000) 
 “Property Address 2: [Land-049] Value: $150,000 (one of three properties 
pledged together for $450,000) 
 “Property Address 3: [The Residence], Temecula, CA 92590 Value: $350,000 
(one of three properties pledged together for $450,000, and second lien pledged at 
$200,000).” The second lien on the Residence is the second deed of trust. 
 F. EX PARTE APPLICATION FOR LEAVE TO INTERVENE 
 On July 17, 2025, Ultim8 applied ex parte for leave to intervene in the case. 
Ultim8 asserted it “should be joined under the rules of compulsory joinder as a necessary 
party since it has an interest in the transaction and facts raised in this action.” 3 In a 

3 In Ultim8’s application, it indiscriminately mixed terminology for joinder 
(§ 389) and mandatory intervention (§ 387, subd. (d)(1)). Mandatory intervention and 
compulsory joinder of an indispensable party “are virtually identical.” (Carlsbad Police 
Officers Assn. v. City of Carlsbad (2020) 49 Cal.App.5th 135, 148.) In the trial court, the 
application was treated as one seeking leave to intervene. We will also treat it as such. 
8 
declaration, Ultim8’s Chief Executive Officer declared that “Blue Vibe, LLC gave 
Ultim8 an interest in several properties one of which is the [Residence] .... Blue Vibe, 
LLC agreed to execute a Deed of Trust on this for a pledge total of Six Hundred and Fifty 
Thousand Dollars ($650,000), including the two other [Land] properties.” 
 In opposing the motion, Trading asserted that Blue Vibe is run by Husband’s son. 
Based upon that alleged fact, Trading asserted the transaction between Blue Vibe and 
Ultim8 was fraudulent. 
 On July 18, 2025, the trial court, with the Honorable Frederick Paul Horn (Judge 
Horn) presiding, held a hearing on Ultim8’s ex parte application. The minute order 
reflects that Ultim8 presented argument during the hearing, but neither a reporter’s 
transcript nor a settled statement is included in the record on appeal. Judge Horn denied 
the ex parte application. The jury trial in the matter was set to start that same day, but 
Judge Horn continued it until August 1, 2025, as Trading and Lowry were pursuing 
settlement discussions. 
 In Court of Appeal case No. E086596, Ultim8 is appealing from Judge Horn’s 
denial of Ultim8’s ex parte application for leave to intervene. Ultim8’s notice of appeal 
was filed in the trial court on July 23, 2025. 
 On July 30, 2025, in the trial court, Lowry filed a notice of settlement of the entire 
case. That same day, Trading filed a notice of settlement of the first amended cross-
complaint and moved to dismiss the first amended cross-complaint. On August 12, 2025, 
a judgment by stipulation, signed

Filed 11/25/26 Culver City Mall v. Wang CA2/2 
NOT TO BE PUBLISHED IN THE OFFICIAL REPORTS 

California Rules of Court, rule 8.1115(a), prohibits courts and parties from citing or relying on opinions 
not certified for publication or ordered published, except as specified by rule 8.1115(b). This opinion has 
not been certified for publication or ordered published for purposes of rule 8.1115. 

IN THE COURT OF APPEAL OF THE STATE OF CALIFORNIA 

SECOND APPELLATE DISTRICT 

DIVISION TWO 

CULVER CITY MALL, LLC, et al., 

 Plaintiffs and Respondents, 

 v. 

STEVE WANG et al., 

 Defendants and Appellants. 

 B344210 

 (Los Angeles County 
 Super. Ct. No. 22STCV38061) 

APPEAL from a judgment of the Superior Court of Los 
Angeles County, William F. Fahey, Judge. Affirmed. 
Mirch Law Firm, Kevin J. Mirch and Marie C. Mirch for 
Defendants and Appellants. 
Dillon Miller Ahuja & Boss, Peter J. Attarian, Jr., 
George B. Blackmar and Gerry C. Schmelter for Plaintiffs and 
Respondents. 
____________________ 

 2 
Defendants Steve and Dinah Wang (the Wangs) appeal the 
trial court’s summary judgment in this breach of contract action 
brought by Plaintiffs Culver City Mall, LLC (Culver City), 
Valencia Town Center Venture, L.P. (Valencia), and Plaza Bonita 
LLC (Plaza Bonita). We affirm. 
FACTUAL BACKGROUND 
 We construe the facts in the light most favorable to the 
Wangs. (Nicoletti v. Kest (2023) 97 Cal.App.5th 140, 144.) The 
Wangs own and operate Burger King restaurants in southern 
California, three of which were located in malls owned by Culver 
City, Valencia, and Plaza Bonita (collectively, Landlords). 
Landlords are all entities affiliated with Westfield, LLC 
(Westfield). 
Landlords initially leased the restaurant premises to 
Shihlin Electric USA Company Limited (Shihlin), an entity that 
operates Burger King restaurants. The leases proffered by 
Landlords are dated March 9, 2010, for Culver City;1 January 4, 
2012, for Valencia; and August 28, 2015, for Plaza Bonita. Steve 
Wang signed each lease in his capacity as president of Shihlin. 
Culver City also proffered three amendments to its lease (dated 
Aug. 29, 2011, Sept. 6, 2012 & July 18, 2014), each also signed by 
Mr. Wang as president of Shihlin. 
In August 2016, an attorney for Shihlin informed Westfield 
that Mr. Wang was a former executive not authorized to enter 
the Plaza Bonita lease on Shihlin’s behalf. Shihlin also confirmed 
he had not been authorized to enter the Culver City or Valencia 
leases. 

1 Culver City’s predecessor, Culver City Mall LP, signed the 
original lease. That entity was later converted to a limited 
liability company. 
 3 
That precipitated months of negotiations among Landlords, 
Shihlin, and the Wangs to assign the three leases from Shihlin to 
the Wangs. In three agreements dated May 3, 2017, Shihlin 
assigned its interests in each lease to the Wangs. The 
assignments also made certain amendments to the existing 
leases, including adding a provision allowing each landlord to 
terminate the lease upon 60 days’ written notice to the Wangs. 
The Wangs maintain they “would never [have] agree[d] to 
an early termination clause,” and they never discussed that 
clause with Westfield. However, the Wangs do not deny they 
operated Burger King restaurants on premises owned by 
Landlords. Moreover, the assignments each state the Wangs 
“operated in the [p]remises since entry into the [l]ease and 
continue[] to do so” as of the date of the assignments. The Wangs 
said they could not authenticate the leases, lease amendments, 
and assignments proffered by Landlords. 
According to Landlords’ records (called “balance due 
analyses”), the Wangs failed to pay rent and other charges 
required by each lease. 
The Culver City deficit began around December 2019. 
Although the Wangs made some payments, those were not 
enough to cover the charges due. 
For the Valencia lease, arrearages began to accrue by 
January 2018, and grew more quickly starting in April 2020. 
Again, although the Wangs made some payments, those were not 
enough to cover the charges due. 
For the Plaza Bonita lease, arrearages began to accrue by 
January 2020. The Wangs made some payments thereafter, but 
not enough to cover the charges due. 
 4 
The Wangs ultimately vacated all three restaurant 
premises: Valencia on January 16, 2022; Culver City on June 7, 
2022; and Plaza Bonita on June 30, 2022. On those dates, 
Landlords’ records show the Wangs owed: $118,484.21 to 
Valencia; $253,299.27 to Culver City; and $138,241.68 to Plaza 
Bonita. 
PROCEDURAL HISTORY 
Landlords filed their complaint against the Wangs in 
December 2022 alleging three breach of contract causes of action, 
one for each lease. Landlords also alleged the leases entitled 
them to recover interest. The Wangs’ answer largely denied 
Landlords’ allegations and asserted 33 affirmative defenses. 
In November 2024, Landlords moved for summary 
judgment. (See Code Civ. Proc., § 437c.2) They sought judgment 
in the amount of $716,288.16, comprising the rent and other 
charges due under the leases ($510,025.16) and the interest on 
those sums ($102,982 to Culver City, $48,232 to Valencia, and 
$55,049 to Plaza Bonita). Among other things, Landlords argued 
they made a prima facie showing of each element of their breach 
of contract causes of action and the Wangs could not show the 
existence of a triable issue of material fact. In the alternative, 
Landlords moved for summary adjudication of each cause of 
action and the Wangs’ affirmative defenses. 
In connection with their motion, Landlords asked the trial 
court to take judicial notice of a document showing Culver City 
Mall LP converted to Culver City Mall LLC, and various 
documents from related cases involving the Wangs, including two 

2 Undesignated statutory references are to the Code of Civil 
Procedure. 
 5 
unlawful detainer actions brought by Plaza Bonita and Culver 
City. 
The Wangs opposed summary judgment on several 
grounds. As relevant here, they argued Landlords’ evidence was 
insufficient to show the leases, amendments, and assignments 
were authentic and unaltered, and thus, Landlords could not 
show valid contracts. They also argued the balance due analyses 
and calculation of interest were inadmissible hearsay. They 
presented evidence from one expert that the proffered lease 
documents contained inconsistencies with regard to page 
numbers, line numbers, fonts, and photocopy machine markings. 
Another expert provided a declaration stating he could not 
calculate damages based upon the documents he was given. 
The Wangs filed a 131-page document, entitled “Objection 
to evidence filed by [Landlords],” containing 163 objections to 
Landlords’ summary judgment declarations and exhibits. The 
Wangs also objected to the trial court taking judicial notice of the 
stipulations for entry of judgment in the unlawful detainer 
actions. 
After a hearing, the trial court granted the motion for 
summary judgment. It sustained the Wangs’ two judicial notice 
objections but denied their objections to Landlords’ summary 
judgment evidence on the ground the Wangs failed to file “the 
mandatory separate proposed order for these objections” required 
by California Rules of Court, rule 3.1354(c).3 
The trial court analyzed two independent grounds for 
granting the summary judgment motion. First, it determined the 

3 All further references to “rule” are to the California Rules 
of Court. 
 6 
Wangs’ separate statement was “mostly non-compliant,” and 
those deficiencies were sufficient reason to grant the motion. 
Second, the trial court considered all “the admissible 
evidence . . . and conclude[d] that there are no material disputed 
issues of fact.” Landlords’ witnesses provided “a sufficient 
foundation” for the lease documents “and also establishe[d] a 
business records exception to a hearsay objection.” The court 
noted the Wangs did not deny they signed the assignments, and 
while their expert “concluded that there were ‘numerous 
problems’ with these documents,” none involved material terms. 
Further, the trial court determined Landlords’ witness 
Romal Wiratunga properly authenticated the balance due 
analyses for each property “as [Landlords’] business records 
showing a total amount of damages of $716,288.16.” That amount 
included interest. While the Wangs’ expert said he could not 
determine damages without further information, that “do[es] not 
raise a material issue of fact as to damages.” The court finally 
noted there was no indication the Wangs’ counsel had attempted 
to obtain discovery from Landlords. Landlords’ motion for 
summary judgment was granted. 
Judgment was entered on February 27, 2025. Culver City 
was awarded $356,281.27, Valencia was awarded $166,716.21, 
and Plaza Bonita was awarded $193,290.68. 
The Wangs timely appealed. (See rule 8.104(a)(1), (d).) 
DISCUSSION 
I. Applicable Law for Summary Judgment 
We review a trial court’s summary judgment de novo. 
(Leyva v. Garcia (2018) 20 Cal.App.5th 1095, 1103 (Leyva).) 
“[S]ummary judgment shall be granted if all the papers 
submitted show that there is no triable issue as to any material 
 7 
fact and that the moving party is entitled to a judgment as a 
matter of law.” (§ 437c, subd. (c).) In making that determination, 
“the court . . . consider[s] all of the evidence set forth in the 
papers, except the evidence to which objections have been made 
and sustained by the court, and all inferences reasonably 
deducible from the evidence.” (Ibid.) 
A burden shifting framework applies to summary judgment 
motions. (See Aguilar v. Atlantic Richfield Co. (2001) 25 Cal.4th 
826, 850 (Aguilar).) First, a moving plaintiff “bears an initial 
burden of production to make a prima facie showing of the 
nonexistence of any triable issue of material fact.” (Ibid.) That 
“showing . . . must be such that it would, if uncontradicted, 
entitle the moving party to judgment as a matter of law.” (Leyva, 
supra, 20 Cal.App.5th at p. 1101.) “A plaintiff . . . meets its 
burden if it proves each element of the cause of action.” (Quidel 
Corp. v. Superior Court (2020) 57 Cal.App.5th 155, 163.) 
Second, if the plaintiff meets his initial burden, “the burden 
shifts to the defendant . . . to show that a triable issue of one or 
more material facts exists as to the cause of action or a defense 
thereto.” (§ 437c, subd. (p)(1).) To do so, the defendant files 
opposition papers which “include a separate statement that 
responds to each of the material facts contended by the moving 
party to be undisputed.” (Id., subd. (b)(3).) “Failure to comply 
with this requirement of a separate statement may constitute a 
sufficient ground, in the court’s discretion, for granting the 
motion.” (Ibid.; see also Kojababian v. Genuine Home Loans, Inc. 
(2009) 174 Cal.App.4th 408, 416 (Kojababian).) 
 8 
II. The Trial Court Properly Overruled the Wangs’ 
Objections to Landlords’ Evidence 
In reviewing summary judgment, we consider “all the 
evidence set forth in the moving and opposition papers except 
evidence for which objections were made and sustained.” (Ryder 
v. Lightstorm Entertainment, Inc. (2016) 246 Cal.App.4th 1064, 
1072; see also § 437c, subd. (c).) We therefore first address the 
Wangs’ argument the trial court improperly overruled their 
objections to Landlords’ evidence on the ground they failed to file 
a separate proposed order. (See rule 3.1354(b)–(c).) We perceive 
no error. 
A. Standard of Review 
The parties dispute whether this issue is reviewed de novo 
or for abuse of discretion. According to the Wangs, Reid v. Google, 
Inc. (2010) 50 Cal.4th 512, 535 (Reid), requires de novo review. 
But the Reid court expressly refused to decide the standard 
applicable to “a trial court’s rulings on evidentiary objections 
based on papers alone.” (Ibid.; see also Doe v. Software One, Inc. 
(2022) 85 Cal.App.5th 98, 103 [“the weight of authority since Reid 
supports applica

leads.text:
Fifth Circuit Court of Appeal
State of Louisiana
__________
No. 26-CA-188
________________
RIVER REGION FEDERAL CREDIT UNION
versus
PRINCE PROPERTIES, LLC, CHRISTINA P. GARY, AND MICHAEL D. GARY
ON APPEAL FROM THE TWENTY-THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT COURT
PARISH OF ST. JAMES, STATE OF LOUISIANA
NO. 41,959, DIVISION "D"
HONORABLE STEVEN C. TUREAU, JUDGE PRESIDING
November 25, 2026
Panel composed of Judges Susan M. Chehardy, 
Fredericka Homberg Wicker, and Scott U. Schlegel
JUDGE
SCOTT U. SCHLEGEL
AFFIRMED
SUS
SMC
FHW

COUNSEL FOR PLAINTIFF/APPELLEE, 
RIVER REGION FCU
 Wilbur W. Reynaud
COUNSEL FOR DEFENDANT/APPELLANT, 
PRINCE PROPERTIES, LLC REPRESENTED BY ITS MANAGER, 
CHRISTINA PRINCE GARY, CHRISTINA P. GARY, AND MICHAEL 
D. GARY
 Robert R. Faucheux, Jr.

26-CA-188 1 
SCHLEGEL, J. 
 Defendants-Appellants, Prince Properties, LLC, Christina P. Gary, and 
Michael D. Gary, appeal the trial court’s October 31, 2025 judgment granted in 
favor of plaintiff-appellee, River Region Federal Credit Union, in the amount of 
$78,717.63, with legal interest from the date of judicial demand. Defendants 
contend that the trial court erred by rendering judgment in favor of River Region 
because its claims against them are prescribed. For the reasons explained more 
fully below, we affirm the trial court’s judgment. 
PROCEDURAL HISTORY AND FACTS 
On December 4, 2023, River Region filed a petition entitled “Suit on a 
Promissory Note” against defendants. In the petition, River Region alleged that on 
June 1, 2017, defendants executed a dation en paiement transferring several lots to 
River Region in order to avoid foreclosure on “a promissory note and collateral 
mortgage originally dated September 22, 2014, which was in default.”1 River 
Region alleged that defendants owed it $260,717.53. River Region agreed to 
attempt to sell the lots at a fair market price and to apply the sales proceeds, less 
any necessary expenses to prepare the lots for sale, against the balance owed by 
defendants. River Region also agreed that it would not charge interest on the 
balance owed by defendants until it sold all of the lots. 
River Region alleged in its petition that it sold the lots for a total of 
$163,500.00, with the last lot sold on February 7, 2022. It further alleged that it 
was entitled to deduct expenses, including $9,410.00 for realtor fees and taxes, as 
well as $29,832.07 incurred for property maintenance, appraisals, surveys, and 
costs to construct a bus turnaround required by St. James Parish prior to approving 
River Region’s request to sell the lots to the general public. After deducting these 

1 A dation en paiement is a contract whereby an obligor gives a thing to the obligee, who accepts it in 
payment of a debt. La. C.C. art. 2655; Dunaway v. Spain, 493 So.2d 577, 579 (La. 1986). 

26-CA-188 2 
expenses from sales proceeds, River Region alleged that defendants owed it a 
balance of $136,549.00.2 
On December 22, 2023, defendants filed an answer to the lawsuit and 
alleged that River Region “breached its fiduciary responsibility” by waiting over 
two and a half years to start selling the lots and “by not selling the lots for fair 
market value and the agreed upon sales price.” Defendants also alleged that River 
Region incurred unnecessary expenses. 
Following a status conference in July 2024, the trial court set the matter for a 
judge trial on February 11, 2025. On January 13, 2025, the trial date was 
continued to April 14, 2025. One week prior to trial on April 7, 2025, defendants 
filed an exception of prescription alleging that pursuant to La. C.C. art. 3498, River 
Region’s suit was prescribed because more than five years had elapsed between the 
time that the final note was due and when River Region demanded payment.3 
Defendants argued that they signed several notes in favor of River Region, 
beginning on November 28, 2011 and ending with the final note signed on June 1, 
2017. Defendants alleged that the due date on the final note was January 1, 2018, 
and that River Region did not send a demand letter for the balance due until 
September 19, 2023, more than five years later. 
However, the trial court did not set the exception of prescription for hearing. 
Instead, on April 9, 2025, it denied the show cause order finding that the exception 
was “untimely filed per [the] pre-trial order.”4 The parties appeared for the bench 
trial on April 14, 2025. Prior to trial, defendants attempted to argue their exception

After obtaining the necessary approvals, however, River Region was initially

Fifth Circuit Court of Appeal
State of Louisiana
__________
No. 26-CA-91
________________
JEFFERSON FIRE FIGHTERS ASSOCIATION LOCAL 1374, ET AL.
versus
ARITA BOHANNON, ET AL.
ON APPEAL FROM THE TWENTY-FOURTH JUDICIAL DISTRICT COURT
PARISH OF JEFFERSON, STATE OF LOUISIANA
NO. 869-035, DIVISION "P"
HONORABLE LEE V. FAULKNER, JR., JUDGE PRESIDING
November 25, 2026
Panel composed of Judges Marc E. Johnson, 
Stephen J. Windhorst, and Timothy S. Marcel
JUDGE
TIMOTHY S. MARCEL
VACATED; REMANDED
TSM
MEJ
SJW

COUNSEL FOR PLAINTIFF/APPELLANT, 
JEFFERSON FIREFIGHTERS ASSOCIATION LOCAL 1374, 
I.A.F.F., INC., ROBERT BURKETT
 Brandon J. Venegas
COUNSEL FOR DEFENDANT/APPELLEE, 
ARITA BOHANNON, DEANO BONANO, JENNIFER VAN 
VRANCKEN, SCOTT WALKER, BYRON LEE, HANS LILJEBERG, 
TIM KERNER, JR. & THE PARISH OF JEFFERSON
 Guice A. Giambrone, III
 Craig R. Watson
 Amanda Plaiscia

26-CA-91 1 
MARCEL, J. 
In this case concerning appointment to the Jefferson Parish Fire 
Civil Service Board, plaintiffs Jefferson Fire Fighters Association Local 
1374, I.A.F.F., Inc., and its president, Robert Burkett, a resident of 
Jefferson Parish, appeal an October 30, 2025 judgment of the trial court 
that denied their Petition for Declaratory Judgment, Writ of 
Mandamus, and Injunctive Relief filed against individual members of 
the Jefferson Parish Council in their official capacities and the Parish of 
Jefferson, (hereafter “Parish defendants”). For the following reasons, 
we vacate the judgment of the trial court and remand this matter to the 
trial court for proceedings consistent with our decision herein. 
BACKGROUND 
Appointment of members to the Jefferson Parish Fire Civil Service 
Board is governed by Louisiana Revised Statute 33:2536, which states 
that the appointment of one board member is to be made from a list of 
four nominees furnished “by the executive head of a regularly chartered 
and established four-year institution of higher education located within 
the area served; or, if there is no such institution in the area served, by 
the executive head of such an institution which is within the state and 
which is the most geographically proximate to the area served.” 
The area served at issue here is the East Bank Consolidated 
Special Service Fire Protection District as defined by Jefferson Parish 
Code of Ordinances, Sec. 13-36. First on August 21, 2019, then on 
August 10, 2022, and again on September 17, 2025, the Jefferson Parish 
Council appointed Mr. Glenn Scorsone to the Fire Civil Service Board, a 
nominee from a list solicited from and furnished by the University of 

26-CA-91 2 
New Orleans.1 Parish defendants aver this appointment is consistent 
with Council practice for more than thirty six years, and that the Parish 
has appointed nominees from lists furnished by UNO since 1989 
without challenge. 
On September 24, 2025, plaintiffs filed a Petition for Declaratory 
Judgment, Writ of Mandamus, and Injunctive Relief seeking to have the 
appointment of Mr. Scorsone declared unlawful, to enjoin the Board 
from recognizing Mr. Scorsone as a lawful member, and a writ of 
mandamus directing the members of the Jefferson Parish Council to 
solicit a list of nominees from Xavier University. Plaintiffs aver in their 
petition that, because Jefferson Parish has no “regularly chartered or 
established four-year institution of higher education” located within the 
East Bank Consolidated Special Service Fire Protection District, Xavier 
University, as the most geographically proximate to the district, is the 
proper institution to furnish the list of Board nominees pursuant to La. 
R.S. 33:2536. 
In their answer to this petition, the Parish defendants argued that 
the Council’s solicitation of a list of nominees from UNO was proper 
because, since July 1, 2000, the University of New Orleans Foundation 
has leased a studio space at 800 Distributors Row in the Elmwood 
Industrial Park area of Jefferson Parish, for the Robert and Jeri Nims 
Center for Entertainment and Multimedia Technology, (the “Nims 
Center”). Defendants argue that plaintiffs are not entitled to 
mandamus relief because the determination of whether a four-year 

1 On July 1, 2026, the University of New Orleans officially changed its name to Louisiana 
State University in New Orleans, LSUNO. For simplicity, we refer to it here by its 
previous name, UNO. 

26-CA-91 3 
institution qualifies under La. R.S. 33:2536 as being “located within the 
area served” necessarily involves factual findings and the exercise of 
judgment. Defendants claim that the Council was acting within its 
discretion in determining that UNO is a four-year institution 
maintaining an academic facility within the geographic boundaries of 
the fire district. 
In response, plaintiffs filed a memorandum with exhibits where 
they pointed out that UNO’s charter, issued under La. R.S. 17:3217(9) 
establishes the university in Orleans Parish. They also state that the 
UNO Foundation is a separate legal entity from the University of New 
Orleans. Plaintiffs further argued that, under the Parish’s 
interpretation of the statute, many other universities could be 
considered “located within” the service area: Louisiana State 
University maintains an office for the LSU AgCenter in the Parish 
Government Building and Tulane University has an Elmwood campus 
less than a hundred yards away from Jefferson Parish Fire 
Headquarters. Plaintiffs argued that the use of the word “shall” in the 
relevant portion of La. R.S. 33:2536 indicates a mandatory rather than 
a discretionary duty. 
A hearing on the petition was held on October 30, 2025, at which 
time the court accepted exhibits from defendants into the record. On 
the same day, the court issued a judgment denying the petition. (The 
court included the following language in the judgment, “In [denying the 
petition], this court acknowledges the intertwine of the Nims Center as 
a division of the University of New Orleans Foundation and thereby 
noting that although division is not impossible, it has not been 

26-CA-91 4 
established as matter of law.”) Plaintiffs’ timely appeal of the judgment 
followed. 
On appeal, plaintiffs raise multiple assignments of error which 
may be summarized as: (1) whether the Council’s duties set forth in La. 
R.S. 33:2536(C)(2)(b) are ministerial or discretionary; (2) what 
constitutes a “regularly chartered and established four-year institution 
of higher education within the area served” under the statute; and (3) 
whether the trial court procedurally erred in dismissing the entire 
petition when the October 30, 2025 hearing was set only on the writ of 
mandamus. We consider these questions in our discussion below. 
DISCUSSION 
A writ of mandamus may be directed to a public officer to compel 
the performance of a ministerial duty required by law. La. C.C.P. art. 
3863. As a general rule, a trial court’s judgment on a writ of mandamus 
is reviewed under an abuse of discretion standard, while the trial 
court’s factual findings are subject to manifest error standard of review. 
Perrilloux v. St. John the Baptist Par. Gov’t by & through Par. Council 
of St. John the Baptist Par., 24-280, p. 6 (La. App. 5 Cir. 10/18/24), 398 
So.3d 1212, 1218. However, questions of law, such as the proper 
interpretation of a statute, are reviewed de novo. Id. (citing Louisiana 
Municipal Association v. State, 04-0227 (La. 1/19/05), 893 So.2d 809, 
836). At issue in appellants’ first assignments of error is the correct 
interpretation of the relevant portions of La. R.S. 33:2536, therefore we 
conduct our review de novo. 
The starting point in the interpretation of any statute is the 
language of the statute itself as what the legislature says in the text of 

26-CA-91 5 
a statute is considered the best evidence of its intent and will. Glorioso 
v. City of Kenner, 19-298, p. 2 (La. App. 5 Cir. 12/18/19), 285 So.3d 601, 
603, (citing Mayeux v. Charlet, 16-1463 (La. 10/28/16, 8), 203 So.3d 
1030, 1036); Par. of Jefferson v. Hous. Auth. of Jefferson Par., 17-272, p. 
8 (La. App. 5 Cir. 12/13/17), 234 So.3d 207, 214; Yount v. Handshoe, 14-
919, p. 7 (La. App. 5 Cir. 5/28/15), 171 So.3d 381, 386. When the law is 
clear and unambiguous and its application does not lead to absurd 
consequences, then the law shall be applied as written and no further 
interpretation may be made in search of the intent of the legislature. 
La. C.C. art. 9. However, when the language of the law is susceptible to 
different meanings, it must be interpreted as having the meaning that 
best conforms to the purpose of the law. La. C.C. art. 10. Finally, when 
the words of the law are ambiguous, their meaning must be sought by 
examining the context in which they occur and the text of the law as a 
whole. La. C.C. art. 12. 
La. R.S. 33:2536 governing fire and police civil service boards 
states in pertinent part2: 
(2) The members of the board shall be appointed by the 
governing body as follows: 
(a) One shall be appointed by the governing body upon its 
own nomination. 

(b)(i) Two members shall be appointed from a list of four 
nominees which shall be furnished, within sixty days after 
the governing authority makes a request by certified letter 
for such list, by the executive head of a regularly chartered 
and established four-year institution of higher education 
located within the area served; or, if there is no such 
institution in the area served, by the executive head of such 
an institution which is within the state and which is the 
most geographically proximate to the area served. 

2 The requirement for two members in this provision is only applicable to five-member 
boards. Here, the Board consists of three members; therefore, only one member is to be 
selected from a higher education institution. La. R.S. 33:2536(N) 

26-CA-91 6 

(ii) If a list of nominations is not submitted within sixty days 
after submission of request for such list, such failure shall be 
considered a failure to perform a ministerial duty required 
by law of a public official or corporate officer. To this end, the 
district attorney for the parish in which the institution is 
located shall provoke the issuance of a writ of mandamus to 
compel the official or officer to act as provided by law. 
… 

This statute sets forth a mandatory scheme for the appointment of 
members of the fire civil service board, as indicated by the language 
“the members of the board shall be appointed by the governing body as 
follows.” Any appointments made in a manner not specified by the 
statute would be unlawful and a writ of mandamus is the proper 
remedy for compelling the governing body to make a proper 
appointment. The additional language of subsection (b)(ii) directed 
towards the executive head of the institution of higher education 
further indicates that the Legislature intended the duties of this statute 
to be ministerial and contemplated mandamus as the proper 
enforcement mechanism for noncompliance. 
The statute does not define “regularly chartered and established 
four-year institution of higher education” or specify how one should 
determine the location or geographical proximity of such an institution. 
The Parish defendants argue that the correct interpretation of this 
statute is that the Legislature intended that the governing body 
exercise its discretion to make a factual determination as to what 
constitutes an institution of higher education located within the service 
area. We disagree. Such an interpretation disregards the plain 
language of the statute; and in particular the phrase “regularly 
chartered and established”. Institutions of higher education are not 

26-CA-91 7 
regularly chartered and established in the abstract, but rather in a 
particular place as specified in the charter document.3 Furthermore, 
the mandates of this statute are not directed towards any official at the 
institution of higher education, but the executive officer in c
