OPINION 
. . . . . . . . . . . 

 Pursuant to the opinion of this court rendered on November 25, 2026, the judgment 
of the trial court is reversed and remanded for further proceedings consistent with the 
opinion. 
 Costs to be paid as stated in App.R. 24. 
 Pursuant to Ohio App.R. 30(A), the clerk of the court of appeals shall immediately 
send a copy of the court’s ruling to each party and note that action on the docket . 
Additionally, pursuant to App.R. 27, the clerk of the court of appeals shall send a certified 
copy of this judgment, which constitutes a mandate, to the clerk of the trial court and note 
the service on the appellate docket. 
For the court, 

MARY K. HUFFMAN, JUDGE 

LEWIS, P.J., concurs. 

EPLEY, J., concurs in judgment only. 

2 
OPINION 
MONTGOMERY C.A. No. 30820 

TERRY W. POSEY, JR. and ANTHONY V. GRABER, Attorneys for Appellant 
GREGORY S. PAGE, Attorney for Appellees 

HUFFMAN, J. 
{¶ 1} Plaintiff-Appellant Bearcreek Farms, Inc. filed a complaint for breach of contract 
and declaratory judgment arising out of a sales transaction to purchase real estate (along 
with improvements and fixtures) against Defendants -Appellees S.L.S. Partnership (SLS) 
and its partners, Kenneth Sexton, Lawrence Lakins, and John Van Horn, and against 
Jacqueline S. Ritter, Inc. d/b/a/ Laffs (JSR), following a dispute over the classification and 
ownership of certain disputed items affixed to the real property purchased by Bearcreek. 
{¶ 2} Bearcreek appeals from the trial court’s judgment granting SLS and its partners 
dismissal of its claims for breach of contract and declaratory judgment, arguing that it made 
sufficient allegations to survive a Civ.R. 12(B)(6) motion to dismiss. Generally, Bearcreek’s 
complaint alleged that, pursuant to the purchase agreement, certain items affixed to the 
property were “fixtures” and thus were conveyed to it at the time of closing despite JSR’s 
(the property tenant) contrary claim. Having reviewed Bearcreek’s complaint, we cannot say 
that Bearcreek could prove no set of facts entitling it to relief. For the reasons outlined below, 
we reverse the judgment of the trial court and remand the matter for further proceedings. 
I. Background Facts and Procedural History 
{¶ 1} Bearcreek entered into a Contract to Purchase Real Estate with SLS and its 
partners for the sale of real property located at 2 E. Center Street in Germantown, Ohio. 
Bearcreek agreed to purchase the property in exchange for SLS’s conveyance of the 
property and the deed in accordance with the terms and conditions of the purchase 

3 
agreement. According to the purchase agreement, the property was sold subject to “one or 
more lease agreements.” At the time of closing, SLS and its partners conveyed the property 
title to Bearcreek via a general warranty deed. 
{¶ 2} JSR was a tenant of the building sold in the transaction. Bearcreek knew about 
JSR’s tenancy and that JSR did business at the property, operating a bar under the name 
“Laffs Pub.” Sometime after the closing, however, a dispute arose between Bearcreek and 
JSR regarding the scope and ownership of certain items affixed to the property ; Bearcreek 
believed that these items, which included a commercial bar, a freezer, and a steel kitchen 
hood, had been conveyed in its purchase. JSR apparently claimed that it, not SLS, owned 
the disputed items as “trade fixtures” which had not been identified in the purchas e 
agreement as part of the sale, and thus the items had not been conveyed in the real estate 
transaction. 
{¶ 3} As a result of this dispute, Bearcreek filed a complaint against SLS, its partners, 
and JSR, seeking a declaratory judgment that the disputed items were “fixtures” owned by 
it as the new property owner. Alternatively, Bearcreek asserted a claim for breach of contract 
against only SLS and its partners, arguing that paragraph 2 of the purchase agreement had 
reflected that: 1) the sale included all appurtenant rights and fixtures on the property; 2) the 
agreement contained no provision indicating that SLS and its partners had additional 
contractual obligations subjecting the property and its fixtures to any other claims of 
ownership, including those of JSR; 3) to the extent any such claims of ownership of fixtures 
or other items at the property were valid, SLS and its partners breached the agreement by 
representing that they had the right and authority to sell the property when they lacked title 
or authority; and 4) Bearcreek suffered damages. 
{¶ 4} JSR filed an answer, asserting that the disputed items were not “fixtures” but 

4 
rather were merely accessories to the bar business and had been put on the premises for 
that purpose, making them JSR’s “trade fixtures” and thus subject to removal by JSR. SLS 
and its partners moved to dismiss Bearcreek’s complaint under Civ.R. 12(B)(6), and the trial 
court granted this motion. Bearcreek then voluntarily dismissed JSR as a party to this action 
so that the trial court’s decision granting SLS and its partners’ motion to dismiss was a final 
appealable order. 
{¶ 5} Bearcreek appeals from the trial court’s dismissal of its claims against SLS and 
its partners. 
II. Assignments of Error 
{¶ 6} We consider Bearcreek’s first two assignments of error together. 
The trial court erred in granting Defendants -Appellees’ Civ.R 12(B)(6) 
Motion to Dismiss Count II of the Complaint (Breach of Contract) because the 
Complaint and its attached exhibits, construed in the light most favorable to 
Bearcreek, state a claim for b reach of the Purchase Agreement’s express 
conveyance of “all buildings, improvements and fixtures.” 
The trial court erred in granting Defendants -Appellees’ Civ.R. 12(B)(6) 
Motion to Dismiss Bearcreek’s claim for breach of the General Warranty 
Covenants set forth in R.C. 5302.06, because the Complaint pleads that a third 
party (JSR) asserts a competing claim of ownership over fixtures conveyed by 
the General Warranty Deed, and such a claim, if established, would breach 
the covenants of seisin, right to convey, against encumbrances, and warranty. 
Civ.R. 12(B)(6) Standard of Review 
{¶ 7} Civ.R. 12(B)(6) provides for dismissal of a complaint for failure to state a claim 
upon which relief can be granted. Under Civ.R. 12(B)(6), a motion to dismiss should only be 

5 
sustained if it appears beyond doubt that a plaintiff can prove no set of facts in support of 
the claim that would entitle the plaintiff to relief. York v. Ohio St ate Hwy. Patrol, 60 Ohio 
St.3d 143, 145 (1991). A motion to dismiss is procedural and tests the sufficiency of the 
complaint, not the merits of the suit. See State ex rel. Hanson v. Guernsey Cty. Bd. of 
Commrs., 65 Ohio St.3d 545, 548 (1992). 
{¶ 8} When considering a motion to dismiss for failure to state a claim, all factual 
allegations must be taken as true, and all reasonable inferences must be drawn in favor of 
the non-moving party. Mitchell v. Lawson Milk Co., 40 Ohio St.3d 190, 192 (1988); Cleveland 
Elec. Illum. Co. v. Pub. Util. Comm., 76 Ohio St.3d 521, 524 (1997). “[T]he movant may not 
rely on allegations or evidence outside the complaint.” State ex rel. Hanson at 548. In other 
words, in order to sustain a Civ.R. 12(B)(6) motion, the trial court must find beyond doubt 
from the allegations and pleadings, without resort to any extraneous material, that there is 
no set of facts which could conceivably be proved by the plaintiff that would allow the case 
to be submitted to a jury. A trial court does not evaluate the merits of a claim when deciding 
on the motion. “A court cannot dismiss a complaint under Civ.R. 12(B)(6) merely because it 
doubts the plaintiff will prevail.” Leichtman v. WLW Jacor Communications, Inc ., 92 Ohio 
App.3d 232, 234 (1st Dist.1994). 
{¶ 9} We conduct a de novo review of trial court decisions that grant or deny a Civ.R. 
12(B)(6) motion to dismiss. Student Doe v. Adkins, 2021-Ohio-3389, ¶ 17 (4th Dist.), citing 
Alexander Local School Dist. Bd. of Edn. v. Village of Albany , 2017-Ohio-8704, ¶ 22 (4th 
Dist.); Menorah Park Ctr. for Senior Living v. Rolston, 2020-Ohio-6658, ¶ 12, citing Lunsford 
v. Sterilite of Ohio, L.L.C ., 2020-Ohio-4193, ¶ 22. Accordingly, we afford “no deference to 
the trial court’s decision,” but instead, independently review it. Id., citing Struckman v. Bd. of 
Edn. of Teays Valley Local School Dist., 2017-Ohio-1177, ¶ 18 (4th Dist.). 

6 
Notice Pleading 
{¶ 10} Ohio is a notice -pleading state. Wells Fargo Bank N.A. v. Horn , 2015-Ohio-
1484, ¶ 13. Generally, a plaintiff is not required to plead the operative facts of his or her case 
with particularity, except in very narrow circumstances, such as fraud. York, 60 Ohio St.3d 
at 145. Thus, “a short and plain statement of the claim showing that the party is entitled to 
relief” is typically sufficient. Civ.R. 8(A). The Ohio Supreme Court has reaffirmed this Ohio 
pleading standard, holding that a plaintiff is not subject to a heightened pleading standard 
and is required only to provide notice of the claim. Maternal Grandmother v. Hamilton Cty. 
Dept. of Job & Family Servs., 2021-Ohio-4096, ¶ 10-11. 
Analysis 
{¶ 11} In its first assignment of error, Bearcreek sets forth several arguments. First, 
Bearcreek contends that the trial court improperly resolved disputed factual questions on 
the pleadings contrary to the foundational rule that Civ.R. 12(B)(6) tests only the legal 
sufficiency of the complaint. Bearcreek next asserts that the court ignored that , pursuant to 
Teaff v. Hewitt, 1 Ohio St. 511 (1853), fixture classification is a factual question that cannot 
be decided without evidence. Third, Bearcreek argues that the trial court adopted a 
construction of the purchase agreement which rendered the express conveyance of “all . . . 
fixtures” in paragraph 2 and in the paragraph 15 survival clause mere surplusage, violating 
Ohio’s anti -surplusage canon. Finally, Bearcreek contends that the court erred when it 
applied, in substance, the federal “plausibility” pleading standard, which Ohio has not 
adopted, as Ohio remains a notice -pleading state. In its second assign ment of error, 
Bearcreek asserts that R.C. 5302.06 imposes four covenants on every general warranty 
grantor and that JSR’s ownership claim over the disputed items trigger ed the covenants of 
seisin, right to convey, against encumbrances, and warranty. Bearcreek also contends that 

7 
fixtures pass automatically within the deed under R.C. 5302.04. 
{¶ 12} “A contract is (1) an agreement, (2) with consideration . . . , (3) between two 
or more parties, and (4) to do or not to do a particular thing.” O’Brien v. Ohio State Univ. , 
2007-Ohio-4833, ¶ 44 (10th Dist.), citing Powell v. Grant Med. Ctr. , 2002-Ohio-443, ¶ 27 
(10th Dist.), quoting Lawler v. Burt, 7 Ohio St. 340, 350 (1857). “The necessary elements of 
a valid contract include an offer, acceptance, contractual capacity, consideration (the 
bargained for legal benefit and/or detriment), a manifestation of mutual assent, and legality 
of object of consideration.” (Citations omitted .) Ayad v. Radio One, Inc. , 2007-Ohio-2493, 
¶ 25 (8th Dist.). There must be a meeting of the minds as to the essential terms of the 
agreement. Id. To prove a breach of contract, a plaintiff must establish (1) the existence and 
terms of a contract, (2) the plaintiff’s performance of the contract, (3) the defendant’s breach 
of the contract, and (4) damage or loss to the plaintiff. O’Brien at ¶ 44, citing Powell at ¶ 27; 
Doner v. Snapp, 98 Ohio App.3d 597, 600 (2d Dist. 1994).

NOT FOR PUBLICATION WITHOUT THE 
APPROVAL OF THE APPELLATE DIVISION 

 SUPERIOR COURT OF NEW JERSEY 
 APPELLATE DIVISION 
 DOCKET NO. A-3971-24 

KAREN LODZINSKI , 

 Plaintiff -Appellant, 

v. 

FIELDSPRING INVESTMENTS, 
LLC, and MICHAEL STADLER, 

 Defendant s-Respondents . 

Argued October 19, 2026 – Decided November 25, 2026 

Before Judges Sabatino, Perez Friscia , and 
Torregross a-O'Connor. 

On appeal from the Superior Court of New Jersey, 
Law Division, Ocean County, Docket No. L -1184-25. 

Peter D. Valenz ano argued the cause for appellant 
(McOmber McOmber & Luber, PC, attorneys ; Peter 
D. Valenz ano, of counsel and on the briefs; Christian 
J. Fechter, on the briefs). 

Brian D. Barr argued the cause for respondents 
(Cooper Leven son PA, attorney s; Jennifer B. Barr and 
Brian D. Barr, on the brief). 

 The opinion of the court was delivered by 

SABATINO, P.J.A.D. 
APPROVED FOR PUBLICATION 

November 25, 2026 

APPELLATE DIVISION 
A-3971 -24 2 
 In this case of first impression, this appeal requires us to consider 
whether the New Jersey Law Against Discrimination ("LAD"), N.J.S.A. 10:5-1 
to -50, can apply to a landlord 's allegedly severe and pervasive sexual 
harassment of a tenant . The trial court dismissed the plaintiff tenant 's 
complaint alleging such harassment , concluding as a matter of law that the 
LAD does not protect commercial tenants from that conduct. 
 Given the broad remedial purposes of the LAD and the recognition of 
such claims by tenants under the anti-discrimination laws of s everal other 
jurisdictions, we vacate the court 's pre -answer dismissal of plaintiff 's lawsuit. 
In appropriate circumstances, the LAD may be construed to protect tenants 
from proven severe or pervasive sexual harassment that creates a hostile 
environment, comparable to the Supreme Court 's holding in Lehmann v. Toys 
'R' Us, Inc. , 132 N.J. 587, 600 -01 (1993), which recogniz ed a cause of action 
under the LAD for workplace sexual harassment. We further conclude that, in 
certain context s, the LAD may protect an individual commercial tenant from 
such sexual harassment as well as residential tenants. 
 The limited pre -discovery record in this case is inad equate to assess at 
this early stage whether plaintiff 's factual contentions are sufficient to establish 
severe or pervasive harassment . The trial court did not make such an 
assessment and limited its ruling to a categorical interpretation of the LAD. 
A-3971 -24 3 
Consequently, having corrected here the court 's mistakenly narrow 
construction of the statute, we remand this case for further development of the 
record and proceedings . 
I. 
 The record before us is confined to the allegations in plaintiff 's 
complaint. In summarizing those allegations , we recognize that, for purposes 
of this appeal, defendants have not refuted the conduct and communications 
described in the complaint , except they note the landlord at one point 
apologized to plaintiff .1 
 The Parties and the Lease of the Premises 
Plaintiff Karen Lodzinski is a self -described "entrepreneur. " Lodzinski 
is the owner of Sunshine Designs Boutique, LLC, a retail business she operates 
functionally as a sole proprietor , despite its legal form as a limited liability 
company . 
Defendant Michael Stadler is the owner and managing member of 
codefendant Fieldspring Investments, LLC ("Fieldspring "), a limited liability 
company based in Lakewood. Together, defendants own or manage a 
commercial building in Point Pleasant. 

1 We likewise provisionally accept the truth of the factual allegations at this 
pre-answer pleadings stage, and our opinion should not be interpreted to credit 
their accuracy or veracity . 
A-3971 -24 4 
At the time of the allegations in the complaint, Lodzinski was in her 
early twenties and Stadler was approximately age seventy. 
On or about August 13, 2022, plaintiff entered into a landlord -tenant 
relationship with defendants to lease 2 their premises for her business. The 
lease term was twenty -eight months through December 2024. Plaintiff alleged 
that her business initially "flourished " at the location, "and she envisioned a 
long and prosperous tenure there. " 
The Alleged Sexually Harassing Conduct 
According to the complaint, from October 2023 until approximately 
August 2024, Stadler engaged in a series of sexually harassing behaviors 
towards plaintiff. The complaint identifie s four incidents of alleged sexual 
harassment during that time frame , when Stadler made several statements to 
plaintiff in person at the premises or in text messages in which he repeatedly 
commented on her physical appearance and his attraction to her. The remarks 
culminated with a text message in or around August 2024 in which Stadler 
asked her to marry him, adding "Sorry, I just can 't help my self [sic]." 

2 The record does not contain a copy of the lease. Nor does it contain the text 
messages quoted by the complaint. 
A-3971 -24 5 
According to plaintiff, after receiving that last text message, she wrote to 
him in response, "That's not appropriate to say to your ten ant." He replied, "I 
know. Sorry." 
Plaintiff alleged that, at this point , she "no longer felt safe being alone in 
the store with . . . Stadler. " She further alleged the last time that she and 
Stadler were alone in the store together on or around September 20, 2024 , he 
"could sense [her] tension and asked her if she was uncomfortable, and she 
confirmed she was ." Plaintiff alleged Stadler then "flippantly " responded that 
a male tenant in another one of defendant s' properties "does not get 
uncomfortable " when Stadler asks to marry him. 
Based on th is series of events, plaintiff alleged it had become clear her 
landlord "would not cease his sexually harassing and discriminatory conduct ," 
and th at she was thereby "forced to vacate the premises and terminate the 
lease." 
Plaintiff Vacates the Premises Before the Lease Ends 
On September 30, 2024, plaintiff vacated the premises , about three 
months before the lease was to expire. In a letter she sent that day to Stadler 
informing him of her decision, plaintiff wrote: "Please be advised the reason 
for the above is with cause and due to unprofessional and inappropriate 
A-3971 -24 6 
communication by the [m]anaging [m]ember, Michael Stadler. " (Emphasis 
added). Plaintiff attached Stadler 's referenced text messages to th e letter. 
Plaintiff 's Complaint and Its Ensuing Procedural History 

 In April 2025, plaintiff filed a one-count complaint in the Law Division 
against Stadler and Fiel dspring , plus several fi ctitious defendants . The 
complaint all eged "hostile environment sexual harassment " in violation of 
Section 10:5-12(g)(2) of the LAD. 
In particular, the complaint alleged that Stadler had "engaged in a 
pattern of unwelcome and offensive conduct " toward her , "including but not 
limited to sexually suggestive comments and physical advances ." Further, the 
complaint asserted that "[d]efendant [Stadler 's] conduct was severe or 
pervasive enough to alter the terms and conditions of [the] lease and create an 
intimidating, hostile, and abusive envir onment for [her] i n the use and 
enjoyment of the commercial property. " Plaintiff also claimed that 
"[d]efendant 's conduct was motivated by [her] sex and constitutes unlawful 
discrimination in the leasing and enjoyment of real property under N.J.S.A. 
10:5-12(g)." 
A-3971 -24 7 
The complaint sought monetary damages ,3 an award of attorney 's fees 
under the LAD, and various forms of injunctive relief including court orders 
mandating that defendants undertake corrective action, traini ng, and other 
remedial measures. 
Defendants ' Motion to Dismiss 
Upon being served, d efendants moved under Rule 4:6-2(e) to dismiss the 
complaint for failure to state a claim upon which relief may be granted . 
Plaintiff opposed the motion, arguing she presented viable claims under the 
LAD that she is entitled to litigate. 
 Following argument on the motion, the tr ial court issued an immediate 
oral decision granting defendants ' dismissal motion. In pertinent part, the 
court stated : 
I understand in an employment situation where you 
have power over someone in that sense that no, you 
can't do that anymore, that that is no longer acceptable 
or when we – and when I say no longer acceptable, to 
say that it was ever acceptable. That 's wrong too. But 
it's no longer – it's now actionable, that an employer 
can't . . . do these type of things. 

 We're talking about a commercial relationship 
where the landlord or a representative of the 

3 At oral argument on th is appeal, plaintiff 's counsel clarified that her claims 
for mone tary damages include quantifiable economic damages for relocation 
costs and lost profits. 
A-3971 -24 8 
landlord . . . says reprehensible things, makes you 
uncomfortable. 

 Does that create a cause of action? There 's no 
case that says that. I found no instance where we have 
extended the law in that regard. Even like [defense 
counsel] said, where does it end? I mean, not 
everything is fixed by the law. 

 Frankly, social norms and taboos are more 
effective than the law a lot of times. I just can think 
of so many situations where this analogous conduct 
would become illegal in an actionable sense. 

 . . . . 

 It is not a LAD case . It could be – it is a 
contract case, a breach of your right to quiet 
enjoyment of your space, and that may be actionable 
in that regard. But I have to agree with defendants, 
we have not gone that far. 

 Now maybe the Appellate Division says we 
should, but I find no legal precedent to say in this type 
of situation where he 's just saying objectionable 
sexual comments to a commercial tenant is actionable 
under the New Jersey Law Against Discrimination . 
And consequently, I 'm going to grant the motion as to 
that aspect of the case . 

[(Emphasis added). ] 

The trial court did not address whether the LAD prohibited the sexual 
harassment of a residential tenant. 
A-3971 -24 9 
The court issued a corresponding order that same day on July 18, 2025 
dismissing plaintiff 's complaint without prejudice "as to [plaintiff 's] LAD 
claims." 
This Appeal 
Plaintiff then filed the present appeal. In response to a finality inquiry 
from staff , plaintiff 's counsel represented that plaintiff is declining to pursue 
any non -LAD claims , and requested that we treat the trial court 's July 18, 2025 
order as a final order for purposes of appeal. We have exercised jurisdiction 
over the appeal , in light of that concession. R. 2:2-3(a). 
II. 
A. 
 The questions of statutory interpretation before us have not yet been the 
subject of published case law in our state. To that end, we provide the 
following background concerning the legislative purposes and judicial 
interpretation of the LAD. 
The Enactment and Evolution of the LAD 
Over eighty years ago, in 1945 , the New Jersey Legislature enacted the 
LAD in an "attempt to 'protect society from the vestiges of discrimination .'" 
L.W. ex rel. L.G. v. Toms River Reg 'l Schs. Bd. of Educ. , 189 N.J. 381, 3 99 
(2007) ( "L.W.") (quoting Cedeno v. Montclair State Univ. , 163 N.J. 473, 478 
A-3971 -24 10 
(2000)). Case law has often remarked that "the LAD 's overarching goal is the 
'eradication "of the cancer of discrimination ."'" Battaglia v. United Parcel 
Serv., Inc. , 214 N.J. 518, 546 (2013) (quoting Fuchilla v. Layman , 109 N.J. 
319, 334 (1988) (quoting Jackson v. Concord Co. , 54 N.J. 113, 124 (1969))) 
(emphasis added); see also Savage v. Twp. of Neptune , 257 N.J. 204, 216 
(2024) ( reiterating the same objective). 
When it was originally ena cted, the "special concern of the 1945 [LAD] " 
was strictly employment -based discrimination, though this singular focus very 
soon thereafter greatly expanded when the Act was amended in 1949 to extend 
the statute to "'all the accommodations, advantages, facilities,

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT OF DELAWARE 
GLOBAL TRADINGS, LLC ) 
Plaintiff, ) 
) 
v. ) Civ. Act. No. N25C-10-238 DJB 
) 
) 
LOFTON ENTERPRISE ) 
GROUP, LLC, & UNKNOWN ) 
OCCUPANTS, ) 
Defendants. ) 
Date Submitted: August 20, 2026 
Date Decided: November 24, 2026 
Memorandum Opinion 
On Plaintiff’s Complaint for Writ of Possession – GRANTED 
David E. Matlusky, Esquire, The Matlusky Firm, Wilmington, Delaware, for 
Plaintiff 
Emery Abdel -Latif, Esquire, Kralizec Law, LLC, Wilmington, Delaware, for 
Defendant 
BRENNAN, J. 
1 

This matter stems from an ejectment action that Plaintiff Global Tradings, 
LLC (hereinafter “Global”) filed against Defendant Lofton Enterprise Group & 
Unknown Occupants (hereinafter “Lofton” or collectively, “Defendants”) seeking to 
remove Defendants from the property located at 2 S. Congress St., Port Penn, DE 
19731 (hereinafter the “Property”).1 
In December of 2022, Lofton executed an unrecorded commercial lease with 
Port Penn Fire Company (hereinafter “Port Penn”), the original owners of the 
Property. 
2 The Property was subsequently sold to IBR Properties, LLC (hereinafter 
“IBR”).3 IBR allowed the Property to proceed to foreclosure, and it was eventually 
sold via Sheriff’s sale at which time it was purchased by Global Tradings.4 
Following its purchase, Global Tradings did not execute a new lease with Lofton.5 
In response to this ejectment action, Lofton asserts the affirmative defense that 
their original lease remains in effect, which precludes ejectment from the Property.6 
Pending before the Court is Global Tradings’ Motion for Writ of Possession.7 As a 
result, the Court is asked to review the statutory framework surrounding Sheriff sales 
1 Global Tradings, LLC v. Lofton Enterprise Group, LLC & Unknown Occupants , 
N25C-10-238 DJB, Docket Item (hereinafter “D.I.”) 1. 
2 D.I. 17, p. 4. 
3 Id. 
4 Id. 
5 Id. 
6 Id. at 4-5. 
7 Id. 
2 

and ejectment actions and consider whether an unrecorded lease survives such a sale. 
Delaware is a race -recording jurisdiction and as a result, even though the lease in 
question at the case at bar pre-dated the foreclosed upon mortgage, it was unrecorded 
and thus extinguished when the property was sold at Sheriff’s sale. As a result, the 
filed Motion for Writ of Possession must be GRANTED. 
I. FACTS 
Lofton executed a commercial lease (hereinafter the “Lease”) for the Property 
on December 13, 2022, to expire May 31, 2027, with Port Penn; the Lease was never 
recorded in the office of the Recorder of Deeds.8 At the time the Lease was executed, 
Port Penn owned the Property, but later sold it to IBR who maintained the Lease .9 
IBR executed a mortgage with Wilmington Savings Fund Society (hereinafter 
“WSFS”) on March 27, 2023, yet that mortgage eventually fell in default.
10 On 
December 27, 2024, WSFS filed a foreclosure action against IBR, and a default 
judgment was eventually entered against an unresponsive IBR on February 7, 
2025.11 
Global Tradings purchased the Property on July 9, 2025, at Sheriff’s s ale. 
Following confirmation, Global Tradings declined to execute a new Lease with 
8 D.I. 17, p. 4, D.I. 11, Ex. B. 
9 Id. 
10 Id. 
11 Id. 
3 

Lofton.12 Global Tradings sought to compel Lofton to vacate the Property and 
eventually filed this ejectment action against Lofton on October 23, 2025. 13 In its 
Answer, Lofton asserted the Lease executed with Port Penn, and then IBR, remained 
in effect following the Sheriff’s sale.14 
II. PROCEDURAL HISTORY 
Global filed its Complaint on October 23, 2025.15 Lofton filed its Answer on 
January 29, 2026.16 Oral argument was heard on February 5, 2026, at which time 
this Court requested supplemental briefing as to the validity of Lofton’s Lease 
following the foreclosure sale.17 Global Tradings filed its Opening Brief on March 
6, 2026.18 Lofton filed its Answering Brief on March 30, 2026.19 Global Tradings 
filed its Reply Brief on April 22, 2026. 20 Oral argument was heard on August 20, 
2026.21 This matter is now ripe for decision. 
III. STANDARD OF REVIEW 
12 Id. 
13 Id. 
14 Id. at 4-5. 
15 D.I. 1. 
16 D.I. 11. 
17 D.I. 12. 
18 D.I. 17. 
19 D.I. 18. 
20 D.I. 20. 
21 D.I. 22. 
4 

An ejectment action requires the landowner who is out of possession to prove 
by a preponderance of evidence that they are “(1) out of possession of the property; 
and (2) have a present right to possess the property.”22 If the landowner successfully 
proves they are entitled to possession of the land in question they may “ be granted 
possession of the disputed property” and a judgment in their favor may be entered.23 
Such judgment “establishes the legal right of the plaintiff to the possession of the 
premises; it is not conclusive as to title.”24 
IV. ANALYSIS 
Global Tradings contends it is entitled to possession of the Property on two 
grounds. First, Global Tradings argues Lofton’s Lease is subordinate to the 
Recorded Mortgage as the Lease was never recorded.25 Second, Global Tradings 
maintains that Lofton’s unrecorded lease was extinguished following the foreclosure 
sale of the Property.26 In support, Global Tradings relies on the Delaware Court of 
22 Taylor v. Vanhorn, 2023 WL 3946342, at *2 (Del. Super. June 9, 2023) (citing 
Justice v. McGinn, 1998 WL 229436, n. 9 (Del. Ch. Apr. 21, 1998) (“Here, the 
Petitioners allege in their complaint that they are in possession of at least a portion 
of the property in dispute. Should that be established, then an action for ejectment 
would not be available at law.”)). 
23 Taylor, 2023 WL 3946342, at *2 (citing Nelson v. Russo, 844 A.2d 301, 302 (Del. 
2004). 
24 Id. (citing 2 Victor B. Wooley, Practice in Civil Actions and Proceedings in the 
Law Courts of the State of Delaware, § 1614 (1906) citing Bright's Lessee 
v. Stevens, 1856 WL 1008 (Del. Super. Apr. 1, 1856). 
25 D.I. 17, p. 6. 
26 Id. 
5 

Chancery’s decision in NVR, Inc. v. Spring Oaks Dev. Purchaser , LLC, which held 
that any unrecorded property interest is extinguished upon a Sheriff’s sale.27 
In response, Lofton first claims this Court does not have jurisdiction to 
adjudicate this matter, and argues jurisdiction rests wholly with the Justice of the 
Peace Court given this litigation surrounds a lease.28 Lofton further argues the Lease 
is not extinguished under 10 Del. C. § 5066 because a lease is a contract and not an 
encumbrance, therefore a lease is akin to a restrictive covenant and easement which 
survives a S heriff’s sale.29 Finally, Lofton submits a S heriff’s sale does not 
automatically extinguish a lease and relies on the holdings in Schwartzman v. Gould 
and Gause v. Richardson.30 
A. Jurisdiction is Proper; A Lease is an Encumbrance on Land 
It is well settled that “[a] n ejectment is an action at law within the jurisdiction 
of the Superior Court.”31 Global Tradings’ Complaint is one for ejectment, which is 
an action at law. Accordingly, this Court has jurisdiction to adjudicate this matter . 
Further, Delaware Courts have recognized that a lease is considered a burden on a 
property’s title that must be cleared to convey unencumbered marketable title 
27 Id. (citing 2025 WL 3515356 (Del. Ch. Dec. 8, 2025). 
28 D.I. 18, p. 3. 
29 Id. 
30 Id. at pp. 6-8 (citing 160 A. 207 (Del. Super. May 3, 1932); 9 Del. 222, 1870 WL 
1132 (Del. Super. Oct. 1, 1870)). 
31 Taylor, 2023 WL 3946342, at *2 (citing Nelson, 844 A.2d at 302); See also 
6 

following Sheriff’s sale of a property.32 A property “interest” includes “leasehold 
interests and rights.”33 Therefore, a lease constitutes an interest in real property that 
may operate as an encumbrance on the Property.34 However, the characterization of 
the Lease as an encumbrance on the Property does not resolve the issue of whether 
the Lease survived the Sheriff’s sale. Such determination turns on the priority of the 
Lease with respect to the mortgage , as well as the legal effect of the sale upon the 
subordinate interest in the Property. 
B. The Lease is Subordinate to the Mortgage and was Extinguished Upon 
Foreclosure of the Property 
Delaware is a race -recording jurisdiction and follows the “first in time, first 
in right” rule codified under 25 Del. C. § 153.35 Lofton’s Lease was never recorded, 
therefore the WSFS mortgage in question takes priority. Because “real property sold 
at a sheriff’s sale is taken free of all nonmortgage liens on the land,”36 the Lease in 
question cannot survive under Delaware’s statutory scheme. Public policy demands 
32 Lewes Inv. Co., LLC v. Estate of Graves, 2013 WL 508486, at *3 (Del. Ch. Feb. 
12, 2013) ( Classified leases as the type of interest that would render title 
unmarketable by stating “[t]he sellers were obligated to deliver ‘good and 
marketable title at closing,’ free and clear of all liens, restrictions, easements, 
encumbrances, leases, tenancies, and other title objections…”) (internal citations 
omitted); see also Pilot Point Owners Ass'n v. Bonk, 2010 WL 3959570, at *3 (Del. 
Ch. Oct. 7, 2010) (internal citations omitted). 
33 2006 WL 4804019, at *7 (Del. Ch. May 30, 2006)). 
34 See Hendry v. Hendry, 2006 WL 4804019, at *7 (Del. Ch. May 30, 2006). 
35 Eastern Savings Bank, FSB v. CACH, LLC, 2014 WL 3827496, at *4 (Del. Super. 
July 31, 2014); 25 Del. C. § 153. 
36 Eastern Savings Bank, 2014 WL 3827496, at *4. 
7 

that when property is sold at Sheriff’s sale, the sale “disencumber[s] lands as much 
as possible from liens” and “require [s] the sheriff to discharge all nonmortgage 
liens….”37 
Title 10, Section 4985 of the Delaware Code, requires that “[r]eal estate sold 
by virtue of execution process shall be discharged from all liens thereon against the 
defendant ... except such liens as have been created by mortgage or mortgages prior 
to any general liens.”38 Title 10, Section 5066 of the Delaware Code, provides that 
property sold following a foreclosure sale is discharged from all encumbrances 
attributable to the former owner.39 Specifically, Section 5066 states: 
The person to whom any lands and tenements shall be sold, or delivered, under 
§ 5065 of this title, and such person ’s heirs and assigns, shall hold the same, 
with their appurtenances, for such estate, or estates, as they were sold, or 
delivered for, discharged from all equity or redemption, and all other 
incumbrances made and suffered by the mortgagor, the mortgagor’s heirs, or 
assigns; and such sale shall be available in law.
40 
The statutory provisions read together support the conclusion that the subordinate 
Lease was extinguished upon the sale of the Property . Delaware Courts have 
consistently applied this principle to extinguish unrecorded equitable interests in 
37 Eastern Savings Bank, FSB v. CACH, LLC, 55 A.3d 344, 347 (Del. 2012). 
38 Eastern Savings Bank, 55 A.3d at 347. (citing 10 Del. C. § 4985). 
39 Id., 55 A.3d at 347 (citing 10 Del. C. § 5066). 
40 Id. 
8 

property upon the completion of a Sheriff’s sale; nothing has been presented to 
support a different conclusion here.41 
Global Tradings’ reliance on NVR, Inc. v. Spring Oaks Dev. Purchaser, LLC, 
is correct.42 In NVR, a corporation entered a Lot Purchase Agreement (hereinafter 
“LPA”) to purchase 158 of 246 lots from the original owner and subsequently 
secured its purchase rights by paying a deposit that was recorded as a mortgage 
against the property.43 Pursuant to the LPA, the sale took place in stages and was 
contingent upon the completion of certain site improvements and the acquisition of 
land permits.44 Prior to the conveyance of the remaining lots under the agreement, 
the original owner took out a second mortgage, which it defaulted upon, thereby 
triggering foreclosure proceedings.45 Ultimately, NVR claimed that any foreclosure 
sale would be subject to its purchase rights under the LPA.46 NVR argued that it had 
superior title over the remaining lots by virtue of the LPA because subordinate 
nonmortgage liens are the only interests that are extinguished upon foreclosure.47 
Having ap

Application of the Pen -Trap Statute and the 
Wiretap Act to Unmanned Aircraft System 
Detection Technologies  
The Pen -Trap Statute, 18 U.S.C. §  3121 et seq., prohibits the “use” of a pen register or 
trap and trace device only if that device has first been “attached or applied” to a “tel-
ephone line or other facility.”  The term “facility” includes neither the end -user devices 
that transmit or receive a communication, nor the “electronic or other impulses” trans-
mitted and received by those end -user devices.  
Under the Wiretap Act, a radio communication may be intercepted under 18 U.S.C. 
§ 2511(2)(g)(i) if it does not fall within one of the statutory categories listed in 18 
U.S.C. §  2510(16). A non-radio electronic communication may be intercepted under 
18 U.S.C. §  2511(2)(g)(i) if it is transmitted by an electronic communication system 
that incorporates elements that make the communication’s contents easily obtainable 
by the general public.  
Detecting unmanned aircraft systems through the use of  acoustic, electrooptical and in-
frared, and radar technology systems generally does not violate either the Pen -Trap 
Statute or the Wiretap Act.  
Detecting unmanned aircraft systems through the use of radiofrequency detection sys-
tems does not violate the Pen -Trap Statute so long as the radiofrequency detection 
device or process is not attached or applied to a telephone line or other facility.  
Using radiofrequency detection systems to conduct spectrum monitoring or to intercept 
remote identification broadcasts generally does not violate the Wiretap Act.  Whether 
the use of radiofrequency detection systems to intercept other communications vio-
lates the Wiretap Act must be determined on a case -by-case basis. 
November  24, 2026 
MEMORANDUM OPINION FOR THE COUNSEL TO THE PRESIDENT 
Drones—also known as unmanned aircraft systems (“UAS”)—present 
an unparalleled opportunity to “reshap [e] the future of aviation.”  Exec. 
Order No. 14307, § 1, 90 Fed. Reg. 24727, 24727 (June  6, 2025).  From 
leisure to logistics, agriculture to emergency response, UAS are changing 
the way Americans live, do business, and are protected by their govern-
ment. Id. But as with any advancement in technology, America’s enemies 
have sought to exploit the proliferation and availability of UAS.  “More 
than 95 countries,” including foreign adversaries, “reportedly operated 
some sort of uncrewed military aircraft in 2021.” 1 UAS are also 
 
1 Kelley M. Sayler & Michael E. DeVine, Cong. Rsch. Serv., R47188, Unmanned 
Aircraft Systems: Roles, Missions, and Future Concepts  at 23 (July  18, 2022); see also  
 
50 Op. O.L.C. __ ( Nov. 24, 2026) 
2 
increasingly employed by malevolent non -state actors and criminal or-
ganizations. 2 The Department of War has therefore assessed UAS as 
“pos[ing] the most significant threat” to overseas “personnel, facilities, 
and assets,” and as presenting an increasing threat within the United 
States.3  
In response, Congress has authorized certain federal departments, as 
well as state, local, tribal, and territorial (“SLTT”) law -enforcement and 
correctional agencies, to conduct a variety of counter -UAS (“C -UAS”) 
operations.  See 6 U.S.C. §  124n (governing Department of Homeland 
Security, Department of Justice, and SLTT operations); 10 U.S.C. §  130i 
(governing Department of War operations 4); id. § 6227 (governing De-
partment of Energy operations); 50 U.S.C. §  3515a (governing Central 
Intelligence Agency operations).  When operating within these statutory 
authorities, authorized personnel are exempted from various criminal 
statutes—including those prohibiting the destruction of aircraft or air-
craft facilities, 18 U.S.C. §  32; unauthorized access of computer sys-
tems, id. § 1030; interception of electronic communications, id. § 2511; 
installation or use of pen registers and trap -and-trace devices, id. 
§ 3121; interference with satellite operations, id. § 1367; and aircraft 
piracy, 49 U.S.C. §  46502. See, e.g. , 6  U.S.C. §  124n(a). 5 But using 
 
Wilson Beaver & Ka’Von Johnson, Heritage Foundation, Countering the Drone Threat: 
Steps for the U.S. Military  2–3 (2025), https://perma.cc/ XY4E-FPS9.  
2 Cole Black, The Houthi Model —Non-State Actors and Multi -Drone Capabilities ,

https://perma.cc/ HE6F-8AEE; see generally Beaver & Johnson.

manned Systems (Dec.  5, 2024), https://perma.cc/ 2NQE-RFP3. 
4 We have not been asked, and therefore do not consider, the Department of War’s 
ability to conduct C -UAS operations under the President’s Article II authority.  
5 These statutory authorities do not relieve compliance with the Communications Act 
or other federal regulations governing access to the radiofrequency spectrum.  See, e.g. , 
47 U.S.C. §  301 (licensing and authorization); id. § 303 (interfering devices); id. § 333 
(jamming); id. § 605 (unauthorized transmissions).  We understand that the Federal

139 Stat. 1938 (2025).  See generally FCC, Counter-UAS (Aug. 18, 2026), https://
perma.cc/ MN8K-PWJM.  
Application of the Pen -Trap Statute and Wiretap Act to UAS Detection Technologies  
3 
these statutory authorities remains subject to certain limitations.  For in-
stance, the C -UAS statute addressing SLTTs limits the types of tech-
nologies that they may employ.  Id. § 124n(d)(2)(A)(iii).  And infor-
mation-sharing amongst federal agencies and between the federal 
government and SLTTs is restricted except under certain circumstances.  
See, e.g. , id. § 124n(e)(4)–(5). 
You have asked us to consider whether the use of acoustic, electro -
optical and infrared (“EO/IR”), radar, and radiofrequency -detection sys-
tems outside the C -UAS statutory authorities violates the Pen -Trap Stat-
ute or Wiretap Act.  We conclude that the use of such UAS -detection 
systems does not generally violate either statute.  Subject to certain lim-
itations and qualifications identified in this opinion, federal and SLTT 
personnel may deploy such systems without relying on the C -UAS stat-
utory authorities. 6 But we caution that the use of radiofrequency -detec-
tion systems that obtain the contents of UAS communications may vio-
late the Wiretap Act, except under the circumstances described herein.  
Part I provides an overview of UAS technology and describes the four 
categories of UAS -detection systems that you requested we consider.  
Part II explains the legal frameworks of the Pen-Trap Statute and Wiretap 
Act. Part III applies those statutes to the UAS-detection system categories. 
I. 
A. 
A UAS is “an unmanned aircraft and associated elements (including 
communication links and the components that control the unmanned air-
craft) that are required for the operator to operate safely and efficiently 
in the national airspace system.”  49 U.S.C. §  44801(12).  It is composed 
of four main elements: an unmanned aircraft, a control component, the 
payload, and the communication architecture.   
 
6 Courts have long held that the Supremacy Clause of the United States Constitution 
protects federal officers “from state prosecutions” and private suits under state law “for 
actions reasonable and necessary in the discharge of their federal responsibilitie s.” Wy-
oming v. Livingston , 443 F.3d 1211, 1217 (10th Cir. 2006).  But SLTT personnel acting 
outside the scope of 6  U.S.C. § 124n(a) may be subject to state eavesdropping laws and 
statutes governing the use of pen registers and trap and trace devices.  See Anne Toomey 
McKenna & Clifford S. Fishman, Wiretapping and Eavesdropping §§ 3:56–3:106, 4:24 
(Dec. 2025) (“ Wiretapping and Eavesdropping ”). This opinion does not interpret those 
laws or provide guidance to SLLT personnel who may be subject to them.   
50 Op. O.L.C. __ ( Nov. 24, 2026) 
4 
The first element is the unmanned aircraft itself.  Federal law defines 
an unmanned aircraft as “an aircraft that is operated without the possi-
bility of direct human intervention from within or on the aircraft.”  Id. 
§ 44801(11). Unmanned aircraft come in a variety of shapes and sizes.  
See Joshua Brungardt & Kurt Carraway, The “System” in UAS , in Intro-
duction to Unmanned Aircraft Systems 57, 58–60 (R. Kurt Barnhart et 
al. eds., 3d ed. 2021).  
The second element is the payload, which is the sum of accessories 
that the unmanned aircraft carries.  See Siva Sivamani Ganesh Kumar & 
Abhishek Gudipalli, A Comprehensive Review on Payloads of Un-
manned Aerial Vehicle , 27 Egyptian J. Remote Sensing & Space Scis. 
637, 638–39 (2024); see also Brungardt & Carraway at 64–67. Payloads 
may include explosives, drugs, and contraband.  See generally Felbab-
Brown; Black; Rivers et al.  But the typical payload includes “[s]ensors 
and video cameras.”  Kumar & Gudipalli, 27 Egyptian J. Remote Sensing 
& Space Scis. at 638.  These onboard devices may record data or transfer 
that data in real -time to terrestrial, airborne, spaceborne, or maritime re-
ceivers. Drone Warfare, Counter-UAS 101 – Radio Frequency (RF) 
Drone Detection  § 1.1 (2025), https://perma.cc/ HK9W-BBVT (“Drone 
Warfare, RF Drone Detection ”). The unmanned aircraft’s payload 
should not be confused with the data it transmits, which are sometimes 
called payload communications.  See 47 C.F.R. §  88.5. For clarity, we 
use the terms “payload” to describe the accessories carried by the un-
manned aircraft and “communications” to describe data transmitted over 
various data links.  
The third element is the control component.  See Brungardt & Carra-
way at 60–61. Unmanned aircraft can be divided into those that are re-
motely piloted and those that are automatic or autonomous.  Id. Remotely 
piloted unmanned aircraft rely on “an interface used by the remote pilot 
to control the flight path of  ” the unmanned aircraft, known as a ground 
control station.  14 C.F.R. § 107.3; see also Brungardt & Carraway at 61.  
By contrast, automatic or autonomous aircraft rely on pre -programmed 
coding to execute missions using onboard GPS, inertial navigation, or 
other technologies.  See Drone Warfare, RF Drone Detection  § 4.2; 
Brungardt & Carraway at 60–61.  
The fourth element—and the most important for purposes of this opin-
ion—is the communication architecture.  See Brungardt & Carraway at 
62–64; see generally Saeed M. Khan, Unmanned Aircraft Systems (UAS) 
Communications , in Introduction to Unmanned Aircraft Systems  at 291, 
Application of the Pen -Trap Statute and Wiretap Act to UAS Detection Technologies  
5 
291–319. UAS typically employ “multiple [radiofrequency] links oper-
ating simultaneously.”  Drone Warfare, RF Drone Detection § 1.1. The 
command and control (“C2”) link “carries pilot inputs from the control-
ler to the [unmanned aircraft] and returns telemetry data about battery 
status, GPS position, altitude, and system health.”  Id. Other links can 
transmit and receive video and other data from payload systems.  See id. 
Unmanned aircraft flying near the ground control station typically use

leads.text:
Matter of Haunted Forest, LLC v Town of Wilson 
 2026 NY Slip Op 06936 
 November 24, 2026 
 Court of Appeals 
 Halligan, J. 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 In the Matter of Haunted Forest, LLC et al., Respondents, 
 v 
 Town of Wilson et al., Appellants. (App. Div. No. CA 24-01568) 

 Decided on November 24, 2026 
 No. 91 

 Craig R. Bucki, for appellants. 
 Justin J. Andreozzi, for respondents. 

 Halligan, J. 
 [*1] 
 The question in this appeal is whether defendants-respondents waived their objection to plaintiffs-petitioners' failure to file a summons as required to commence a plenary action under CPLR 304 (a). Our precedent, including Matter of Fry v Village of Tarrytown (89 NY2d 714 [1997]), makes clear that defects such as this one are waivable. Because defendants-respondents failed to timely assert a defense based on this infirmity, we agree with the Appellate Division that they waived it. Accordingly, we affirm the denial of their untimely request to assert the defense. 
 I. 
 The facts of this case are not in dispute. Plaintiff-petitioner Haunted Forest LLC hosted seasonal fall events, including a corn maze and hayride, on farmland owned by plaintiff-petitioner Tracy A. Quinn (together, "petitioners") near the Town of Wilson (the "Town"). In the fall of 2021 and 2022, petitioners obtained special use permits for those events. When petitioners sought to renew their permit for the fall of 2023, the Town Zoning Board (the "Board") determined that petitioners had to complete an environmental assessment under the State Environmental Quality Review Act ( see ECL 8-0101 et seq. ; 6 NYCRR 617.1 et seq. ). 
 Petitioners thereafter asserted claims against the Town and the Board (together, "respondents") in a hybrid article 78 proceeding and plenary action. Petitioners challenged the Board's actions under CPLR article 78 and asserted plenary causes of action against respondents for, among other things, tortious interference with business relations and violations of petitioners' state and federal constitutional rights. CPLR 304 (a) provides, as relevant here, that "[a]n action is commenced by filing a summons and complaint," and "[a] special proceeding is commenced by filing a petition." It is undisputed that petitioners filed a combined petition and complaint and a notice of petition, and that their special proceeding pursuant to article 78 was properly commenced under CPLR 304 (a). It is also undisputed that petitioners did not file a summons as required to commence a plenary action with respect to their remaining claims. 
 Respondents filed a pre-answer motion to dismiss the petition and complaint, and in that motion raised no jurisdictional defenses to petitioners' plenary causes of action or objections to petitioners' failure to file or serve a summons. Respondents thereafter filed a verified answer responding to petitioners' allegations on the merits, again without raising jurisdictional defenses or objections based on petitioners' nonfiling of a summons. Supreme Court granted the petition in part, including on the merits of the article 78 claims. Respondents then moved to amend their answer to plead additional defenses, including that petitioners' failure to file a summons deprived the court of subject matter jurisdiction over petitioners' plenary causes of action. Supreme Court denied that portion of respondents' motion on the ground that respondents had waived any jurisdictional defenses to the lack of summons by failing to timely assert them. 
 The Appellate Division reversed Supreme Court's determination on petitioners' article 78 claims and dismissed them for lack of ripeness because the challenged actions were not final (240 AD3d 1340, 1341-1342 [4th Dept 2025]). The Court affirmed the denial of respondents' request to amend their answer to assert a jurisdictional defense, reasoning that "petitioners' failure to file a summons is a defect in personal jurisdiction, not subject matter jurisdiction," and that respondents "waived a defense based on that defect by failing to raise it in their pre-answer motion to dismiss" ( id. at 1342). 
 The Appellate Division granted leave to appeal ( see 242 AD3d 1578 [4th Dept 2025]). 
 II. 
 Respondents contend that petitioners' failure to file a summons as required by CPLR 304 (a) deprived the court of subject matter jurisdiction over their plenary causes of action. If it did, respondents may raise an objection to that defect "at any time" since defects in subject matter jurisdiction "may not be waived" ( Henry v New Jersey Tr. Corp. , 39 NY3d 361, 367 [2023]). If that defect was instead waivable, then Supreme Court properly denied respondents' untimely motion to assert a defense on that basis. 
 The Appellate Division Departments have reached different conclusions on this question. As noted, the Fourth Department held below that petitioners' failure to file a summons was not a defect of subject matter jurisdiction, and that respondents waived an objection on that basis by failing to timely raise it (240 AD3d at 1342). The Second and Third Departments, in contrast, have held that because the filing of a summons is "necessary to institute an action," the nonfiling of a summons is "a nonwaivable, jurisdictional defect" that "render[s] the action a nullity" ( Park Premium Enters., Inc. v Norben Lofts, LLC , 220 AD3d 661, [*2] 662 [2d Dept 2023], quoting O'Brien v Contreras , 126 AD3d 958, 958 [2d Dept 2015]; accord Sangiacomo v County of Albany , 302 AD2d 769, 770-771 [3d Dept 2003]). 
 Our cases confirm that defects like the one at issue here do not implicate the court's subject matter jurisdiction. In Fry , the petitioner sought to initiate an article 78 proceeding, but one of the initiatory documents was defective because it was only a " proposed order to show cause" rather than an executed order (89 NY2d at 716-717). The respondents answered without objecting to the defect ( id. at 717). The trial court nonetheless dismissed the proceeding sua sponte, concluding that it had not been commenced and therefore "no jurisdiction was acquired over respondents" ( id. ). On appeal to this Court, respondents argued that it was proper to dismiss the proceeding sua sponte because the filing error deprived the court of subject matter jurisdiction ( id. at 718). 
 We rejected that contention. First, we noted that the unexecuted order to show cause in Fry was "of no legal effect" ( id. at 717). We explained that "its filing did not satisfy the provision of the commencement-by-filing statute," which resulted in an "attendant failure to properly commence the special proceeding" ( id. ). Second, we deemed it "beyond dispute" that the court had subject matter jurisdiction—which we described as "the [court's] power, conferred by the Constitution or statute, to entertain the case before it"—over the article 78 proceeding ( id. at 718, citing Village Law § 7-712-c, and CPLR 7804). Third, we held that "strict compliance with the filing system" is not "a requirement of subject matter jurisdiction" ( id. ). On that score, we noted not only the filing statute's lack of an express "limit[ation] or condition" on the court's " 'competence' to entertain particular categories of actions," but also that "the purpose and the structure of the filing requirements . . . do not evince an implicit limitation on subject matter jurisdiction" ( id. at 718-719). We explained that the filing requirements serve other purposes, such as revenue raising via "the payment of a filing fee when an action is commenced," and "the need to pinpoint the moment of 'commencement' " for statute of limitations purposes ( id. at 719). The petitioner in Fry had paid the filing fee, and we concluded that "the court's principal interest in the filing system was satisfied" ( id. ). As to the second purpose, we stated that, "[i]nsofar as the sufficiency of the papers filed at commencement is linked to . . . waivable matters of primary concern to the parties, not the court, defects in filing should be waivable as well" ( id. at 720). So, while "the proceeding would have been subject to dismissal" due to the defective filing, we concluded that respondents had waived that basis for dismissal by "appear[ing] in the proceeding and litigat[ing] its merits without raising this objection" ( id. at 722). 
 So too here. Respondents acknowledge that petitioners' plenary causes of action fall within Supreme Court's general jurisdiction, and thus "[i]t is beyond dispute that Supreme Court has subject matter jurisdiction" over those causes of action ( id. at 718; see NY Const, art VI, § 7 [a]; see also Matter of Ballard v HSBC Bank USA , 6 NY3d 658, 663-664 [2006]). And, as in Fry , respondents "appeared in the proceeding and litigated its merits without raising" any objection to petitioners' failure to file a summons (89 NY2d at 722). Those conclusions are sufficient to resolve this appeal, since "a defect in compliance with the commencement-by-filing system does not deprive a court of subject matter jurisdiction and, accordingly, is waived absent a timely objection by the responding party" ( Harris v Niagara Falls Bd. of Educ. , 6 NY3d 155, 158 [2006], citing Fry , 89 NY2d 714). 
 Respondents and the dissent would distinguish Fry because it involved "the sufficiency of the filed papers" rather than a complete failure to file an initiatory document (dissenting op at 8, quoting Fry , 89 NY2d at 719). They contend that distinction is important because if initiatory papers are not filed, no action is commenced and the proceeding is "a nullity" ( id. at 5, quoting Harris , 6 NY3d at 158). Courts lack authority over such proceedings, they say, and that equates to an absence of subject matter jurisdiction requiring dismissal of the action even if a party does not timely object ( id. at 2). 
 This view cannot be squared with our precedent. As an initial matter, we agree that if a party does not file an initiatory document as CPLR 304 (a) requires, the proceeding will be subject to dismissal ( see Matter of Gershel v Porr , 89 NY2d 327, 330, 333 [1996]; Matter of Mendon Ponds Neighborhood Assn. v Dehm , 98 [*3] NY2d 745, 747 [2002]). FN1 The question is what effect, if any, such a failure has on the court's jurisdiction. Although the view that such a failure implicates subject matter jurisdiction may have some intuitive appeal, this Court has rejected it. In each case where this Court has considered a party's failure to comply with the commencement-by-filing regime, we have either explicitly or implicitly recognized that such an error is subject to waiver if not timely challenged. For example, in Fry , we deemed the defective initiatory document that was filed to be "of no legal effect" and observed that, as a consequence, petitioners "fail[ed] to properly commence the special proceeding" (89 NY2d at 717). We nonetheless concluded that the defect that arose was waivable ( id. at 723). Similarly, in Harris v Niagara Falls Board of Education , where the plaintiff failed to obtain a new index number or pay a filing fee, we stated broadly that, "[u]nder the procedure mandated by the CPLR, 'service of process without first paying the filing fee and filing the initiatory papers is a nullity, the action or proceeding never having been properly commenced' "—yet still we held that the error was waivable (6 NY3d at 158-159, quoting Gershel , 89 NY2d at 330). 
 Respondents and the dissent contend that the rule set forth in Fry and Harris applies only where a party has filed initiatory documents and (in the dissent's words) "thus commenced the proceeding" (dissenting op at 7). Our case law does not support that distinction. While we have affirmed dismissals when no initiatory documents were filed, we have done the same where such documents were filed, and we have furt

leads.caseName: Sapp v. Clark Wilson, Inc.
leads.text:
Sapp v Clark Wilson, Inc. 
 2026 NY Slip Op 06935 
 November 24, 2026 
 Court of Appeals 
 Cannataro, J. 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 Dianna Sapp, et al., Plaintiffs, Tameake Macklin, et al., Appellants, 
 v 
 Clark Wilson, Inc., et al., Respondents, et al., Defendants. 

 Decided on November 24, 2026 
 No. 90 

 Pavita Krishnaswamy, for appellants. 
 Craig M. Flanders, for respondents. 

 Cannataro, J. 
 [*1] 
 [*2] We are asked to determine on this appeal whether defendants were entitled to summary judgment dismissing plaintiffs' illusory tenancy claims. Plaintiffs, formerly homeless individuals who received emergency housing placements in privately owned apartments through the Neighborhood Based Cluster Transitional Residence Program, assert that they are entitled to vacancy leases pursuant to the Rent Stabilization Code (9 NYCRR § 2520.1 et seq. ) as a remedy for an alleged illusory tenancy scheme perpetrated by defendants. We answer the question in the negative on two independent bases. First, plaintiffs are neither tenants nor subtenants and lack standing to assert causes of action pursuant to the Rent Stabilization Code. Second, there exists no triable issue of material fact as to whether defendants engaged in an illusory tenancy scheme intended to deprive plaintiffs of the protections of the Rent Stabilization Code. We therefore affirm the order of the Appellate Division. 
 I. 
 The Neighborhood Based Cluster Transitional Residence Program (Transitional Residence Program), operated by the New York City Department of Homeless Services (DHS) until 2016, provided homeless families with temporary, emergency housing placements in privately owned apartments throughout New York City. Plaintiffs are formerly homeless individuals placed by DHS into apartments owned by certain defendants (the owners) under the auspices of the Transitional Residence Program. FN1 
 Between 2002 and 2008, the owners leased apartments to a for-profit service provider, defendant We All Care Inc., which then contracted with DHS to participate in the Transitional Residence Program. In 2008, DHS changed the terms of the Transitional Residence Program to require that service providers be nonprofit entities. Because it could no longer directly contract with DHS, beginning in 2009, We All Care subleased its apartments to defendant nonprofit Church Avenue Merchants and Block Association (CAMBA), which already had a separate contract with DHS as a service provider. Pursuant to the terms of its contract with DHS, CAMBA was required to accept any families that DHS referred to it on a 24-hour-a-day, 7-day-a-week basis, and to provide certain services, including, for example, temporary housing services, assessment services, social services, permanent housing preparation services, and childcare services. In exchange, DHS paid CAMBA a per diem rate of $107.49 per occupied apartment, per day. The contract further contemplated, by its plain terms, that a family was supposed to occupy an apartment for a maximum period of six months. Pursuant to its sublease agreement, CAMBA then paid rent to We All Care at a per diem rate of $75.50 per occupied apartment, per day upon its receipt of contract payments from DHS. CAMBA was the service provider in 2011 when plaintiffs were first placed by DHS into the owners' apartments. 
 Following the termination of its relationship with CAMBA in 2014, We All Care began subleasing its apartments to defendant nonprofit We Always Care Inc. We Always Care contracted with DHS as the service provider on substantially similar terms to DHS's agreement with CAMBA. We Always Care, pursuant to its sublease agreement, then paid We All Care $76.15 per occupied apartment, per day. The owners ceased participating in the Transitional Residence Program in 2015 and sought to remove plaintiffs from the apartments they had been occupying. 
 Plaintiffs commenced multiple, separate actions against defendants alleging, inter alia, that defendants had engaged in an illusory tenancy scheme intended to deprive plaintiffs of the protections of the Rent Stabilization Code and seeking, as relevant here, a declaration that they were rent-stabilized tenants and an order directing the owners to offer them vacancy leases for the units they had been occupying. FN2 Plaintiffs' actions were ultimately consolidated into this action. The owners thereafter moved for summary judgment dismissing plaintiffs' first, second, and third causes of action, all of which were premised on plaintiffs' illusory tenancy scheme theory. Supreme Court granted the owners' motion, concluding that plaintiffs lacked standing to seek vacancy leases because they were not tenants as defined by the Rent Stabilization Code. Certain plaintiffs appealed. 
 The Appellate Division affirmed on alternate grounds (206 AD3d 1014 [2d Dept 2022]). Assuming without deciding that plaintiffs had standing, the Appellate Division held that the owners demonstrated, as a matter of law, that they had not engaged in an illusory tenancy scheme ( see id. at 1016). The Court further rejected plaintiffs' claim that additional discovery was needed, concluding that plaintiffs' illusory tenancy claims would fail regardless of how certain alleged issues of fact were ultimately resolved ( see id. at 1018-1019). 
 One Justice dissented, and would have denied summary judgment, opining that there were [*3] issues of fact or a need for further discovery that precluded an award of summary judgment ( see generally id. at 1020-1029 [Duffy, J., dissenting]). The Appellate Division granted plaintiffs' motion for leave to appeal to this Court and certified the following question: "Was the decision and order of this Court dated June 29, 2022, properly made?" (2025 NY Slip Op 79882[U] [2d Dept 2025]). 
 II. 
 It is well-settled that the proponent of a summary judgment motion has the initial burden of making a prima facie showing that they are entitled to judgment as a matter of law ( see Alvarez v Prospect Hosp. , 68 NY2d 320, 324 [1986] [internal citations omitted]). If that showing is made, the burden shifts to the nonmoving party to establish the existence of triable issues of material fact ( see id. , citing Zuckerman v City of New York , 49 NY2d 557, 562 [1980]). Of course, the facts must be viewed in the light most favorable to the nonmoving party, but "bald, conclusory assertions or speculation" or the " 'shadowy semblance of an issue' are insufficient" to defeat the motion ( Stonehill Capital Mgt. LLC v Bank of the W. , 28 NY3d 439, 448 [2016], quoting S.J. Capelin Assoc. v Globe Mfg. Corp. , 34 NY2d 338, 341 [1974]). 
 III. 
 In New York City, the Rent Stabilization Law (Administrative Code of City of NY § 26-501 et seq. ) is administered by the Division of Housing and Community Renewal (DHCR), which promulgates regulations "for rent stabilization based on statutory criteria and by prohibiting owners of regulated units from charging more rent than those regulations allow" ( Matter of 160 E. 84th St. Assoc. LLC v New York State Div. of Hous. & Community Renewal , 43 NY3d 275, 278 [2024]). Those regulations are codified in the Rent Stabilization Code (9 NYCRR § 2520.1 et seq. ). Turning first to plaintiffs' standing under the Rent Stabilization Code, it is axiomatic that " '[w]hen presented with a question of statutory interpretation, our primary consideration is to ascertain and give effect to the intention of the [l]egislature' " (43 NY3d at 282, quoting Kuzmich v 50 Murray St. Acquisition LLC , 34 NY3d 84, 91 [2019]). Thus, " '[i]nasmuch as the clearest indicator of legislative intent is the statutory text, the starting point . . . must always be the language itself, giving effect to the plain meaning thereof' " ( id. , quoting Kuzmich , 34 NY3d at 90). Relevant here, "administrative regulations are generally subject to the same interpretive rules and canons of construction as statutes" ( Cruz v Banks , 45 NY3d 599, 605 [2026]). 
 Plaintiffs assert that they are entitled to vacancy leases pursuant to the Rent Stabilization Code as a remedy for the illusory tenancy scheme; however, we have never held that parties who are neither tenants nor subtenants, as those terms are defined in the Rent Stabilization Code, can bring claims arising under it, and we decline to do so on these facts. Thus, because they are neither tenants nor subtenants under the Rent Stabilization Code, plaintiffs lack standing to seek such relief. Tenant, as defined by the Rent Stabilization Code, is "[a]ny person or persons named on a lease as lessee or lessees, or who is or are a party or parties to a rental agreement and obligated to pay rent for the use or occupancy of a housing accommodation or is entitled to occupy the housing accommodation as a tenant pursuant to any other provision of this Code" (9 NYCRR 2520.6 [d]). Accordingly, to be considered tenants, plaintiffs are required to satisfy two elements: they must (1) be "named on a lease" as lessees or be "parties to a rental agreement" and (2) be "obligated to pay rent for the use or occupancy" of the apartments. As to the first requirement, plaintiffs are neither "named on a lease" nor "parties to a rental agreement." Rather, the relevant leases for the apartments occupied by plaintiffs were subleases between We All Care as the prime tenant and either CAMBA or We Always Care as the subtenant. As to the second requirement, plaintiffs did not pay rent and were not obligated to pay rent for the apartments they occupied. DHS, pursuant to [*4] its contracts with either CAMBA or We Always Care, paid the relevant service provider at a per diem rate for each occupied apartment per day. CAMBA or We Always Care then paid rent at a separate per diem rate to We All Care out of the money received from DHS as required by the terms of the sublease agreements. 
 Nor are plaintiffs subtenants within the meaning of the Rent Stabilization Code. A subtenant is "[a]ny person lawfully occupying the housing accommodation pursuant to an agreement with the tenant by authority of the lease or by virtue of rights afforded pursuant to section 226-b of the Real Property Law" (9 NYCRR 2520.6 [k]). Plaintiffs do not "have an agreement with the tenant"—We All Care—such that they can properly be considered subtenants. The sublease agreements between We All Care and CAMBA or We Always Care were entered into "in connection" with the agreements between DHS and CAMBA or We Always Care for the purpose of "provid[ing] apartment units on a temporary basis and related services" to "homeless families as part of" the Transitional Residence Program. For this reason, and contrary to the assertion by the dissent ( see dissent at 19-20), plaintiffs have no relationship with any party in the leasing chain of the type that would confer standing under the Rent Stabilization Code. 
 Many plaintiffs here have occupied their apartments for years, and it is undoubtedly true that they and their families have formed strong bonds with their neighbors and within their respective communities. Nor do we doubt that plaintiffs possess a genuine desire to remain in those apartments to maintain the employment and educational opportunities that stable housing has afforded them. That does not, however, transform plaintiffs into tenants or subtenants within the meaning of the Rent Stabilization Code. 
 IV. 
 Even if plaintiffs could assert claims under the Rent Stabilization Code, they still fail to raise a triable issue of material fact to overcome the owners' showing that they did not engage in an illusory tenancy scheme as a matter of law. The Rent Stabilization Code prohibits an "owner or other person" from "engag[ing] in any practice, including but not limited to illusory or collusive rental practices which deprive a tenant in possession of his or her
