 Halligan, J. 
 [*1] 
 The question in this appeal is whether defendants-respondents waived their objection to plaintiffs-petitioners' failure to file a summons as required to commence a plenary action under CPLR 304 (a). Our precedent, including Matter of Fry v Village of Tarrytown ( 89 NY2d 714 [1997]), makes clear that defects such as this one are waivable. Because defendants-respondents failed to timely assert a defense based on this infirmity, we agree with the Appellate Division that they waived it. Accordingly, we affirm the denial of their untimely request to assert the defense. 
 I. 
 The facts of this case are not in dispute. Plaintiff-petitioner Haunted Forest LLC hosted seasonal fall events, including a corn maze and hayride, on farmland owned by plaintiff-petitioner Tracy A. Quinn (together, "petitioners") near the Town of Wilson (the "Town"). In the fall of 2021 and 2022, petitioners obtained special use permits for those events. When petitioners sought to renew their permit for the fall of 2023, the Town Zoning Board (the "Board") determined that petitioners had to complete an environmental assessment under the State Environmental Quality Review Act ( see ECL 8-0101 et seq. ; 6 NYCRR 617.1 et seq. ). 
 Petitioners thereafter asserted claims against the Town and the Board (together, "respondents") in a hybrid article 78 proceeding and plenary action. Petitioners challenged the Board's actions under CPLR article 78 and asserted plenary causes of action against respondents for, among other things, tortious interference with business relations and violations of petitioners' state and federal constitutional rights. CPLR 304 (a) provides, as relevant here, that "[a]n action is commenced by filing a summons and complaint," and "[a] special proceeding is commenced by filing a petition." It is undisputed that petitioners filed a combined petition and complaint and a notice of petition, and that their special proceeding pursuant to article 78 was properly commenced under CPLR 304 (a). It is also undisputed that petitioners did not file a summons as required to commence a plenary action with respect to their remaining claims. 
 Respondents filed a pre-answer motion to dismiss the petition and complaint, and in that motion raised no jurisdictional defenses to petitioners' plenary causes of action or objections to petitioners' failure to file or serve a summons. Respondents thereafter filed a verified answer responding to petitioners' allegations on the merits, again without raising jurisdictional defenses or objections based on petitioners' nonfiling of a summons. Supreme Court granted the petition in part, including on the merits of the article 78 claims. Respondents then moved to amend their answer to plead additional defenses, including that petitioners' failure to file a summons deprived the court of subject matter jurisdiction over petitioners' plenary causes of action. Supreme Court denied that portion of respondents' motion on the ground that respondents had waived any jurisdictional defenses to the lack of summons by failing to timely assert them. 
 The Appellate Division reversed Supreme Court's determination on petitioners' article 78 claims and dismissed them for lack of ripeness because the challenged actions were not final ( 240 AD3d 1340 , 1341-1342 [4th Dept 2025]). The Court affirmed the denial of respondents' request to amend their answer to assert a jurisdictional defense, reasoning that "petitioners' failure to file a summons is a defect in personal jurisdiction, not subject matter jurisdiction," and that respondents "waived a defense based on that defect by failing to raise it in their pre-answer motion to dismiss" ( id. at 1342 ). 
 The Appellate Division granted leave to appeal ( see 242 AD3d 1578 [4th Dept 2025]). 
 II. 
 Respondents contend that petitioners' failure to file a summons as required by CPLR 304 (a) deprived the court of subject matter jurisdiction over their plenary causes of action. If it did, respondents may raise an objection to that defect "at any time" since defects in subject matter jurisdiction "may not be waived" ( Henry v New Jersey Tr. Corp. , 39 NY3d 361 , 367 [2023]). If that defect was instead waivable, then Supreme Court properly denied respondents' untimely motion to assert a defense on that basis. 
 The Appellate Division Departments have reached different conclusions on this question. As noted, the Fourth Department held below that petitioners' failure to file a summons was not a defect of subject matter jurisdiction, and that respondents waived an objection on that basis by failing to timely raise it (240 AD3d at 1342). The Second and Third Departments, in contrast, have held that because the filing of a summons is "necessary to institute an action," the nonfiling of a summons is "a nonwaivable, jurisdictional defect" that "render[s] the action a nullity" ( Park Premium Enters., Inc. v Norben Lofts, LLC , 220 AD3d 661 , [*2] 662 [2d Dept 2023], quoting O'Brien v Contreras , 126 AD3d 958, 958 [2d Dept 2015]; accord Sangiacomo v County of Albany , 302 AD2d 769, 770-771 [3d Dept 2003]). 
 Our cases confirm that defects like the one at issue here do not implicate the court's subject matter jurisdiction. In Fry , the petitioner sought to initiate an article 78 proceeding, but one of the initiatory documents was defective because it was only a " proposed order to show cause" rather than an executed order ( 89 NY2d at 716-717 ). The respondents answered without objecting to the defect ( id. at 717 ). The trial court nonetheless dismissed the proceeding sua sponte, concluding that it had not been commenced and therefore "no jurisdiction was acquired over respondents" ( id. ). On appeal to this Court, respondents argued that it was proper to dismiss the proceeding sua sponte because the filing error deprived the court of subject matter jurisdiction ( id. at 718 ). 
 We rejected that contention. First, we noted that the unexecuted order to show cause in Fry was "of no legal effect" ( id. at 717 ). We explained that "its filing did not satisfy the provision of the commencement-by-filing statute," which resulted in an "attendant failure to properly commence the special proceeding" ( id. ). Second, we deemed it "beyond dispute" that the court had subject matter jurisdiction—which we described as "the [court's] power, conferred by the Constitution or statute, to entertain the case before it"—over the article 78 proceeding ( id. at 718 , citing Village Law § 7-712-c, and CPLR 7804). Third, we held that "strict compliance with the filing system" is not "a requirement of subject matter jurisdiction" ( id. ). On that score, we noted not only the filing statute's lack of an express "limit[ation] or condition" on the court's " 'competence' to entertain particular categories of actions," but also that "the purpose and the structure of the filing requirements . . . do not evince an implicit limitation on subject matter jurisdiction" ( id. at 718-719). We explained that the filing requirements serve other purposes, such as revenue raising via "the payment of a filing fee when an action is commenced," and "the need to pinpoint the moment of 'commencement' " for statute of limitations purposes ( id. at 719). The petitioner in Fry had paid the filing fee, and we concluded that "the court's principal interest in the filing system was satisfied" ( id. ). As to the second purpose, we stated that, "[i]nsofar as the sufficiency of the papers filed at commencement is linked to . . . waivable matters of primary concern to the parties, not the court, defects in filing should be waivable as well" ( id. at 720). So, while "the proceeding would have been subject to dismissal" due to the defective filing, we concluded that respondents had waived that basis for dismissal by "appear[ing] in the proceeding and litigat[ing] its merits without raising this objection" ( id. at 722). 
 So too here. Respondents acknowledge that petitioners' plenary causes of action fall within Supreme Court's general jurisdiction, and thus "[i]t is beyond dispute that Supreme Court has subject matter jurisdiction" over those causes of action ( id. at 718; see NY Const, art VI, § 7 [a]; see also Matter of Ballard v HSBC Bank USA , 6 NY3d 658, 663-664 [2006]). And, as in Fry , respondents "appeared in the proceeding and litigated its merits without raising" any objection to petitioners' failure to file a summons ( 89 NY2d at 722 ). Those conclusions are sufficient to resolve this appeal, since "a defect in compliance with the commencement-by-filing system does not deprive a court of subject matter jurisdiction and, accordingly, is waived absent a timely objection by the responding party" ( Harris v Niagara Falls Bd. of Educ. , 6 NY3d 155, 158 [2006], citing Fry , 89 NY2d 714 ). 
 Respondents and the dissent would distinguish Fry because it involved "the sufficiency of the filed papers" rather than a complete failure to file an initiatory document (dissenting op at 8, quoting Fry , 89 NY2d at 719 ). They contend that distinction is important because if initiatory papers are not filed, no action is commenced and the proceeding is "a nullity" ( id. at 5, quoting Harris , 6 NY3d at 158 ). Courts lack authority over such proceedings, they say, and that equates to an absence of subject matter jurisdiction requiring dismissal of the action even if a party does not timely object ( id. at 2). 
 This view cannot be squared with our precedent. As an initial matter, we agree that if a party does not file an initiatory document as CPLR 304 (a) requires, the proceeding will be subject to dismissal ( see Matter of Gershel v Porr , 89 NY2d 327, 330, 333 [1996]; Matter of Mendon Ponds Neighborhood Assn. v Dehm , 98 [*3] NY2d 745, 747 [2002]). FN1 The question is what effect, if any, such a failure has on the court's jurisdiction. Although the view that such a failure implicates subject matter jurisdiction may have some intuitive appeal, this Court has rejected it. In each case where this Court has considered a party's failure to comply with the commencement-by-filing regime, we have either explicitly or implicitly recognized that such an error is subject to waiver if not timely challenged. For example, in Fry , we deemed the defective initiatory document that was filed to be "of no legal effect" and observed that, as a consequence, petitioners "fail[ed] to properly commence the special proceeding" (89 NY2d at 717). We nonetheless concluded that the defect that arose was waivable ( id. at 723). Similarly, in Harris v Niagara Falls Board of Education , where the plaintiff failed to obtain a new index number or pay a filing fee, we stated broadly that, "[u]nder the procedure mandated by the CPLR, 'service of process without first paying the filing fee and filing the initiatory papers is a nullity, the action or proceeding never having been properly commenced' "—yet still we held that the error was waivable (6 NY3d at 158-159, quoting Gershel , 89 NY2d at 330 ). 
 Respondents and the dissent contend that the rule set forth in Fry and Harris applies only where a party has filed initiatory documents and (in the dissent's words) "thus commenced the proceeding" (dissenting op at 7). Our case law does not support that distinction. While we have affirmed dismissals when no initiatory documents were filed, we have done the same where such documents were filed

leads.caseName: Sapp v. Clark Wilson, Inc.
leads.text:
Sapp v Clark Wilson, Inc. 
 2026 NY Slip Op 06935 
 November 24, 2026 
 Court of Appeals 
 Cannataro, J. 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 Dianna Sapp, et al., Plaintiffs, Tameake Macklin, et al., Appellants, 
 v 
 Clark Wilson, Inc., et al., Respondents, et al., Defendants. 

 Decided on November 24, 2026 
 No. 90 

 Pavita Krishnaswamy, for appellants. 
 Craig M. Flanders, for respondents. 

 Cannataro, J. 
 [*1] 
 [*2] We are asked to determine on this appeal whether defendants were entitled to summary judgment dismissing plaintiffs' illusory tenancy claims. Plaintiffs, formerly homeless individuals who received emergency housing placements in privately owned apartments through the Neighborhood Based Cluster Transitional Residence Program, assert that they are entitled to vacancy leases pursuant to the Rent Stabilization Code (9 NYCRR § 2520.1 et seq. ) as a remedy for an alleged illusory tenancy scheme perpetrated by defendants. We answer the question in the negative on two independent bases. First, plaintiffs are neither tenants nor subtenants and lack standing to assert causes of action pursuant to the Rent Stabilization Code. Second, there exists no triable issue of material fact as to whether defendants engaged in an illusory tenancy scheme intended to deprive plaintiffs of the protections of the Rent Stabilization Code. We therefore affirm the order of the Appellate Division. 
 I. 
 The Neighborhood Based Cluster Transitional Residence Program (Transitional Residence Program), operated by the New York City Department of Homeless Services (DHS) until 2016, provided homeless families with temporary, emergency housing placements in privately owned apartments throughout New York City. Plaintiffs are formerly homeless individuals placed by DHS into apartments owned by certain defendants (the owners) under the auspices of the Transitional Residence Program. FN1 
 Between 2002 and 2008, the owners leased apartments to a for-profit service provider, defendant We All Care Inc., which then contracted with DHS to participate in the Transitional Residence Program. In 2008, DHS changed the terms of the Transitional Residence Program to require that service providers be nonprofit entities. Because it could no longer directly contract with DHS, beginning in 2009, We All Care subleased its apartments to defendant nonprofit Church Avenue Merchants and Block Association (CAMBA), which already had a separate contract with DHS as a service provider. Pursuant to the terms of its contract with DHS, CAMBA was required to accept any families that DHS referred to it on a 24-hour-a-day, 7-day-a-week basis, and to provide certain services, including, for example, temporary housing services, assessment services, social services, permanent housing preparation services, and childcare services. In exchange, DHS paid CAMBA a per diem rate of $107.49 per occupied apartment, per day. The contract further contemplated, by its plain terms, that a family was supposed to occupy an apartment for a maximum period of six months. Pursuant to its sublease agreement, CAMBA then paid rent to We All Care at a per diem rate of $75.50 per occupied apartment, per day upon its receipt of contract payments from DHS. CAMBA was the service provider in 2011 when plaintiffs were first placed by DHS into the owners' apartments. 
 Following the termination of its relationship with CAMBA in 2014, We All Care began subleasing its apartments to defendant nonprofit We Always Care Inc. We Always Care contracted with DHS as the service provider on substantially similar terms to DHS's agreement with CAMBA. We Always Care, pursuant to its sublease agreement, then paid We All Care $76.15 per occupied apartment, per day. The owners ceased participating in the Transitional Residence Program in 2015 and sought to remove plaintiffs from the apartments they had been occupying. 
 Plaintiffs commenced multiple, separate actions against defendants alleging, inter alia, that defendants had engaged in an illusory tenancy scheme intended to deprive plaintiffs of the protections of the Rent Stabilization Code and seeking, as relevant here, a declaration that they were rent-stabilized tenants and an order directing the owners to offer them vacancy leases for the units they had been occupying. FN2 Plaintiffs' actions were ultimately consolidated into this action. The owners thereafter moved for summary judgment dismissing plaintiffs' first, second, and third causes of action, all of which were premised on plaintiffs' illusory tenancy scheme theory. Supreme Court granted the owners' motion, concluding that plaintiffs lacked standing to seek vacancy leases because they were not tenants as defined by the Rent Stabilization Code. Certain plaintiffs appealed. 
 The Appellate Division affirmed on alternate grounds (206 AD3d 1014 [2d Dept 2022]). Assuming without deciding that plaintiffs had standing, the Appellate Division held that the owners demonstrated, as a matter of law, that they had not engaged in an illusory tenancy scheme ( see id. at 1016). The Court further rejected plaintiffs' claim that additional discovery was needed, concluding that plaintiffs' illusory tenancy claims would fail regardless of how certain alleged issues of fact were ultimately resolved ( see id. at 1018-1019). 
 One Justice dissented, and would have denied summary judgment, opining that there were [*3] issues of fact or a need for further discovery that precluded an award of summary judgment ( see generally id. at 1020-1029 [Duffy, J., dissenting]). The Appellate Division granted plaintiffs' motion for leave to appeal to this Court and certified the following question: "Was the decision and order of this Court dated June 29, 2022, properly made?" (2025 NY Slip Op 79882[U] [2d Dept 2025]). 
 II. 
 It is well-settled that the proponent of a summary judgment motion has the initial burden of making a prima facie showing that they are entitled to judgment as a matter of law ( see Alvarez v Prospect Hosp. , 68 NY2d 320, 324 [1986] [internal citations omitted]). If that showing is made, the burden shifts to the nonmoving party to establish the existence of triable issues of material fact ( see id. , citing Zuckerman v City of New York , 49 NY2d 557, 562 [1980]). Of course, the facts must be viewed in the light most favorable to the nonmoving party, but "bald, conclusory assertions or speculation" or the " 'shadowy semblance of an issue' are insufficient" to defeat the motion ( Stonehill Capital Mgt. LLC v Bank of the W. , 28 NY3d 439, 448 [2016], quoting S.J. Capelin Assoc. v Globe Mfg. Corp. , 34 NY2d 338, 341 [1974]). 
 III. 
 In New York City, the Rent Stabilization Law (Administrative Code of City of NY § 26-501 et seq. ) is administered by the Division of Housing and Community Renewal (DHCR), which promulgates regulations "for rent stabilization based on statutory criteria and by prohibiting owners of regulated units from charging more rent than those regulations allow" ( Matter of 160 E. 84th St. Assoc. LLC v New York State Div. of Hous. & Community Renewal , 43 NY3d 275, 278 [2024]). Those regulations are codified in the Rent Stabilization Code (9 NYCRR § 2520.1 et seq. ). Turning first to plaintiffs' standing under the Rent Stabilization Code, it is axiomatic that " '[w]hen presented with a question of statutory interpretation, our primary consideration is to ascertain and give effect to the intention of the [l]egislature' " (43 NY3d at 282, quoting Kuzmich v 50 Murray St. Acquisition LLC , 34 NY3d 84, 91 [2019]). Thus, " '[i]nasmuch as the clearest indicator of legislative intent is the statutory text, the starting point . . . must always be the language itself, giving effect to the plain meaning thereof' " ( id. , quoting Kuzmich , 34 NY3d at 90). Relevant here, "administrative regulations are generally subject to the same interpretive rules and canons of construction as statutes" ( Cruz v Banks , 45 NY3d 599, 605 [2026]). 
 Plaintiffs assert that they are entitled to vacancy leases pursuant to the Rent Stabilization Code as a remedy for the illusory tenancy scheme; however, we have never held that parties who are neither tenants nor subtenants, as those terms are defined in the Rent Stabilization Code, can bring claims arising under it, and we decline to do so on these facts. Thus, because they are neither tenants nor subtenants under the Rent Stabilization Code, plaintiffs lack standing to seek such relief. Tenant, as defined by the Rent Stabilization Code, is "[a]ny person or persons named on a lease as lessee or lessees, or who is or are a party or parties to a rental agreement and obligated to pay rent for the use or occupancy of a housing accommodation or is entitled to occupy the housing accommodation as a tenant pursuant to any other provision of this Code" (9 NYCRR 2520.6 [d]). Accordingly, to be considered tenants, plaintiffs are required to satisfy two elements: they must (1) be "named on a lease" as lessees or be "parties to a rental agreement" and (2) be "obligated to pay rent for the use or occupancy" of the apartments. As to the first requirement, plaintiffs are neither "named on a lease" nor "parties to a rental agreement." Rather, the relevant leases for the apartments occupied by plaintiffs were subleases between We All Care as the prime tenant and either CAMBA or We Always Care as the subtenant. As to the second requirement, plaintiffs did not pay rent and were not obligated to pay rent for the apartments they occupied. DHS, pursuant to [*4] its contracts with either CAMBA or We Always Care, paid the relevant service provider at a per diem rate for each occupied apartment per day. CAMBA or We Always Care then paid rent at a separate per diem rate to We All Care out of the money received from DHS as required by the terms of the sublease agreements. 
 Nor are plaintiffs subtenants within the meaning of the Rent Stabilization Code. A subtenant is "[a]ny person lawfully occupying the housing accommodation pursuant to an agreement with the tenant by authority of the lease or by virtue of rights afforded pursuant to section 226-b of the Real Property Law" (9 NYCRR 2520.6 [k]). Plaintiffs do not "have an agreement with the tenant"—We All Care—such that they can properly be considered subtenants. The sublease agreements between We All Care and CAMBA or We Always Care were entered into "in connection" with the agreements between DHS and CAMBA or We Always Care for the purpose of "provid[ing] apartment units on a temporary basis and related services" to "homeless families as part of" the Transitional Residence Program. For this reason, and contrary to the assertion by the dissent ( see dissent at 19-20), plaintiffs have no relationship with any party in the leasing chain of the type that would confer standing under the Rent Stabilization Code. 
 Many plaintiffs here have occupied their apartments for years, and it is undoubtedly true that they and their families have formed strong bonds with their neighbors and within their respective communities. Nor do we doubt that plaintiffs possess a genuine desire to remain in those apartments to maintain the employment and educational opportunities that stable housing has afforded them. That does not, however, transform plaintiffs into tenants or subtenants within the meaning of the Rent Stabilization Code. 
 IV. 
 Even if plaintiffs could assert claims under the Rent Stabilization Code, they still fail to raise a triable issue of material fact to overcome the owners' showing that they did not engage in an illusory tenancy scheme as a matter of law. leads.text:
Escrown LLC v Arepas NYC Corp. 
 2026 NY Slip Op 06949 
 November 24, 2026 
 Appellate Division, First Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 Escrown LLC, Plaintiff-Respondent, 
 v 
 Arepas NYC Corp., et al., Defendants-Appellants. 

 Decided and Entered: November 24, 2026 
 Index No. 655905/20|Appeal No. 7590|Case No. 2025-06582| 
 Before: Scarpulla, J.P., Shulman, Rosado, Michael, Hagler, JJ. 

 Sanchez & Associates, Goshen (Oscar Sanchez of counsel), for appellants. 
 Fox Rothschild LLP, New York (Brett A. Berman of counsel), for respondent. 

 [*1] 
 Appeal from order, Supreme Court, New York County (Lyle E. Frank, J.), entered on or about August 20, 2025, deemed appeal from judgment, same court and Justice, entered October 8, 2025, awarding plaintiff $587,238.40, unanimously modified, on the law, to vacate the award of prejudgment interest in the amount of $126,186.48, remand for further proceedings consistent with this order, and otherwise affirmed, without costs. 
 In this action for breach of a lease, Supreme Court properly awarded damages to plaintiff for the amounts of rent and additional rent accruing under the lease despite its delay in delivering possession of the premises. 
 Initially, contrary to defendants' contention, the appeal from the August 20, 2025 order assessing damages does not bring up for review the court's September 17, 2024 order granting summary judgment as to liability in plaintiff's favor ( see CPLR 5501[a] [1], [c]). Although defendants purport to appeal from both orders, defendants did not file a notice of appeal from the summary judgment order (CPLR 5501[c]) nor did they file a notice of appeal from the final judgment entered October 8, 2025. 
 In any event, the court properly found that defendants were liable for breach of the lease. Although Real Property Law § 223-a implies a right to rescind a lease for failure to give possession, the statute expressly permits the parties to waive its application, as the parties elected to do here under section 3.02(b) of the lease. The liability disclaimer, in section 3.02(b) of the lease , for failure to give possession, did not render the lease obligations illusory , but "may reasonably be read to be limited to instances of a holdover, construction problems or regulatory failures, outside [the landlord's] control" ( Matter of Daval-Ogden, LLC v Highbridge House Ogden, LLC , 103 AD3d 422, 422 [1st Dept 2013]). 
 Here, defendants did not establish any intentional conduct by plaintiff that precluded defendant tenant's use of the premises. Plaintiff's work in the premises was contemplated by the lease, and the pandemic-related construction delays were largely "outside [the landlord's] control" ( id. ). Defendant's affirmative defenses seeking to avoid the application of section 3.02(b) did not preclude an award of damages in plaintiff's favor, because plaintiff submitted competent evidence to establish damages at the hearing. 
 Additionally , an award of damages in plaintiff's favor was not precluded by plaintiff's refusal to provide the keys to the premises until defendants provided the requisite insurance. Section 3.02(a) of the lease provides that "in the event that Tenant has not complied with the insurance requirements set forth in this lease . . . Landlord shall not have tendered possession of the Premises to tenant." The record reflects that defendants' insurance broker acknowledged that the correct insurance coverage was not procured at any point after possession was deemed given. 
 [*2] 
 Plaintiff was entitled to full enforcement of the guaranty until at least 36 months after the rent commencement date, "whether or not any portion of the Premises is occupied." Supreme Court also properly declined to limit damages against defendant guarantor under Administrative Code of City of NY § 22-1005 (the guaranty law). Defendants acknowledged that they never took possession of the premises, which precluded them from establishing the guaranty law's requirement that defendant tenant "was required to cease serving patrons food or beverage for on-premises consumption or to cease operation under executive order number 202.3" (Administrative Code § 22-1005[1][a]). 
 In addition to the rent and additional rent, Supreme Court properly found that plaintiff was entitled to recover the broker's fees incurred in reletting the premises under section 18.02(b) of the lease. Defendants' argument that plaintiff was not entitled to collect the broker's fees associated with the new tenant's lease because it never paid the original broker fee is not supported by the record. In any event, plaintiff's purported failure to pay the broker fee associated with defendants' lease does not preclude recovery of the separately incurred fees associated with reletting the premises under section 18.02(b). 
 However, the award of $126,186.48 in prejudgment interest is not sufficiently supported by the hearing record ( see Chrysler E. Bldg., L.L.C. v Keenwawa, Inc. , 217 AD3d 494, 495 [1st Dept 2023]). Under section 1.04(c), plaintiff is entitled to interest on payments when due, at a rate of "the lesser of (i) the base rate from time to time announced by JPMorgan Chase, N.A. (or such other bank in New York, New York, as shall be designated by Landlord in a notice to Tenant) to be in effect at its principal office in New York, New York plus 10%" or the statutory maximum of 16% ( see Banking Law § 14-a[1]). At the damages hearing, however, the representative from plaintiff's managing agent's office testified that he had not personally calculated the interest charged, and he did not know if the calculation was made based on multiple periods or one final interest calculation. 
 [*3] 
 On this record, plaintiff did not meet its burden to establish that it was entitled to prejudgment interest of $126,186.48, which constituted more than 20% of the total $596,904.79 contract damages requested at the hearing. On remand, the prejudgment interest award should be supported by competent, nonconclusory evidence showing how the calculation was made, at what intervals the relevant interest rate was applied, and if any interest was compounded ( see Chrysler E. Bldg., L.L.C. , 217 AD3d at 495; see also Halgene Watch Ltd. v Alex Capital Fund, LLC , 242 AD3d 413, 414 [1st Dept 2025] [damages not established where "the spreadsheet, even if it could be said to reflect plaintiffs' member's knowledge of the facts, obscures the precise prime rate on which plaintiffs relied to calculate the amounts outstanding, which appears to have varied from the actual prime rate in effect for certain intervals"]). 
 We have considered the remaining contentions and find them unavailing. 
 THIS CONSTITUTES THE DECISION AND ORDER OF THE SUPREME COURT, APPELLATE DIVISION, FIRST DEPARTMENT. 
 ENTERED: November 24, 2026

Torres v 120 Broadway Holdings, LLC 
 2026 NY Slip Op 06971 
 November 24, 2026 
 Appellate Division, First Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 Rafael Torres, et al., Plaintiffs-Appellants, 
 v 
 120 Broadway Holdings, LLC, et al., Defendants-Respondents. 
 Miroslaw Chrostowski, Plaintiff-Appellant, 
 v 
 120 Broadway Holdings, LLC, et al., Defendants-Respondents. 
 Andrei Percuin, Plaintiff-Appellant, 
 v 
 120 Broadway, LLC, et al., Third-Party Defendants-Respondents, Tri-State Dismantling Corp., Defendant. [And Third-Party Actions] 

 Decided and Entered: November 24, 2026 
 Index No. 159374/18|Appeal No. 7575-7576|Case No. 2025-03655 2025-03669| 
 Before: Manzanet-Daniels, J.P., Webber, Mendez, González, Rodriguez, JJ. 

 Shulman & Hill, PLLC, New York (Timothy W. Norton of counsel), for Rafael Torres and Marta Cecilia Benites Jaramillo, appellants. 
 Roth & Khalife LLP, New York (Ronald H. Roth of counsel), for Miroslaw Chrostowski, appellant. 
 Pollack, Pollack, Isaac & DeCicco, LLP, New York (Jillian Rosen of counsel), for Andrei Perciun, appellant. 
 Wood Smith Henning & Berman LLP, New York (Matthew D. Lavoie of counsel), for 120 Broadway, LLC, 120 Broadway Holdings, LLC, 120 Broadway Properties, LLC, 120 Broadway Condominium and Silverstein Properties, Inc., respondents. 
 Ropers Majeski P.C., New York (Jonathan P. Sellers of counsel), for JRM Construction Management, LLC, respondent. 
 Gartner + Bloom, PC, New York (Lee Tarr of counsel), for Rite-Way Internal Removal, Inc., respondent. 

 [*1] 
 Order, Supreme Court, New York County (Lyle E. Frank, J.), entered on or about May 19, 2025, which denied the motion of plaintiffs Rafael Torres and Marta Cecilia Benitez Jaramillo for summary judgment on their Labor Law § 240(1) claim, unanimously affirmed, without costs. Order, same court and Justice, entered on or about May 30, 2025, which granted the motions of defendants 120 Broadway LLC, 120 Broadway Holdings, LLC, 120 Broadway Condominium, 120 Broadway Properties, LLC, Silverstein Properties, Inc., JRM Construction Management LLC, and Rite-Way Internal Removal, Inc. for summary judgment dismissing the respective complaints of plaintiffs Torres, Andrei Percuin, and Miroslaw Chrostowski as against them, and denied the motion of Percuin for summary judgment on his Labor Law §§ 240(1), 241(6), 200 and common-law negligence claims, unanimously modified, on the law, to deny defendants' motions, except for defendant Rite-Way Internal Removal, Inc.; grant the motion of plaintiff Percuin for summary judgment on his Labor Law § 241(6) claim predicated on Industrial Code (12 NYCRR) § 23-3.3(b) and (c); and otherwise affirmed, without costs. 
 In this Labor Law action stemming from a ceiling collapse, plaintiffs Torres, Chrostowski, and Percuin were laborers employed by third-party defendant asbestos removal company, ETS Contracting. Plaintiffs were working on the 40th floor of a building at 120 Broadway in Manhattan at the time of the ceiling collapse. Defendants 120 Broadway LLC, 120 Broadway Holdings, LLC, 120 Broadway Condominium, and 120 Broadway Properties, LLC are the owners and/or lessees of the building, and defendant Silverstein Properties, Inc. manages the building. Silverstein, on behalf of 120 Broadway Holdings, entered into a construction manager agreement with defendant JRM Construction Management LLC for a multi-floor gut renovation. JRM hired a number of subcontractors, including the demolition company Rite-Way Internal Removal, Inc. Silverstein entered into an agreement with ETS for asbestos abatement. 
 Plaintiffs began their work on the 40th floor on July 23, 2018. Prior to the arrival of ETS at the project, Rite-Way performed demolition work on the 40th floor, which was finished on July 11, 2018. At the time of the collapse, plaintiffs had finished their asbestos abatement work and were disassembling their decontamination unit when the ceiling suddenly collapsed upon them. 
 [*2] 
 Defendant Rite-Way is not a proper Labor Law defendant, nor are the common-law claims against it viable. Rite-Way's contract was to perform specific demolition as listed on drawings provided to it by JRM. Its contract specifically excludes any shoring, and it finished its work approximately two weeks prior to the accident ( see Bell v Bengomo Realty, Inc ., 36 AD3d 479, 480 [1st Dept 2007]). There is no evidence in the record that Rite-Way deviated from JRM's instructions, nor was it responsible under the contract to provide continuing inspections of the worksite for stability ( see id. ; see also Klewinowski v City of New York , 103 AD3d 547, 548 [1st Dept 2013], lv denied 21 NY3d 855 [2013] [contractor who installed temporary light pole not a Labor Law defendant where it did not remain on site after installation and had no contractual duty to maintain it]). 
 JRM, however, is a proper Labor Law defendant. While its contract with the building owner was one for construction management, the terms of the agreement required it to coordinate and oversee its subcontractors, as well as take reasonable precautions for the safety of "employees on the Work and other persons who may be affected thereby." No other general contractor was present, JRM held authority to control activity at the work site including stopping work due to unsafe practices, and it was JRM who turned the site over to plaintiffs' employer, the asbestos abatement contractor ( see Walls v Turner Constr. Co., 4 NY3d 861, 863-864 [2005]; see also Naughton v City of New York, 94 AD3d 1, 7, 9-10 [1st Dept 2012]). While JRM argues that it was not responsible for supervising plaintiffs' employer, it was responsible for the safety of the site ( see Calle v 686 Broadway Realty, LLC , 247 AD3d 521, 522 [1st Dept 2026]). Defendants' argument that they did not control the site at the time of the accident because asbestos abatement was ongoing is unpersuasive ( see Moracho v Open Door Family Med. Ctr., Inc. , 74 AD3d 657, 658 [1st Dept 2010]; Perez v Society of N.Y. Hosp ., 225 AD2d 467, 467 [1st Dept 1996]). Moreover, ample time existed after demolition and prior to turning the area over for asbestos abatement to inspect the area and shore the partially demolished ceiling. 
 [*3] 
 Issues of fact as to whether the collapse of the ceiling was foreseeable bar summary resolution of plaintiffs' Labor Law § 240(1) claims. While defendants assert that there were no visual signs of cracking or sagging and that the collapse was due to a preexisting construction defect, the ceiling had been partially demolished, and large sections of it and other elements in the room had been removed ( see Jones v 414 Equities LLC , 57 AD3d 65 [1st Dept 2008]). Issues of fact as to foreseeability also preclude summary judgment on plaintiffs' common-law negligence and Labor Law § 200 claims ( see Bernardez v 70 Franklin Place LLC , 205 AD3d 642, 643 [1st Dept 2022]). Defendants are not entitled to dismissal of those claims, however, as they failed to make a prima facie showing of entitlement to that relief ( see Garcia v Soho AOA Owner, LLC , 234 AD3d 572, 573 [1st Dept 2025]). Defendants also failed to show that, as a matter of law, the collapse was caused by a latent defect, incapable of discovery through inspection (see Bentley v All—Star, Inc ., 179 AD3d 618, 618—619 [1st Dept 2020]). 
 Plaintiff Percuin is entitled to summary judgment on his Labor Law § 241(6) claim predicated on Industrial Code (12 NYCRR) § 23-3.3(b) and (c). The record does not support defendants' claims that inspections were performed during the demolition work. The witnesses who testified as to inspections or a walk-through did not participate in that process. Nothing in the record demonstrates that inspections were held ( see Vasquez v Urbahn Assoc. Inc. , 79 AD3d 493, 494 [1st Dept. 2010]; Perez v ZZZ Carpentry, Inc. , 248 AD3d 1065, 1068-1069 [2d Dept 2026]). 
 THIS CONSTITUTES THE DECISION AND ORDER OF THE SUPREME COURT, APPELLATE DIVISION, FIRST DEPARTMENT. 
 ENTERED: November 24, 2026

leads.text:
U.S. Bank Trust, N.A. v Joseph 
 2026 NY Slip Op 06972 
 November 24, 2026 
 Appellate Division, First Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 U.S. Bank Trust, N.A., Plaintiff-Respondent, 
 v 
 Andre Joseph, et al., Defendants, West Fork Funding, L.L.C., Defendant-Appellant. 

 Decided and Entered: November 24, 2026 
 Index No. 809664/21|Appeal No. 7560|Case No. 2025-03871| 
 Before: Manzanet-Daniels, J.P., Kennedy, Mendez, González, Rodriguez, JJ. 

 Rosenberg Fortuna Filosa & Laitman, LLP, Garden City (Anthony R. Filosa of counsel), for appellant. 
 Day Pitney LLP, New York (Christina A. Livorsi of counsel), for respondent. 

 [*1] 
 Order, Supreme Court, Bronx County (Naita A. Semaj), entered on or about April 24, 2025, which, to the extent appealed from as limited by the briefs, denied defendant West Fork Funding, L.L.C.'s CPLR 3211(a)(8) motion to dismiss the complaint and granted the CPLR 306-b cross-motion by plaintiff, U.S. Bank Trust, N.A., to extend the time in which to serve defendant, unanimously affirmed, with costs. 
 The motion court providently granted plaintiff's cross-motion in the interest of justice and denied defendant's motion to dismiss. 
 This action was not time-barred and thus, the court had the authority to entertain plaintiff's cross-motion for an extension of time in which to serve defendant West Fork ( cf. Schwartz v Chan , 162 AD3d 408, 409 [1st Dept 2018], lv denied 32 NY3d 904 [2018]). Plaintiff adequately demonstrated that the statute of limitations did not expire. Although the original note holder, nonparty BAC Home Loans Servicing, LP commenced an action in 2009 in which it declared the entire balance due, it and the borrower entered into a modification agreement on April 1, 2010, that allowed the borrower to resume monthly payments, thereby de-accelerating the loan ( see Goshen Mtge., LLC v DePalma , 186 AD3d 1203, 1206 [2d Dept 2020], lv denied 37 NY3d 903 [2021]). Even if plaintiff is estopped from contesting a later note holder's acceleration of the loan on July 24, 2015, when that note holder, though found to have lacked standing, brought a second action to foreclose upon the same mortgage, plaintiff still timely brought this action on July 12, 2021, which was within the six-year limitation period ( see id. ; Ditech Fin. LLC v Temple , 252 AD3d 180, 186-187 [3d Dept 2026]). And the Foreclosure Abuse Prevention Act (L 2022, ch 821) does not bar bilateral agreements to this effect ( see HSBC Bank USA, N.A. v Nicholas , 252 AD3d 201, 204 [1st Dept 2026]). 
 To the extent West Fork argues that it lacked constructive notice of the modification agreement, which it asserts was not recorded, this Court declines to consider the argument, as it was not raised before the motion court ( see Chateau D'If Corp. v City of New York , 219 AD2d 205, 209 [1st Dept 1996], lv denied 88 NY2d 811 [1996]), and, in any event, whether the modification agreement was recorded is not evident from the record. 
 [*2] 
 Turning to the merits of plaintiff's cross-motion, any lack of diligence was not so significant as to constitute a major factor warranting against granting the cross-motion in the interest of justice ( see Leader v Maroney, Ponzini & Spencer , 97 NY2d 95, 105 [2001]). Plaintiff brought this action on July 12, 2021, and included West Fork as a defendant based on West Fork's acquisition of the property pursuant to a judicial sale following a condominium lien foreclosure action against the borrower. The deed for the sale listed West Fork's address as 305 Broadway, Suite 200, New York, New York, where plaintiff sought service. The affidavit of service stated that West Fork was served at that address through service on Matthew Mannion, identified as West Fork's owner. At the time, plaintiff had no reason to believe that the address was incorrect or that Mannion was not an owner of West Fork. Although West Fork argues that plaintiff was long aware of the address of West Fork's sole member, Adam Plotch, the evidence West Fork pointed to consisted of papers submitted by Plotch in the prior action on the same loan brought by a prior note holder, not by plaintiff. West Fork points to no evidence that plaintiff, as opposed to that prior note holder, had this information. 
 Plaintiff also adequately established the meritorious nature of its cause of action ( see Leader , 97 NY2d at 105). 
 Finally, plaintiff adequately showed that West Fork would not be substantially prejudiced by the extension ( see id . at 106). West Fork learned about the action no later than August 23, 2021, when it filed its original answer, a little over a month after the action was commenced ( cf. Williams v Nassau County Med. Ctr. , 6 NY3d 531, 539, 539 n 3 [2006]). West Fork has not adequately explained how it would be adversely affected by the short delay in serving it. 
 In view of the foregoing, this Court does not reach West Fork's remaining contentions. 
 THIS CONSTITUTES THE DECISION AND ORDER OF THE SUPREME COURT, APPELLATE DIVISION, FIRST DEPARTMENT. 
 ENTERED: November 24, 2026

leads.caseName: Zavala Family Inc. v. Super. Ct.
leads.text:
Filed 11/24/26 
CERTIFIED FOR PUBLICATION 
 
IN THE COURT OF APPEAL OF THE STATE OF CALIFORNIA 
 
SECOND APPELLATE DISTRICT 
 
DIVISION EIGHT 
 
ZAVALA FAMILY INC.  et al.,  
 Petitioners; 
 v. 
THE SUPERIOR COURT OF 
LOS ANGELES COUNTY,  
 Respondent; 
LOS ANGELES COUNTY 
METROPOLITAN 
TRANSPORTATION 
AUTHORITY,  
 Real Party in Interest. 
B352255 
Los Angeles County 
Super. Ct. No. 25VECV05690 
 
PETITION for a writ of mandate from an order of the 
Superior Court of Los Angeles County.  Shirley K. Watkins, 
Judge.  Petition denied. 
California Eminent Domain Law Group, Glenn L. Block; 
Pierson Ferdinand and Paul J. Beard II, for Petitioners. 
No appearance for Respondent. 
FBT Gibbons, Keith E. McCullough, S. Christopher Yoo 
and Andrew M. Jones for Real Party in Interest. 
2 
 _________________________ 
We encounter the intersection of eminent domain and 
unlawful detainer.  Real party Los Angeles Metropolitan 
Transportation Authority (Metro) acquired, under threat of 
condemnation, real property that petitioners Zavala Family Inc. 
and Jose Zavala had leased to run a scrap metal recycling 
business.  When petitioners remained on the premises after 
Metro’s acquisition, Metro sought possession of the premises 
through an unlawful detainer action.  The parties dispute 
whether the unlawful detainer action can proceed, or whether 
Metro must instead seek possession through procedures set forth 
in the Eminent Domain Law (Code Civ. Proc., § 1230.010 et seq.).  
(Undesignated statutory references are to the Code of Civil 
Procedure.)  The trial court, rejecting the arguments in 
petitioners’ demurrer, concluded Metro’s unlawful detainer action 
could proceed.  Petitioners seek a writ of mandate directing the 
trial court to sustain their demurrer.  We deny their petition.  We 
do not conclude that an unlawful detainer action will always be 
an appropriate method for determining a tenant’s possessory 
interest in real property acquired under threat of condemnation; 
rather, we reject petitioners’ limited arguments against the use of 
unlawful detainer in this case.  
I. 
We take the facts from the unlawful detainer complaint 
and consider, for context, undisputed facts admitted in the writ 
petition pleadings or reflected in documents attached to Metro’s 
March 25, 2026 unopposed motion for judicial notice, which we 
grant.  We deny two other requests for judicial notice:  one 
petitioners filed February 9, 2026, seeking notice of filings in 
other pending eminent domain actions, and one Metro filed 
3 
February 17, 2026, seeking notice of petitioners’ answer to the 
complaint.  The documents attached to these two earlier requests 
do not bear upon our resolution of the issues presented in this 
writ proceeding.  (OneTaste Inc. v. Netflix, Inc. (2025) 
116 Cal.App.5th 174, 194 [denial of judicial notice proper for 
irrelevant and unnecessary documents].)   
Since at least April 2017, petitioners have operated a scrap 
metal recycling business on a parcel of real property located in 
Van Nuys, California.  Petitioners leased these premises from 
Franz J. Neuwirth and Gretchen V. Newell, Trustees of The Etzel 
Trust UTA January 7, 2021 (collectively, “Etzel Trust”).  The 
written lease is not in the record before us.  
 In September 2023, Metro sent petitioners written notice of 
its intent to acquire the premises to construct the East San 
Fernando Valley Light Rail Transit Project.  The notice informed 
petitioners of their potential eligibility for relocation benefits 
under the Uniform Relocation Assistance and Real Property 
Acquisition Policies Act of 1970 (42 U.S.C. § 4601 et seq.).  The 
notice stated, in bolded text, that petitioners “will not be required 
to move without at least 90 days advance written notice of the 
day by which [they] must vacate.” 
 In February 2024, Metro sent petitioners written notice 
that it had made an offer to purchase the premises in December 
2023 and again advised petitioners of their potential eligibility 
for relocation benefits.  The notice advised, in bolded text, “you 
are not requested or required to move as a result of this notice” 
and if Metro “acquires the property, you will be given at least 90 
days written notice before you will be required to move.” 
 Four months later, in June 2024, the Etzel Trust 
contracted to sell the real property to Metro.  The Etzel Trust 
4 
conveyed the property to Metro through a grant deed recorded on 
January 23, 2025. 
 About a month later, on February 21, 2025, Metro sent 
petitioners a 30-day notice to vacate the premises.  Subsequently, 
it sent a second 30-day notice on March 14, 2025, and a third 30-
day notice on May 14, 2025.  Petitioners continued to occupy the 
premises. 
 Approximately five months after the third notice, on 
October 6, 2025, Metro filed an unlawful detainer action seeking 
immediate possession of the premises.  The complaint alleged 
Metro “acquired the Premises for public use” and, consequently, 
by operation of section 1265.110, “any leasehold interest in the 
Premises held by Defendants was . . . terminated effective on 
[Metro’s] acquisition of the Premises” in January 2025.  The 
complaint alleged that because petitioners have not entered into 
a new lease or other agreement with Metro permitting their 
continued occupation of the premises, petitioners “became a 
holdover tenant without any leasehold interest” subject to 
eviction under section 1161, subdivision (1). 
 Three days later, Metro filed a complaint in eminent 
domain to “acquire improvements . . . located on” the premises 
petitioners occupied to further “the East San Fernando Valley 
Light Rail Transit Project.”  
 Petitioners demurred to the unlawful detainer complaint.  
Petitioners asserted the trial court lacked jurisdiction (see 
§ 430.10, subd. (a)) over the premises at issue in the unlawful 
detainer case because section 1230.050 operated to confer 
exclusive jurisdiction over the premises to the eminent domain 
court.  Petitioners also asserted the complaint failed to state facts 
sufficient to constitute a cause of action (§ 430.10, subd. (e)) 
5 
because, in their view, section 1265.110, which terminates a lease 
upon acquisition of property for public use, only terminates a 
tenant’s liability for rent, and does not affect a tenant’s 
possessory rights.  In petitioners’ view, Metro needed to seek 
possession of the premises in accord with the Eminent Domain 
Law and its procedural safeguards, most notably section 
1255.410, which concerns prejudgment possession.  Finally, 
petitioners asserted the complaint must be dismissed because the 
eminent domain and unlawful detainer cases concerned the same 
parties and the same causes of action.  (§ 430.10, subd. (c).)   
 The trial court overruled the demurrer.  
 Petitioners filed a petition for writ of mandate in this court 
requesting that we vacate the trial court’s order and instruct that 
court to instead sustain the demurrer without leave to amend.  
Metro filed a preliminary opposition.  Petitioners filed a 
preliminary reply.  
We temporarily stayed the unlawful detainer action and 
directed the trial court to show cause why the petitioners’ 
requested relief should not be granted.  Thereafter, Metro filed a 
return, and petitioners filed a reply. 
II. 
 “ ‘The standard of review for an order overruling a 
demurrer is de novo.  The reviewing court accepts as true all facts 
properly pleaded in the complaint in order to determine whether 
the demurrer should be overruled.  [Citation.]’  [Citation.]  We 
must also consider matters that are properly the subject of 
judicial notice.”  (Big Valley Band of Pomo Indians v. Superior 
Court (2005) 133 Cal.App.4th 1185, 1190.)  “We do not accept as 
true the pleader’s deductions, contentions, or conclusions of law, 
as this court must decide questions of law independently.”  (Doe 
6 
3, Family Services Organization v. Superior Court (2025) 
110 Cal.App.5th 571, 582 (Doe 3).)   
 “To the extent the trial court’s ruling on a demurrer 
presents a question of statutory interpretation, we will interpret 
the statute de novo as well.  [Citation.]  Our task in interpreting 
a statute is to determine the Legislature’s intent in order to 
effectuate the law’s purpose, first by looking at the plain and 
commonsense meaning of the statutory language.  [Citations.]  
We examine the language in the context of the statutory scheme 
as a whole to determine the law’s scope and purpose, and to 
harmonize the various parts of the enactment.  [Citation.]  ‘If the 
language of the statute is ambiguous, we “can look to legislative 
history [citation] and to rules or maxims of construction” to 
resolve the ambiguity.  [Citation.]’ ”  (Doe 3, supra, 
110 Cal.App.5th at p. 582.)   
 In this proceeding, petitioners renew several of their 
demurrer arguments for why Metro cannot proceed by unlawful 
detainer.  That is, petitioners assert section 1230.050 requires a 
condemning entity to secure possession of any property taken for 
public use through the Eminent Domain Law, section 1265.110 
cannot authorize an unlawful detainer action because it does not 
terminate a lease, and Metro must comply with section 
1255.410’s procedures to obtain possession.  To the extent 
petitioners’ demurrer raised other arguments against an 
unlawful detainer proceeding, including that dismissal is 
required under section 430.10, subdivision (c), because of another 
action pending, we do not address them.  (See Golden Door 
Properties, LLC v. County of San Diego (2020) 50 Cal.App.5th 
467, 554–555 [“ ‘Even when our review . . . “is de novo, it is 
limited to issues which have been adequately raised and 
7 
supported in [the appellant’s opening] brief” ’ ”and “ ‘ “[i]ssues not 
raised in an appellant’s brief are deemed” ’ ” forfeited]; see also 
In re Reno (2012) 55 Cal.4th 428, 458, fn. 15 [writ review is 
typically limited to only those issues properly raised].)  We 
emphasize, then, the limited nature of the petition, its challenge 
to the unlawful detainer process, and its arguments for relief.  
Just by way of example, petitioners have not advanced, and we 
will not address, arguments against the unlawful detainer 
process based on Metro’s simultaneous seeking of improvements 
in eminent domain or those improvements’ existence, nature, and 
relationship to the acquired premises.  (Cf. Chhour v. Community 
Redevelopment Agency (1996) 46 Cal.App.4th 273, 282–283.) 
A. 
 Petitioners assert that under section 1230.050 and, in 
particular, under the Law Revision Commission’s comment to 
that section, an eminent domain court has exclusive jurisdiction 
to determine possession of property acquired for public use and 
that Metro’s unlawful detainer action is, for that reason, 
impermissible.  Section 1230.050 grants the court presiding over 
an eminent domain action “the power” to “[d]etermine the right to 
possession of the property, as between the plaintiff and the 
defendant, in accordance with” the Eminent Domain Law and to 
“[e]nforce any of its orders for possession by appropriate process.”  
(§ 1230.050, subds. (a)–(b); see § 1230.010.)  The Law Revision 
Commission’s comment explains that, “[i]n general,” section 
1230.050 “codifies judicial decisions which hold that, after an 
eminent domain proceeding is begun, the court in which that 
proceeding is pending has the exclusive power to determine the

NOT FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST'S HAWAI#I REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER 
Electronically Filed 
Intermediate Court of Appeals 
CAAP-24-0000649 
24-NOV-2026 
08:00 AM 
Dkt. 97 SO 
NO. CAAP-24-0000649 
IN THE INTERMEDIATE COURT OF APPEALS 
OF THE STATE OF 
HAWAI#I 
ONE WAILEA DEVELOPMENT LLC, Appellant-Appellant, v.
MAUI PLANNING COMMISSION, Appellee-Appellee
and WAILEA SF-S PARTNERS LP, Appellee/Intervenor-Appellee 
APPEAL FROM THE CIRCUIT COURT OF THE SECOND CIRCUIT 
(CASE NO. 2CCV-23-0000154) 
SUMMARY DISPOSITION ORDER 
(By: Leonard, Presiding Judge, Hiraoka and Guidry, JJ.) 
The Maui County 
Planning Commission granted a Special 
Management Area Use 
Permit to One Wailea Development LLC in 
June 1999. The Planning Commission decided to "close and/or 
terminate" the Permit on February 14, 2023. LLC appealed the 
Planning Commission's Findings of Fact, Conclusions of Law, 
Decision and Order Closing Subject SMA Permit SM1 1999/0010 to 
the Circuit Court of the Second Circuit. The circuit court 
affirmed the Decision and Order, granted the Planning 
Commission's motion for sanctions, and entered a Final Judgment.
1 
LLC filed this secondary appeal. We affirm. 
In May 1999, Michael J. Szymanski  contracted to buy 
21.3 acres of real Property on Maui from Wailea Resort Company. 
Szymanski then formed LLC; he is its sole member and manager. 
Szymanski planned to use LLC to develop the Property into twenty 
single-family home lots. 
1 The Honorable Kirstin M. Hamman presided.  
 
NOT FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST'S HAWAI#I REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER 
The Property is located in a Coastal Zone Management 
Special Management Area (SMA). Development in an SMA requires a 
permit. Hawaii Revised Statutes (HRS) § 205A-28 (2017). LLC 
applied to the Maui County Planning Department for an SMA use 
permit in June 1999. The Planning Commission's SMA Rules 
required the applicant to provide "documentation of ownership or 
authorization by the owners of the parcel on which the proposed 
action is to occur[.]" SMA Rules § 12-202-12(c)(2)(A).
2  LLC's 
application included a letter from Wailea Resort Co. authorizing 
LLC to apply for the SMA use permit. 
By letter dated November 24, 1999, the Planning 
Department informed LLC that the Planning Commission had approved 
its permit application, subject to conditions. LLC had to start 
construction by November 30, 2001, and construction had to be 
completed within five years. 
Beginning in October 2001 LLC asked for, and received, 
several extensions of the deadline to begin construction because 
Szymanski was "working with the seller to complete the sale" of 
the Property. 
The Szymanski-Wailea Resort Co. transaction did not go 
well. In July 2002, Title Guaranty Escrow Services filed an
Interpleader Action for funds it held in escrow. Title Guar. 
Escrow Servs., Inc. v. Wailea Resort Co., 146 Hawai#i 34, 38, 456 
P.3d 107, 111 (2019) (Title Guaranty). Szymanski and Wailea 
2 SMA Rules § 12-202-12 (eff. Sept. 28, 1997) provided: 
(c) Assessment applications shall be filed in
accordance with the following: 
. . . . 
(2) Any applicant seeking an assessment shall submit
an application form, provided by the department,
to the central coordinating agency. The 
application shall require the following
information and documentation: 
(A) Identification of the applicant along with
documentation of ownership or
authorization by the owners of the parcel
on which the proposed action is to
occur[.] 
2 
NOT FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST'S HAWAI#I REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER 
Resort Co. filed cross-claims. Id. Each claimed the other had 
breached their Land Sales Contract. 
In September 2002 LLC asked for a 90-day extension of 
the deadline to complete construction because it was in "the 
final stages of closing the transaction and are awaiting the 
partial mortgage release from the seller's Japanese lender." The 
Planning Department stated it would hold LLC's request "in 
abeyance until December 31, 2002, however, 
this will be the last deferral to be granted. After this date 
the request will be forwarded to the Maui Planning Commission for 
appropriate action." 
In December 2002 LLC asked for another extension of the 
deadline to complete construction. In January 2003 the Planning 
Department asked Wailea Resort Co. whether it continued to 
authorize LLC to proceed to develop the Property. In February 
2003 LLC's attorney told the Planning Department about the 
Interpleader Action and opined that LLC was likely to "obtain a 
decree of specific performance requiring [Wailea Resort Co.] to 
comply with the Contract and convey the [P]roperty to Szymanski." 
It appears that the Planning Department took no further action 
pending resolution of the Interpleader Action. 
In 2004 the trial court presiding over the Interpleader 
Action granted summary judgment on Szymanski's and Wailea 
Resort Co.'s cross-claims. The court ruled that Szymanski 
breached the Land Sales Contract and was not entitled to specific 
performance by Wailea Resort Co. The 2004 Summary Judgment was 
certified as final under Hawai#i Rules of Civil Procedure (HRCP) 
Rule 54(b). Szymanski appealed. 
We affirmed. Title Guar. 
Escrow Servs., Inc. v. Szymanski, No. 27254, 2009 WL 1112604 
(Haw. App. Apr. 27, 2009) (SDO), cert. rejected
, 2009 WL 2974724 
(Haw. Sept. 17, 2009). The only issue remaining was who should 
receive the interpleaded funds. 
Szymanski nevertheless continued to challenge the 2004 
Summary Judgment. He moved to vacate the 2004 Summary Judgment, 
arguing the judge who entered it should have recused. See Title 
Guaranty
, 146 Hawai#i at 39, 456 P.3d at 112. The motion was 
denied. Id.
 at 40, 456 P.3d at 113. Szymanski moved for 
3 
NOT FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST'S HAWAI#I REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER 
reconsideration. Id. Reconsideration was denied. Id.
Szymanski appealed. We affirmed. Title Guar. Escrow Servs., 
Inc. v. Wailea Resort Co., No. CAAP–12–0000711, 2016 WL 4555771 
(Haw. App. Aug. 31, 2016) (mem. op.), cert. rejected, 2017 WL 
127710 (Haw. Jan. 12, 2017), cert. rejected, 2018 WL 5817276 
(Haw. Nov. 7, 2018), cert. denied. sub nom., Szymanski v. Wailea 
Resort Co., 583 U.S. 827, 138 S. Ct. 164, 199 L. Ed. 2d 39 
(2017). 
Undaunted, "Szymanski filed yet another motion to 
vacate" the 2004 Summary Judgment based on the trial judge's 
failure to recuse. Title Guaranty, 146 Hawai#i at 41, 456 P.3d 
at 114. 
The motion was denied. Id. at 42, 456 P.3d at 115. 
Szymanski appealed. 
We affirmed. Title Guar. Escrow Servs., 
Inc. v. Wailea Resort Co., Nos. CAAP-14-0001138 and 
CAAP-16-0000034, 2018 WL 3198379 (Haw. App. June 29, 2018) (SDO), 
aff'd in part, vacated in part, 146 Hawai#i 34, 456 P.3d 107 
(2019). 
On certiorari, the supreme court affirmed the denial of 
the motion to vacate the 2004 Summary Judgment. Title Guaranty, 
146 Hawai#i at 46, 456 P.3d at 119 (holding that "the ICA did not 
err in applying the law of the case doctrine with respect to 
Szymanski's 2014 Renewed Motion to Vacate Judge Loo's 2004 
Summary Judgment Orders that again asserted Judge Loo should have 
been disqualified"). The 2019 Title Guaranty decision 
conclusively affirmed that Szymanski breached the Land Sales 
Contract and was not entitled to specific performance by Wailea 
Resort Co. The supreme court also held that we erred by 
affirming the circuit court's disbursal of the escrowed funds to 
Wailea Resort Co., and remanded to the circuit court for 
disposition of the funds. Id. at 48-49, 456 P.3d at 121-22. 
On October 6, 2020, the Planning Department notified 
LLC it had determined that LLC had neither an ownership interest 
in, nor authorization from Wailea Resort Co. to develop, the 
Property. The Planning Department closed LLC's Permit. 
LLC requested a contested case hearing. A hearing 
officer was appointed. The hearing officer proposed findings of 
fact and conclusions of law, and recommended a decision. The 
4
 
NOT FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST'S HAWAI#I REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER 
Planning Commission adopted the hearing officer's report and 
recommendation, and entered the Decision and Order on 
February 14, 2023. LLC requested reconsideration. The Planning 
Commission denied reconsideration. 
LLC appealed to the circuit court. The circuit court 
affirmed the Decision and Order. The court also granted the 
Planning Commission's motion for HRCP Rule 11 sanctions against 
LLC. The Final Judgment was entered on June 6, 2024. LLC moved 
for reconsideration. Reconsideration was denied. This secondary 
appeal followed. 
(1) LLC contends the circuit court "made numerous 
procedural errors, and numerous factual and legal errors." But 
in this secondary appeal, we apply the standards in HRS 
§ 91-14(g) (2012 & Supp. 2019) to the Planning Commission's 
Decision and Order, not to the circuit court's order affirming 
it. Sierra Club v. D.R. Horton-Schuler Homes, LLC, 136 Hawai#i 
505, 515–16, 364 P.3d 213, 223–24 (2015). 
LLC contends the Decision and Order was arbitrary and 
capricious and should be vacated under HRS § 91-14(g)(6). LLC 
challenges the Planning Commission's findings of fact (FOF) 
nos. 55 and 56. The Planning Commission's other findings of 
fact, which are unchallenged, are binding on appeal. Okada 
Trucking Co. v. Bd. of Water Supply, 97 Hawai#i 450, 459, 40 P.3d 
73, 82 (2002). 
The Decision and Order stated: 
55. The Supreme Court remanded the matter to the Circuit
Court only as to the deposit issue: "[W]e vacate the ICA's
judgment on appeal only as to the disbursal of escrow funds
to [WRC]. This case is remanded to the circuit court for 
further proceedings consistent with this opinion."
(December 24, 2019 Hawaii Supreme Court decision[.]) 
56. As a result of these court appeals regarding the
status of the Land Sales Contract, it has now been
judicially determined that: 
a. Szymanski was the party in breach of obligations
under the Land Sales Contract; 
b. Szymanski is not entitled to an order directing
that the Land Sales Contract should be specifically
performed such that Szymanski would become the party
entitled to be the owner and successful buyer of the
Subject Property; 
5 
 
NOT FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST'S HAWAI#I REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER 
c. The Land Sales Contract has been terminated, and 
d. The only remaining issue to be determined is a
question of who is entitled to receive the
interpleaded escrow funds of $50,000 and associated
interest. (December 24, 2019 Hawaii Supreme Court
decision[.]) 
The label finding of fact or conclusion of law does not 
determine the standard of review. Pave v. Prod. Processing, 
Inc., 152 Hawai#i 164, 171, 524 P.3d 355, 362 (App. 2022). 
Whether a determination is a finding of fact, a conclusion of 
law, or a mixed finding and conclusion is a question of law 
freely reviewable on appeal. Id. FOF nos. 55 and 56 were 
actually conclusions of law construing the 2019 Title Guaranty 
decision. 
We review an agency's conclusions of law de novo under 
the right/wrong standard. Sierra Club, 136 Hawai#i at 516, 364 
P.3d at 224. The supreme court's 2019 
Title Guaranty decision 
conclusively affirmed that Szymanski breached the contract to buy 
the Property and was not entitled to specific performance by 
Wailea Resort Co. 
FOF nos. 55 and 56 were right. 
The Planning Commission then concluded: 
13. Szymanski and [LLC] do not have any ownership
interest in the Subject Property nor any contractual right
to purchase or acquire an interest in the Subject Property
and have no authorization from the owner of the Subject
Property to pursue a SMA permit. Consequently, [LLC] and
Szymanski do not qualify for and are not entitled to be a
holder of an SMA permit for the Subject Property. 
14. Accordingly, it is appropriate for the
Department to close and/or terminate the subject SMA permit.

must provide "documents of ownership or authorization by the

leads.caseName: Foxfield Construction v. Associates in Sleep Medicine
leads.text:
2026 IL App (3d) 250573-U 
No. 3-25-0573 
Order filed November 24, 2026 
NOTICE: This order was filed under Illinois Supreme Court Rule 23 and is not 
precedential except in the limited circumstances allowed under Rule 23(e)(1). 

IN THE 
APPELLATE COURT OF ILLINOIS 
THIRD DISTRICT 

FOXFIELD CONSTRUCTION, LTD., Plaintiff-Appellant, 
v. 
ASSOCIATES IN SLEEP MEDICINE, LLC, SIGMA VENTURES, LLC, MB FINANCIAL 
BANK, NATIONAL ASSOCIATION as successor in interest to American Chartered Bank, 
HARMON ELECTRICAL SYSTEMS, LLC, TRANSFORM CONSTRUCTION, LLC d/b/a TC 
Security Sales, KMG CONSTRUCTION, INC., SPRINGBROOK CENTER OWNERS 
ASSOCIATION, OTHER UNKNOWN OWNERS AND LIENHOLDERS, UNKNOWN 
NECESSARY PARTIES and NON-RECORD CLAIMANTS, Defendants 
(Associates in Sleep Medicine, LLC and Sigma Ventures, LLC, Defendants-Appellees). 
Appeal from the Circuit Court of Du Page County. 
Honorable Robert G. Gibson, Judge, Presiding. 
Nos. 17-CH-1390, 17-CH-1664 

JUSTICE DA VENPORT delivered the judgment of the court. 
Presiding Justice Hettel and Justice Brennan concurred in the judgment. 

ORDER 
¶ 1 Held: The circuit court abused its discretion in granting Rule 304(a) certification. Appeal 
dismissed. 

¶ 2 Plaintiff, Foxfield Construction, Ltd. (Foxfield) , obtained certification under Rule 304(a) 
(Ill. S. Ct. R. 304(a) (eff. Mar. 8, 2016) ) to immediately appeal a summary judgment ruling 
extinguishing its mechanic’s lien claim against defendants, Associates in Sleep Medicine, LLC 

- 2 - 
(ASM) and Sigma Ventures, LLC (Sigma). The court reasoned that the immediate appeal of a 
“fairly narrow” issue would conserve judicial resources by avoiding the possibility of a lengthy 
retrial in the event of a reversal. We conclude the court abused its discretion in granting Rule 304(a) 
certification. The appeal’s narrow scope and the claims still pending below undercut the potential 
benefits of immediate review while raising the prospect of piecemeal appeals. We thus vacate the 
certification and dismiss the appeal for want of jurisdiction. 
¶ 3 I. BACKGROUND 
¶ 4 This appeal arises from a construction dispute. Sigma authorized ASM, its tenant with 
whom it shares common ownership, to construct a building on Sigma -owned land. In May 2016, 
ASM contracted with Foxfield, a general contractor, to construct a two-story office building. The 
construction contract required ASM to make $1.8 million in payments over the course of the 
project. 
¶ 5 A. Foxfield’s Mechanic’s Lien 
¶ 6 Before submitting each of its requests for a progress payment, Foxfield issued a sworn 
contractor’s statement as required by section 5(a) of the Mechanics Lien Act (Act) (770 ILCS 
60/5(a) (West 2016)). 
¶ 7 ASM paid five progress payments totaling $1,326,591.42. In April 2017, ASM received a 
temporary certificate of occupancy for the building’s newly constructed first floor. The next month, 
Foxfield issued its sixth invoice for $369,582.50, noting a $118,184 balance would remain after 
payment of the invoice. 
¶ 8 ASM did not pay the sixth invoice. In a letter to Foxfield, it declined to make any more 
payments until it was “assured that all defects (flooring, walls, doors, ceiling grid, and others 

- 3 - 
discovered) are corrected.” ASM later identified specific deficiencies in the work but did not assign 
values to those claimed deficiencies. 
¶ 9 In June 2017, Foxfield recorded a mechanic’s lien against the premises for $473,589.10. 
By then, Foxfield had issued six sworn statements under section 5(a), which requires the contractor 
seeking payment to disclose “the names and addresses of all parties furnishing labor, services, 
material, fixtures, apparatus or machinery, or forms or form work and of the amounts due or to 
become due to each.” 770 ILCS 60/5(a) (West 2016). 
¶ 10 In July 2017, the parties attempted mediation and Foxfield continued to demand that ASM 
pay its latest invoice. Thereafter, ASM instructed Foxfield to stop all work under the contract. 
¶ 11 B. Pleadings 
¶ 12 In October 2017, Foxfield sued ASM, Sigma, and others unrelated to this appeal (a lender, 
subcontractor-lien claimants, and unknown lienholders, owners, and necessary parties). Count I 
sought to foreclose the mechanic’s lien, count II alleged breach of contract against ASM, and count 
III alleged quantum meruit in the alternative to count II. ASM and Sigma answered the complaint, 
denying its material allegations. 
¶ 13 ASM countersued for breach of contract (count I) and indemnification (count II). Sigma 
countersued for slander of title (count V) and conversion (count VII). Both ASM and Sigma 
countersued for defamation (count III), “ declaration of false sworn statements and invalid lien ” 
(count IV), consumer fraud (count VI), fraud in the inducement of the contract (count VIII), and 
“fraudulent sworn contractor statements” (count IX). 
¶ 14 Foxfield answered counts I and II of the counterclaim, denying its material allegations, and 
moved to dismiss the remaining counts. On Foxfield’s motion, the court dismissed counts III, VI, 

- 4 - 
VII, and VIII of the counterclaim. The court allowed count IX to stand as brought by ASM and 
dismissed that count as brought by Sigma. 
¶ 15 C. Cross-Motions for Summary Judgment 
¶ 16 After discovery, ASM and Sigma moved for summary judgment on counts I and II of 
Foxfield’s complaint and as to liability on count I of the counterclaim. Foxfield, in turn, moved for 
summary judgment on counts I, II, and V of the counterclaim. 
¶ 17 The court granted summary judgment against Foxfield on c ount I of its complaint. It held 
the mechanic’s lien was invalid because Foxfield’s sworn contractor statements did not strictly 
comply with section 5, noting the statements (1) failed to identify the architect-subcontractor,
1 
Virtual Energy Solutions, LLC (VES), and (2) overstated the contract price for architectural work 
by $15,000. The court observed, “There are other violations of Section 5 by Foxfield, but the VES 
omission is the most glaring and egregious and invalidates [Foxfield’s] lien.” The court denied the 
cross-motions in all other respects, noting the facts underlying the breach-of-contract claims were 
“about as clear as mud.” 
¶ 18 D. Surviving Claims 
¶ 19 On entry of the partial summary judgment, counts II and III of the complaint remained, as 
did counts I, II, I V, V, and IX of the counterclaim. 
¶ 20 Count II of the complaint alleges ASM breached the construction contract by failing to pay 
Foxfield’s sixth invoice, and by ordering Foxfield to stop all work without notice or an opportunity 
to cure. Count III of the complaint is Foxfield’s alternative claim for quantum meruit. 

1Foxfield disputes the architect’s status as a subcontractor. 

- 5 - 
¶ 21 Count I of the counter claim alleges Foxfield departed from the contract in numerous 
respects and performed much of the work in an un workmanlike manner . Count II of the 
counterclaim seeks to enforce an indemnification provision against Foxfield for ASM’s resulting 
losses. The remaining three surviving claims —counts IV, V , and IX of the counterclaim —arise 
directly from Foxfield’s sworn contractor statements. 
¶ 22 Count IV alleges the sworn statements were defective in multiple respects. First, it alleges 
the statements failed to identify all parties furnishing services and the amounts due each. Second, 
it alleges the statements incorrectly listed amounts as paid in full . Third, it alleges the sworn 
statements falsely identified Foxfield as the party furnishing services provided by subcontractors. 
Fourth, it alleges Foxfield’s own itemizations fluctuated materially from statement to statement—
its rough-carpentry figure moving from $255,000 to $87,700 to $207,700 to $225,705, and its 
finish-carpentry figure from zero to $167,300 to $158,206 to $38,206 and back to zero. Count IV 
seeks a declaration that Foxfield’s sworn statements were “false” and its mechanic’s lien was 
invalid. 
¶ 23 Count V is Sigma’s slander -of-title count. It alleges Foxfield recorded the lien with 
knowledge (or reckless disregard) that it was not entitled to the claimed sum of $473,589.10, and 
that it recorded the lien with actual malice, thereby disparaging Sigma’s title. It incorporates all of 
count IV’s allegations and adds that Foxfield knew (or recklessly disregarded), before recording 
its lien, that its sworn statements violated section 5 and its lien was therefore invalid. Count V 
seeks both actual and punitive damages. 
¶ 24 Count IX is ASM’s “fraudulent sworn contractor’s statements ” count. It alleges Foxfield 
knowingly included material misrepresentations in its sworn statements, intending for ASM to pay 
Foxfield in reliance on them. The count lists the alleged misrepresentations, as follows: in all six 

- 6 - 
statements, Foxfield falsely claimed it was providing the architectural services; in four of the six 
statements, Foxfield falsely claimed the architectural services had been paid in full; and in the fifth 
and sixth statements , Foxfield falsely claimed the $87,700 rough- carpentry subcontract had 
increased to $207,000 and then to $225,705.44. ASM alleges that as a result of the alleged 
misrepresentations, it paid Foxfield $181,315 for the rough-carpentry work, while Foxfield 
remitted only $87,700 to the subcontractor and retained the remaining $93,615. ASM further 
alleges it paid Foxfield $50,000 for architectural services Foxfield did not itself provide. Count IX 
seeks punitive damages. 
¶ 25 E. Motion for Immediate Appeal 
¶ 26 In August 2025, Foxfield moved to certify the lien ruling for immediate appeal under Rule 
304(a). In the alternative, it requested certification of a question of law under Rule 308 (Ill. S. Ct. 
R. 308 (eff. Oct. 1, 2019)). It also asked the court to stay the proceedings pending appeal. The legal 
question Foxfield wished to present on appeal was a narrow one: whether an architect’s services 
must be listed in a contractor’s sworn statement under section 5 of the Act. It argued an appeal 
before trial would “avoid the significant risk of multiple trials in the event” of a reversal. 
¶ 27 ASM and Sigma opposed the motion. Alternatively, they requested that if the court grants 
Foxfield’s Rule 304(a) motion, it should also enter Rule 304(a) language on the portion of the 
decision denying summary judgment on whether Foxfield breached the contract (insofar as that 
issue was relevant to the validity of the mechanic’s lien). 
¶ 28 The court granted Foxfield’s motion for Rule 304(a) certification. It noted that, absent 
certification, the case would proceed to what would “likely be a lengthy trial” given the numerous 
pending issues and factual disputes. It believed a subsequent reversal of the lien ruling could result 
in a retrial, which would delay rather than expedite the case’s resolution. Characterizing the issue 

- 7 - 
presented for appeal as “fairly narrow” and “not particularly fact specific,” it concluded that 
fairness to both sides favor ed appellate review “sooner rather than later” and that such review 
would conserve judicial resources. 
¶ 29 Having ruled on Rule 304(a) grounds, the court found Foxfield’s Rule 308 request moot. 
Lastly, the court denied defendants’ cross-request for Rule 304(a) language, noting twice that the 
appellate court could affirm the judgment on any basis in the record. 
¶ 30 Foxfield filed a timely notice of appeal. Thereafter, defendants moved to dismiss the appeal 
for lack of proper certification under Rule 304(a). Foxfield filed an objection, and we took the 
motion with the case. 
¶ 31 II. ANALYSIS 
¶ 32 Generally, this court only has jurisdiction to review a final order disposing of every claim 
raised in an action. AT&T v. Lyons & Pinner Elec tric Co., 2014 IL App (2d) 130577, ¶ 19. Rule 
304(a) provides an exception to this principle, allowing an appeal from a final order as to fewer 
than all claims “if the trial court has made an express
