II. SUMMARY DISPOSITION RULINGS 
 This Court reviews a trial court’s decision on a motion for summary disposition de novo. 
PNC Nat’l Bank Ass’n v Dep’t of Treasury, 285 Mich App 504, 505; 778 NW2d 282 (2009). The 
trial court did not specify whether it was acting under MCR 2.116(C)(8) or (10) in granting 
summary disposition. To the extent the court and the parties relied on materials outside the 
pleadings, the relief is to be considered as granted under MCR 2.116(C)(10). For claims where 
materials outside the pleadings were not relied on, MCR 2.116(C)(8) is appropriate. See Spiek v 
Dep’t of Transp, 456 Mich 331, 338; 572 NW2d 201 (1998). 
 “A motion for summary disposition brought under MCR 2.116(C)(8) tests the legal 
sufficiency of the complaint on the basis of the pleadings alone. The purpose of such a motion is 
to determine whether the plaintiff has stated a claim upon which relief can be granted.” Beaudrie 
v Henderson , 465 Mich 124, 129 -130; 631 NW2d 308 (2001). “All well -pleaded factual 
allegations are accepted as true and construed in a light most favorable to the nonmovant.” Maiden 
v Rozwood, 461 Mich 109, 119; 597 NW2d 817 (1999). “The motion should be granted if no 
factual development could possibly justify recovery.” Beaudrie, 465 Mich at 129-130. 
 A motion brought under MCR 2.116(C)(10), on the other hand, tests the factual support 
for the claim. Spiek, 456 Mich at 337. “In evaluating such a motion, a court considers the entire 
record in the light most favorable to the party opposing the motion, including affidavits, pleadings, 
depositions, admissions, and other evidence submitted by the parties.” Corley v Detroit Bd of Ed, 
470 Mich 274, 278; 681 NW2d 342 (2004). Summary disposition is appropriate when there are 
no genuine issues of material fact and the moving party is entitled to judgment as a matter of law. 
Kisiel v Holz, 272 Mich App 168, 170; 725 NW2d 67 (2006). 
A. STANDING 
 The principal issue on appeal is whether the trial court erred by granting summary 
disposition of plaintiff’s foreclosure-related claims for lack of standing. We conclude that the trial 
court erred by treating the incorrect redemption deadline in the sheriff’s deed as insufficient to 
constitute an irregularity in the foreclosure procedure. 
 The general nature of foreclosure by advertisement is well established. In the event of 
certain defaults, a lender may post a notice that the mortgage on mortgaged premises will be 
foreclosed, MCL 600.3208, after which there is to be a public sale “by the sheriff, undersheriff, or 
a deputy sheriff of the county, to the highest bidder,” MCL 600.3216. The person making the sale 
must execute “a deed of the premises bid off by him.” MCL 600.3232. 
 Even af ter the sheriff’s sale, the mortgagor retains an opportunity to reclaim the lost 
property. A sheriff’s deed “is void if the mortgagor . . . redeems the entire premises sold by paying 
the amount required . . . within the applicable time limit . . . to the purchaser . . . or to the register 
of deeds in whose office the deed is deposited.” MCL 600.3240(1). See also Bryan v JPMorgan 
Chase Bank, 304 Mich App 708, 713; 848 NW2d 482 (2014) (“Pursuant to MCL 600.3240, after 
a sheriff’s sale is completed, a mortgagor may redeem the property by paying the requisite amount 
within the prescribed time limit . . . .”). But “[i]f a mortgagor fails to avail him or herself of the 
right of redemption, all the mortgagor’s rights in and to the property are extinguished.” Id., citing

Matter of Target Corp. v County of Monroe Indus. Dev. Agency 
 2026 NY Slip Op 06899 
 November 20, 2026 
 Appellate Division, Fourth Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 IN THE MATTER OF TARGET CORPORATION, PETITIONER, 
 v 
 COUNTY OF MONROE INDUSTRIAL DEVELOPMENT AGENCY AND ONE MEDLEY CENTER, LLC, RESPONDENTS. 

 Supreme Court of the State of New York, Appellate Division, Fourth Judicial Department 
 Decided on November 20, 2026 
 481 OP 25-01531 
 Present: Whalen, P.J., Lindley, Ogden, Nowak, And Delconte, JJ. 

 FOGEL & BROWN P.C., SYRACUSE (MICHAEL A. FOGEL OF COUNSEL), FOR PETITIONER. 
 HARRIS BEACH MURTHA CULLINA PLLC, BUFFALO (ALLISON B. FIUT OF COUNSEL), FOR RESPONDENT COUNTY OF MONROE INDUSTRIAL DEVELOPMENT AGENCY. 

 Proceeding pursuant to EDPL 207 (initiated in the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court in the Fourth Judicial Department) to annul a determination of respondent County of Monroe Industrial Development Agency. 
[*1]
 It is hereby ORDERED that the determination is unanimously confirmed without costs and the petition is dismissed. 
 Memorandum: In this original proceeding pursuant to EDPL 207, petitioner seeks annulment of a determination of respondent County of Monroe Industrial Development Agency (COMIDA) condemning certain contractual rights of petitioner, which operates a retail store in Irondequoit, just west of the site of the shopping center once known as the Medley Centre and the Irondequoit Mall. 
 A public hearing regarding the proposed condemnation was scheduled, and COMIDA notified petitioner of the public hearing by sending a copy of the notice of public hearing and an accompanying letter by both certified mail and Federal Express to the address provided by petitioner to the tax assessor for billing purposes, as required by EDPL 202 (C) (1), within the time period set forth in EDPL 202 (C) (2). The documents informed petitioner that the hearing would address the "[p]roposed condemnation of certain real property interests held by [petitioner] . . . with respect to" certain parcels of land. The documents further informed petitioner that the purpose of the public hearing was to consider the acquisition of the property, the public purpose of the proposed acquisition, and the details of the proposed project. Despite that notice, no one appeared on petitioner's behalf at the public hearing, and the only people who spoke at the hearing expressed support for the proposed condemnation of petitioner's contractual rights. It is undisputed that the notice of public hearing did not inform petitioner that, if it wished to raise a subsequent challenge to the condemnation, it could "do so only on the basis of issues, facts, and objections raised at [the] hearing" (EDPL 202 [C] [2]). The letter that accompanied the notice did, however, contain that language in bold, underlined, and capital letters. 
 The condemnation was approved following the hearing, and COMIDA sent petitioner a synopsis of its determination and findings. Approximately one month later, petitioner commenced this proceeding contending, inter alia, that the notice of the public hearing was insufficient because it failed to inform the public and petitioner of the public use to be served by the proposed public project and describe the details of the property rights sought to be condemned and failed to state in the notice that property owners who subsequently wished to challenge condemnation via judicial review could do so only on the basis of issues, facts, and [*2] objections raised at the hearing. We reject petitioner's contention regarding the sufficiency of the notice regarding the public hearing. 
 Pursuant to the EDPL, the condemnor must provide "notice of the purpose, time, date, and location of [the] public hearing" (§ 202 [C] [1]), and we conclude that COMIDA's notice and accompanying letter to petitioner satisfied those requirements. Section 202 does not require the condemnor to describe the proposed public project sought to be undertaken. Indeed, the entire objective of the public hearing is for the condemnor to "outline the purpose . . . of the public project and any other information it considers pertinent" (EDPL 203). Notice of the purpose of the public hearing , which is required by EDPL 202, is not the same as notice of the purpose of the proposed public project , which is the objective of the public hearing and is not required to be contained in the notice of the hearing ( see EDPL 203). 
 We further conclude that the notice of public hearing and the letter accompanying the notice sent to petitioner were sufficient to inform petitioner that "property owners who may subsequently wish to challenge condemnation of their property via judicial review may do so only on the basis of issues, facts, and objections raised at such hearing," as mandated by EDPL 202 (C) (2). While the notice of public hearing did not include the statutorily required language, the statutory warning is directed only at owners of property sought to be condemned, not the public at large. Petitioner cites no authority in support of its assertion that the letter sent to petitioner, which accompanied the notice of public hearing and contained the statutory warning, should not be considered as part of the notice sent to the property owner contemplated by EDPL 202 (C) (1) and (2). 
 Petitioner raises numerous substantive contentions regarding the determination to condemn its contractual rights. We conclude that "such contentions are not properly before this Court, as . . . petitioner did not appear at the public hearing, and thus, failed to raise or present [those contentions]" ( Matter of River St. Realty Corp. v City of New Rochelle , 181 AD3d 676, 678 [2d Dept 2020]; see Matter of One Point St. , Inc. v City of Yonkers Indus. Dev. Agency , 170 AD3d 851 , 853 [2d Dept 2019]; Sun Co. v City of Syracuse Indus. Dev. Agency , 209 AD2d 34, 44 [4th Dept 1995], appeal dismissed 86 NY2d 776 [1995]). We reject petitioner's contention that EDPL 207 (A) permits it to seek judicial review of COMIDA's determination and findings even though it did not appear at the public hearing. That statute provides that "[a]ny person or persons jointly or severally, aggrieved by the condemnor's determination and findings made pursuant to [EDPL 204], may seek judicial review thereof by the appellate division of the supreme court, in the judicial department embracing the county wherein the proposed facility is located by the filing of a petition in such court within thirty days after the condemnor's completion of its publication of its determination and findings pursuant to [EDPL 204]." While EDPL 207 (A) allows petitioner, as an aggrieved party, to commence a proceeding pursuant to EDPL article 2, it does not allow petitioner to raise arguments and objections in such a proceeding that were not raised at the public hearing. 
 We thus confirm the determination and dismiss the petition.
